Built on `@react-aria`/`@react-stately` — the first runtime dependency `packages/ui` has ever taken on. The panel is portal-rendered (`useOverlayPosition`) so it escapes ancestor `overflow` clipping, needed by several Phase-2 dialog sites even though neither Phase-1 site below does yet. **Phase 1** migrated exactly two call sites — the ticket-type editor's Workflow select (searchable, `ticket-type-editor-screen.tsx`) and its Field-type select (non-searchable, `fields-editor.tsx`). Test cases 10.81–10.83. **Phase 2 Wave A** migrated 3 more sites in `apps/web`: the members-invite page's Channel and Role selects (`apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/members/page.tsx` — only the Role picker carries a dedicated case, 3.132; the Channel select has none of its own) and the Style select (`apps/web/src/style-toggle.tsx`, cases 13.344–13.346). **A fourth `apps/web` site joined on 2026-09-18: the members roster's per-row role control** (same file, cases 13.824–13.828) — the first `Select` whose callers pass a per-instance `aria-label` to tell N structurally identical controls apart, and the first whose callers had to be written against the component's actual accessible-name behaviour (react-aria's `aria-labelledby` makes the trigger's name `<value> <aria-label>`, so an exact-string query matches nothing and an absence assertion anchored to that name can never fire; measured, and recorded in `test-cases/13`). **Phase 2 Wave B** migrated 5 more sites in `packages/app-core`'s workflow-builder UI: the canvas node's Category select (`state-node.tsx`), two rule-editor selects — the Field picker and the Earlier-move picker (`require-field-editor.tsx`, `require-different-user-editor.tsx`), both carrying the same `string` → `string | null` unset treatment so an unrecognized rule value shows the Select's own placeholder rather than falsely displaying its first option — and two repeated-instance target-state selects, one per dropped/outgoing state (`state-mapping-dialog.tsx`, `workflow-rebind-dialog.tsx`); the latter is a genuinely separate component from the former despite the near-identical UI, because it authors a one-shot map between two UNRELATED workflows that rides its own migration request, never a `stateMapping` keyed inside one workflow's own version chain (design decision 10). Test cases 10.84–10.89. **Phase 2 Wave C** migrated the final 5 sites (4 files) in `packages/app-core`'s ticket-action views: the transition dialog's Move-to select (`transition-dialog.tsx`, Task 1), the reopen dialog's Reopen-to select (`reopen-dialog.tsx`, Task 2), the new-ticket dialog's Type and Parent selects (`new-ticket-dialog.tsx`, two selects in one file, Task 3 — Parent's `''` value is a real, always-selectable "None (project root)" option, added as a synthetic first `SelectOption` rather than treated with this rollout's usual value-or-null unset pattern), and the ticket list's Group-by select (`ticket-list.tsx`, Task 4 — no `string | null` migration needed, `grouping` is always one of 5 valid values). Test cases 3.51, 3.53, 3.65, 3.72, 3.79, 3.157, 3.164–3.166, 12.384, 12.386, 12.388. **THE ROLLOUT IS NOW COMPLETE: all 15 of the original audit's native `<select>` elements are migrated** — Phase 1's 2, Wave A's 3, Wave B's 5, Wave C's 5 — confirmed by a repo-wide sweep of `packages/app-core/src`, `packages/ui/src`, `apps/web/app` and `apps/web/src` finding zero remaining `<select>` JSX in scope (only comments/docblock prose, several of it deliberately narrating the pre-migration history of sites already converted). There is no Wave D and no further phase planned. **Focus restoration (E4-17, 2026-09-21):** because the panel is portal-rendered, its option rows are DOM-focused *outside* the component's own subtree — so when the panel unmounted, the focused node left with the portal and the browser dropped focus to `<body>`, which is what a keyboard user hit on both close paths a person actually uses (Escape after Enter-opening, and Enter to pick): focus was thrown out of the surrounding sheet to the top of the document. `SelectPanel` now wraps its content in `@react-aria/focus`'s `FocusScope restoreFocus`, which captures the active element at render time — before `useListBox`'s own `autoFocus` child mounts, which is why the capture is a render-time ref rather than a layout effect — and restores it on unmount, behind a guard that leaves a deliberately moved focus alone, so a blur-away close is unaffected. Case 10.90; the same contract 13.420 (the account menu) and 13.446 (the Filters sheet) already state for their own components, and `Select` was the one that stranded. **Focus visibility on the searchable trigger (E4-21 / P23, 2026-09-21, cases 10.91–10.92):** the searchable branch suppressed its input's outline (`input:focus { outline: none; }`) and replaced it with nothing, so the one control whose entire job is to be typed into had no visible focus indicator — and because the removal is the product's own declaration, no user-agent default could survive it (WCAG 2.2 §2.4.7, Level AA). The ring now goes on the wrapper, keyed on `:focus-within` rather than on the input, since the wrapper div carries no `tabIndex` and the inner input is what takes focus; `outline-offset: 1px` is `.gn-field__input`'s own value, so the searchable and non-searchable branches of the control look identical while focused. **The trigger now draws a chevron, and `appearance` chooses its coat (owner request 2026-09-22, cases 13.1342–13.1344):** the single non-searchable trigger rendered no arrow at all and wore the field coat unconditionally, so the one control whose whole job is "a list will open under this" was indistinguishable from a plain text field. `SelectProps` gains `appearance?: 'sunken' | 'raised'` (default `'sunken'` — the shipped field treatment, and what every call site that omits the prop still gets), and the single non-searchable trigger renders a `ChevronDownIcon` (new, in `select-icons.tsx`, 16px `currentColor` `aria-hidden`) in a `.gn-select__chevron` wrapper on BOTH appearances — the arrow is an affordance of a dropdown, not a property of a coat, and one component must not have two shapes by appearance. `SearchableSelect` and the `multiple` branch deliberately get none (a typeable field wearing a `SearchIcon`; chips plus an open button) — both arms are controlled in case 13.1342. The chevron is `aria-hidden`, so no trigger's accessible name changes. `'raised'` paints `var(--gn-surface-raised)` + `var(--gn-shadow-raised)` (the `.gn-card` pair) and is ADDITIVE: the trigger keeps `gn-field__input`, which is where its 44px `min-height` floor comes from. **The raised rule's selector is compound and its position is load-bearing, both measured:** `[data-style="neo"] .gn-field__input` is `(0,2,0)` and repaints any field sunken under `neo` — the shipped default — so a bare `.gn-select__trigger--raised` at `(0,1,0)` would have rendered the owner's raised pill PRESSED with every case in the repo green; it takes the field class to reach `(0,2,0)` and sits after the override it beats, since at equal specificity only source order decides.
- ⚙️ **Client `DataSource` contract & view types** — coordination amendment 10 pinned as code: `DataSource` (`ingest`, a typed `query` surface mirroring the server reads, `subscribe(workspaceId, afterSeq, cb)`), the `StreamItem` frames (amendments 13 + 19 — **five** members since Plan 6 Task 8: `event`, `purge`, `scope-revoked`, `caught-up`, `error`, the event member carrying a `LedgerEvent` so it holds the `workspaceSeq` the resume protocol is defined in terms of), and the view types every client renders from (`BoardView`, `ListRow`, `TicketRead`, `AttentionItem`, `UserPreferences`, …). Views consume only this interface and never import HTTP code. **THIRTEEN methods since Plan 6 Task 14's fix round**: `getTicketTypes(workspaceId)` was added because `GET /v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/ticket-types` had shipped in Plan 5 and no seam reached it, so the web shell hardcoded a four-entry ticket-type ladder and presented it as the workspace's own — see the New-ticket control below. It returns the domain's `TicketTypeDef` rather than a client view model, exactly as `getWorkflowDef` returns `WorkflowDef`, because the wire body already carries that type and there is nothing to rename. Scaffold only — the online HTTP + WebSocket source and the offline replica implement these same signatures later. `packages/app-core/src/`
- ⚙️ **Online stream subscriber** — `createStreamSubscriber({baseUrl, webSocketFactory?, random?})`, amendment 13's client half and the first implementation of `DataSource.subscribe`. It speaks the pinned frames verbatim and reconnects with exponential backoff from 500 ms capped at 30 s with ±20% jitter drawn from an injected `random`. **ONE SOCKET PER CLIENT, multiplexed, since 2026-09-23 (cases 12.962–12.968).** It used to open a socket per `subscribe()` call, and since every `useLiveQuery` instance subscribes once, a board page opened **six** — against a server cap of **eight per user** (`DEFAULT_MAX_SOCKETS_PER_USER`) whose own reasoning assumes about one socket per tab. A reload or a second tab crossed the cap, `requireConnectionBudget` answered **HTTP 429 during the upgrade**, and a 429 on a handshake reaches the browser as close code **1006** with no close frame and no server-side error log — so the client looked broken while the log looked clean. Measured over forty minutes on the dev stack: **205 `/v1/stream` requests, 160 of them 429**; with no established socket the debounced re-read never fired and a newly created ticket appeared only after a manual page load. Subscribers now share one connection and one ROOM per workspace, fanned out locally, which is what the protocol already assumed (`routes.ts`: *"One socket multiplexes several workspaces"*). Two consequences are contract, not accident: a **late joiner to a room gets no replay** — the hub refuses a duplicate subscribe and there is no unsubscribe frame, so the room's cursor belongs to whoever opened it — and **`scope-revoked` ends one ROOM, not the connection**, the socket closing only when the last room goes. The single production consumer passes `afterSeq: 0` and uses the callback as a change signal before its own full read, so the first costs it nothing. The socket is an injected `WebSocketLike` seam — Plan 10's Tauri and React Native shells reuse it, and nothing in it assumes the DOM socket's deferred `close`. Two decisions carry their reasons at the site: the resume cursor advances from `caught-up`'s `seq` **and** from an event's `envelope.workspaceSeq` (never the per-entity `seq`), because `stream/hub.ts` sends `caught-up` exactly once per subscription and "only `caught-up` advances it" would guarantee unbounded replay on a long-lived connection — and it advances only after the consumer callback returns, since a returning synchronous callback is the only durability signal this seam has and over-advancing loses an event permanently while under-advancing costs a replay the consumer already dedupes. And `scope-revoked` is TERMINAL: delivered once, then the subscription shuts down, because reconnecting into a workspace you were just revoked from earns `not-a-member` forever. **It answers a TEXT `ping` with nothing, and that is a deletion rather than an omission (case 12.328):** the arms that declared `PingFrame`, parsed it and replied `{type:'pong'}` spoke a protocol no server implements — the heartbeat at `stream/routes.ts:319` is `socket.ping()`, a WebSocket PROTOCOL control frame the platform socket answers below JavaScript, and the server's message door answers `bad-message` to any text frame that is not a `subscribe`. Case 12.360 keeps them deleted, and 12.361 records the one residual a docblock carries and no test can: never inject a raw `ws` socket into this seam. `parseFrame` is hand-rolled rather than calling the domain's `serverStreamFrameSchema` — that schema is stricter than a client should be about id shape and a value import would resolve through `./dist` — and the schema is used as the test's ORACLE instead, pinning that everything it accepts this parser accepts. `packages/app-core/src/online/stream.ts`
- ⚙️ **Client submit factory** — `makeSubmittedFactory({actorId, origin, now?})`, the one door every claim the web client makes leaves through. **In tests, the door is real (case `18.431`):** the vitest setup of `apps/web` and `packages/app-core` wraps `newSubmittedEvent` so any envelope whose payload the registered domain schema would refuse throws at build time (a hand-built payload the server would reject can no longer pass a mocked `ingest`); a case that builds a refused payload on purpose sets `__gnAllowRefusedPayloads`. It mints nothing itself: the ULID and the `clientTime` stamp come from the domain's `newSubmittedEvent`, so the web client, the desktop client and the offline replica cannot grow three ideas of what a claim is; the factory adds only the per-session half (who is signed in, which origin, which clock), and `serverTime`/`seq` stay absent by construction. Proven equal, field for field, to the domain builder's own output, and proven to mint claims the envelope door admits. `packages/app-core/src/submit.ts`
- ⚙️ **Provenance rendering** — `actorLabel`, `formatDate`, `formatDateTime`, `formatStateProvenance`: honesty contract 1 as code. A missing display name falls back to the raw actor id — never blank, never a fabricated "system". **The display-name chain it heads is name → email → id as of 2026-09-22** (owner request: *"Everywhere for id, show the Name; if name is empty/blank, show the email"*): the EMAIL step lives one module down in `member-label.ts`'s `memberLabel`, which is what the roster JOIN's value is built with, so an address reaches a claim line by riding the join rather than by `actorLabel` learning to look one up — it is handed a claim's `{actorId, actorName}` and has no roster to reach for. `actorLabel`'s own order is untouched and load-bearing: the reserved `SYSTEM_ACTOR_AUTO_CLOSE` is checked FIRST, ahead of any label a join could produce, so no roster row can rename a decision no person made and auto-close is never given an address (case `13.1293`). **ONE rule, ONE home — `packages/app-core/src/member-label.ts`** — where it had been copied privately into the members page and the visibility editor; the surfaces that hold a roster member (the sheet's Assignee picker and `@`mention list, the board filter's person rows, the workflow builder's named-people editors and rule summaries, the phone's mention list) all call it, and the surfaces that hold only a claim call `actorLabel`. Every instant is rendered by the domain's one `formatIstInstant`, never by the device: the suite renders the same claim from `Pacific/Kiritimati` and `Pacific/Niue` and demands both the same words AND the IST words, so a formatter that is merely consistently wrong fails too. A day claim (`2026-08-30`) is shown as the day it already is rather than shifted through a zone it never had, an unparseable claim renders verbatim, and a calendar-impossible day claim renders verbatim rather than throwing at a rendering surface — the plan's unguarded `istDayBounds` call would have thrown on `2026-02-30`. The unfold text reads the SERVER clock, so no claimed clock can move a ticket onto a day it was never marked on. `packages/app-core/src/provenance.ts`
- ⚙️ **Pre-check state cache** — `ClientStateCache` / `createClientStateCache()`, a snapshot of what this client has SEEN, existing only to fuel the local rule-engine pre-check. It is never rendered as truth: `withCacheFeed(source, cache)` decorates a `DataSource` so ordinary `getTicket`/`getWorkflowDef` reads FEED it and stream frames invalidate it, and nothing is ever SERVED from it — a cache hit that short-circuited a read would put a snapshot on screen as a fact. Any stream event touching an entity DROPS the snapshot rather than patching it optimistically. Its one non-obvious member is `markChildrenComplete(parentId, children)` / `hasCompleteChildren`: `childrenOf` can only answer "the children I have seen", the parent-terminal invariant needs "all of them", and a partial child set reads to the rule engine as a parent with nothing open under it. Any ticket event voids EVERY vouch — targeted invalidation would leave a vouched-but-emptied child set behind, which is the pre-check's one route to a false pass. Nothing feeds a vouch yet; until a producer does (Plan 6 Task 7 or the board/list reads), moves into terminal states answer not-evaluated rather than passed. `packages/app-core/src/cache.ts`, `packages/app-core/src/cache-feed.ts`
- ⚙️ **Local pre-check** — `precheckEvent(submitted, cache, deps?)` runs the REAL `@gisik-nokma/rule-engine` in the browser build (spec honesty contract 2) for instant, named-reason refusal previews, plus `PARENT_TERMINAL_RULE` (`hierarchy.parent-terminal`) for the owner's reopen moment on `ticket.created`/`ticket.reparented`, read through the same registered payload schemas the server's door uses rather than a cast. It is advisory: the server stays the authority. The line it holds is that a `passed` is never manufactured out of ABSENCE — five gates downgrade to `not-evaluated` instead, each closing a way the cache's silence would otherwise read as a fact: an uncached ticket or definition; an unwalkable workflow-version chain at EITHER end (a missing intermediate both invents `stranded-state` refusals and silently disarms four-eyes, which skips entries it cannot resolve; a cached definition OLDER than the version the ticket's own snapshot names makes the forward fold a no-op, so the state resolves cleanly against the wrong vocabulary and the client evaluates the pre-publish rules the server has already replaced); an accept into a terminal state with no vouched-complete child set; an accept that moves a ticket OUT of a terminal state while its parent is not cached (gate 5, E3-19 — the engine's child-side guard reads an unresolved parent as no parent); the hand-rolled `ticket.closed` mirror applies gate 3's discipline too since E6-8 (a vouched open child previews `parent-terminal-with-open-children`, an unvouched child set defers); and — since Plan 3 landed `ticket.created`/`ticket.reparented` as engine cases — a hierarchy claim of either type, entirely, because every engine accept for them is decided behind a ticket-type definition and this cache holds none. What survives for those two is the `hierarchy.parent-terminal` refusal, which reads only cached, server-served state. A roles-bearing `restrict-to` refusal downgrades too — memberships live server-side — while an assignee-only one stands, because the snapshot holds the assignee. `completeForPrecheck` stamps `seq: 0`, a position the ledger cannot hold, so the stand-in envelope is refused by the very door it would have to pass to become a fact. The standing canary that asserted the shared engine had no case for `ticket.created`/`ticket.reparented` FIRED on Plan 3 Chain A's landing (2026-08-31), which is what it was for; it is superseded in place by one aimed at the next drift — that the engine reaches a ticket-type door this cache cannot answer, pinned in both directions so it goes red whether the dispatcher cases are removed or the adapter starts answering `null`. `packages/app-core/src/precheck.ts`
- ⚙️ **Live query hook** — `useLiveQuery(source, workspaceId, queryKey, load, debounceMs = 200, initial?)`, the refetch loop every view hook in the web client rides on: load once, then re-run `load` (debounced) on every `event`/`purge` frame the workspace stream delivers. `queryKey` names WHAT is being asked for (the project id, for a board): a changed key clears the previous answer and re-asks, and an answer that arrives for a key already left is dropped rather than rendered. The clear is a passive effect, so the window in which the previous project's data sits under the new project's heading is bounded to the single render between commit and effect rather than lasting the whole load — shortened, not removed. The key drives the reload and the WORKSPACE drives the subscription — two effects, so a key change never re-opens the stream (`subscribe` resumes from cursor `0`, and each re-open would replay the workspace from the start). Deliberately refetch-based rather than patch-based — the stream is an invalidation signal and the server projections stay the one source of rendered truth; folding raw events into rendered state is Plan 10's replica, built on reducers. Speaks only to `DataSource`, never to a URL or a socket. `packages/app-core/src/views/use-live-query.ts` **`initial: {key, data}`** is an answer the caller already holds for one key: served for that key from its first render until the key's own load answers (a `null` answer replaces it), never for another key — the note page uses it so a note it just found is not reset to "no longer shared" for a round trip (R7, cases 18.460–18.461).
- ⚙️ **Derived progress text** — `formatRollup(rollup)` renders `"5 of 8 done · 2 restricted"`. Counts are over ALL direct children with no visibility filtering: the denominator never shrinks to what the viewer can see, and children the viewer cannot see are NAMED in the restricted count rather than pretended absent (spec §6, invariant 5). `packages/app-core/src/views/rollup-text.ts`
- ⚙️ **Board view** — `Board` + `useBoard(source, workspaceId, projectId)`. Columns are exactly the attached workflow's states, empty ones included and blocked ones marked; a project whose ticket types sit on different workflows gets one group per workflow rather than a merged column set that would invent columns no definition declares. Grouping is a rearrangement and never a filter — the same tickets grouped two ways render the same tickets, and each column's count badge agrees with the cards under it. Cards fold their state behind "who · when" and unfold to `"marked Doing by Anselma Marak on 19 Aug 2026"`, falling back to the raw actor id when a claim carries no display name; a reopen renders its `cause` as "reopened — live work added" instead of an anonymous flip; a claim still in flight to the server carries a "claim in transit" chip, which is a CLIENT-SIDE `BoardCard` flag and not a fourth `IngestResult` status. **A claimed due date now draws on the card (ruling E5-2, 2026-09-21), and a date that has PASSED draws it in the danger tone.** Until this ruling the Board carried no due date at all — `BoardCard` had none while `TicketCard.dueDate` was already on every card the board is projected from and `ListRow` read it — so a ticket a week overdue was indistinguishable from an undated one on the project's DEFAULT tab, while the sheet, the List, My Work, the Calendar and the Timeline all carried the date; the export draws the label in the card's meta line and the ruling is the reason the four places disagreeing was a defect rather than a style. The label is `formatDate(due.date)` — the product's one date formatter, the same one the List's due cell uses — and the claimant rides along as the span's `title`, the export's meta line being one bit and a card the densest surface in the product. **Lateness is computed from a `today` PROP, never from a device clock**: `Board` takes an optional IST day string (`BoardProps.today`), `apps/web`'s project page hands it the same `istToday()` it already hands the Calendar and Timeline tabs, and with no `today` the label draws in the ordinary tone and no danger tone does — a danger tone with no clock behind it would paint every past date the same colour as every future one, which is exactly why `.gn-list__due` never transcribed the export's own late arm. Comparing two `YYYY-MM-DD` strings needs no date arithmetic and no zone: `<` means a ticket due TODAY is not late. **The export's OTHER meta bit, the ticket key, is still not drawn and is a real wire gap rather than an oversight** — `CCSO-1183` is composed on the single-ticket read (`apps/server/src/routes/tickets.ts`), and `TicketCard` carries no workspace prefix, no project prefix and no per-project number, so a card has nothing to compose one from; the key is a PRODUCT decision already filed as such (the List view's own bullet below), not something this ruling could invent. Every instant goes through the domain's one `formatIstInstant`, guarded from two absurd zones by tests that hand the worker back exactly the `TZ` they borrowed. **These zone batteries are REGRESSION GUARDS, not live discriminations:** `formatIstInstant` and `formatDate` are constant +05:30 arithmetic over the UTC getters (`packages/domain/src/clock-skew.ts:51`, `packages/domain/src/ist-day.ts`) and read no local zone, so every zone prints one string against today's code and the zone loop cannot fail — measured 2026-09-02 against a `toLocale*` control in the same run that answered a different calendar day. The `TZ` probe establishes that the KNOB moves and nothing more. The teeth are the mutation: swapping in a device-reading formatter kills these cases, and each block now names its own kill count at the site. Pointing the hook at another project re-asks rather than re-rendering the last one. A test guard holds that no view module imports anything but react, the shared packages and its own relatives, and calls no network API — reading `from`, bare, dynamic and `require` specifiers, matching on whole package names rather than prefixes, and walking `src/views/` recursively. **AN EPIC IS NOT A CARD HERE (owner, 2026-09-20): *"epics should never show up in the board, timeline and calendar views. they can only be in the list views."*** `boardNarrowing` drops a rank-1 card BEFORE `total` increments, so the column badge and the `N of M` strip both agree with the grid — counting it in `total` while never drawing it would make `shown !== total` true on every project holding an epic and tell a person with no filter in force that a filter is hiding work. The epic is read through the workspace's own rank-1 predicate (`isEpicType`, falling back to `isBuiltinEpicType` while the roster loads), never a name or an id match. **And every card carries a priority BADGE** (spec 2026-09-22, superseded in part 2026-09-23 — see below): the level in the keys row, `title`-attributed with its claimant exactly as the due label is, drawn on EVERY card — P2 is the birth default and its being drawn is the point, since the level is a fact about the ticket rather than something the badge has to earn. Cases `13.1237`–`13.1238`. `packages/app-core/src/views/board.tsx`, `packages/ui/src/ui.css` **The card carries its ticket key (owner, 2026-09-22):** `TicketCard.key` — `<workspace prefix><project prefix>-<number>` composed by `assembleTicketCards` from the same three ledger facts the single-ticket read uses, or `null` when any is missing — travels on every card route, and the board draws the ticket key in its keys row, key first — **superseded 2026-09-23, see the priority-badge sentence below for the row's current shape (`[parent key badge] key [priority badge] · <due>`)**; the offline replica answers `null`. Cases `13.1278`–`13.1281`. **The priority badge gains an ICON and its own INK per level, the whole card is TINTED by priority, and two hierarchy badges join it (owner request, 2026-09-23), superseding the "only P1 takes the tone" arm of spec 2026-09-22 above.** The badge draws a hand-drawn 24×24 `currentColor` glyph left of its `P1`/`P2`/`P3` text — a red fire, a green leaf, a frozen-blue snowflake (`packages/ui/src/icons/priority-icons.tsx`) — and P1/P2 REUSE the existing `danger`/`success` ink roles (`--gn-danger`/`--gn-success`), never a new one; P3 gets one new role, `--gn-priority-p3`, a cyan-leaning blue chosen to stay visually distinct from `accent`/`textAccent`. The card's OWN surface (`.gn-board-card--p1`/`--p2`/`--p3`) is washed by a new alpha-tint role per priority (`priorityP1Tint`/`priorityP2Tint`/`priorityP3Tint`, `packages/ui/src/tokens.ts`) — layered over `--gn-surface-raised`, never the sunken column behind it — measured to clear WCAG AA 4.5:1 for the priority ink, the card's title/body text, AND the move-arrows' ghost buttons composited a further layer down, across all three styles and both themes (`packages/ui/test/tokens.test.ts`, "the priority tint composites legibly…"). This is a scoped, owner-authorised reopening of a standing refusal on record against a general-purpose danger/success wash (`.gn-visibility__standing-mode`'s own comment, `ui.css`) — the new roles are named for the priority feature specifically, not a general tint another styling task could reach for. **AMENDED 2026-09-29 (styling refresh Plan A Task 6, cases 20.051–20.059): this tint, its three roles and `--gn-priority-p3` are RETIRED — the card paints no priority tint, the ink is neutral except Urgent (P1 `danger`, P2 `textMuted`, P3 `textSubtle`), the parent badge is text2 and underlined with an `aria-hidden` `›` before the key, and the badge/arrows/Close are borderless ghost controls in a footer (see §17).** **A parent-key badge** (`.gn-board-card__parent-key`) sits LEFT of the card's own key in the keys row, a real clickable button opening the immediate parent's sheet, drawn only when the parent is visible (server) or live-and-visible-offline (replica) AND its key can be composed — a `null` key draws nothing, the same rule the card's own key already follows. **An epic chip** (`.gn-board-card__epic`) sits on the card's TOP LINE, above the title — a flag icon plus the epic's truncated title, clickable to the epic's sheet — reusing the SAME "no existence leak" rule the epic-grouping walk already applies (an unreadable or soft-deleted ancestor is indistinguishable from having none). **CORRECTED 2026-09-23 (owner bug report):** the chip shipped `display: inline-flex`, and since `.gn-board-card` sets no `display: flex` of its own, the chip shared a line with the title button whenever both fit — a real board card read "⚑ Open questionsHSN digit count". Now `display: flex` with `width: fit-content`, so the chip is genuinely its own line, sized to its content. Cases `13.1467`–`13.1468`. **When the immediate parent IS the epic, the parent badge is suppressed** — a VIEW-layer dedup in `board.tsx`, not a data-layer one, so every door that builds a `BoardCard` (server read, online mapper, replica) gets the rule automatically. Both badges carry NO existence leak, unlike the single-ticket route's `ParentRef.restricted` arm (spec §6) — a board is scanned as a grid, not read one ticket at a time, so a badge naming a ticket that opens to nothing would be an unbounded leak; `BoardTicketCard.parent`/`.epic` (`packages/domain/src/read-models.ts`) fold an unreadable ancestor to `null`, exactly as `ListCard.epicId` already does one ancestor further up. Server derivation: `apps/server/src/read/ancestry.ts`'s `boardAncestryFor` (both facts from ONE recursive walk, sharing `epicAncestors`' own `ancestryCte`, moved there from `routes/list.ts` verbatim) and `keysForAncestors`. Offline: `replica-data-source.ts`'s `boardHierarchyOf`, deleted-safe at every hop, key always `null` (the replica cannot compose one). Cases `13.1451`–`13.1470` (`test-cases/13-hig-per-screen.md`).
  - ✅ **Styling refresh (2026-09-29):** the card's content follows the rules (title-first, three groups, `›` between parent and key, neutral priority ink, ghost footer, no tick). Cases 20.051–20.059.
- ⚙️ **`moveOutcome` — the transition gate, as a pure function (board-prototype-port plan Task 12, 2026-09-16; ticketFields/Ruling 25 and the whitespace trim/Ruling 26, same day)** — the one place Tasks 13 (move arrows) and 14 (drag-and-drop) both route a proposed ticket move through before anything is submitted. Built entirely over `transitionOptions` (immediately above) rather than reading `def.states`/`def.transitions` directly — a second derivation of "what moves are legal" would drift from the engine that actually enforces it. Three outcomes: `refused` (the target is not a declared edge from this state; carries every OTHER move that state DOES declare, by name, so the caller need not guess), `direct` (a declared edge whose rules are all already met — submit it), `needs-dialog` (a declared edge with at least one rule still unmet — open `TransitionDialog`). A move back onto the current state refuses like any other undeclared target, since `transitionOptions` already excludes `to === fromStateId`. Ships no UI. Takes `ticketFields` (Ruling 25) and checks a `require-field` rule against it through `fieldAlreadyClaimed` (`packages/app-core/src/views/field-claims.ts`) — the SAME predicate `TransitionDialog` reads, extracted rather than re-derived a second time, so an edge whose only rule is a field the ticket already carries answers `direct`, matching the dialog's own already-skips-that-input behaviour exactly rather than opening a dialog with nothing left to fill in. **`fieldAlreadyClaimed` TRIMS, whitespace-only counts as unset (Ruling 26)** — mirroring, not importing, `evaluateRequireField`'s own tested semantics (`packages/rule-engine/test/engine.test.ts`, "require-field and require-evidence refuse a blank value, not only an absent one"; Task 9's controller ruling); before Ruling 26 a ticket with `dueDate: '   '` answered `direct` here and the server refused it for real, with no display path on Tasks 13/14 — the same silent-failure shape `transitionOptions`'s own docblock warns against. The agreement is pinned by a real round trip against the exported engine dispatcher, not a self-comparison: `packages/app-core/test/views/field-claims.test.ts` (13.489). **This trim also changes `TransitionDialog`'s own rendering** — a blank-but-present field now correctly prompts instead of being silently skipped — a FIX, not a regression (the engine required this all along; the dialog was out of step), confirmed by the full 21/21 `transition-dialog.test.tsx` suite still green. `require-comment`/`require-evidence` have no "already satisfied" reading before a submission exists, so either always answers `needs-dialog`. `restrict-to`/`require-different-user`-only edges answer `needs-dialog` too, though the dialog they open prompts for nothing — a DELIBERATE choice (Ruling 25), not an oversight: both are server-decided, this client cannot certify either satisfied, and routing to `direct` would submit blind with no display path Tasks 13/14 were scoped to carry for the server's refusal. `packages/app-core/src/views/board-moves.ts`, `packages/app-core/src/views/field-claims.ts`; `packages/app-core/src/views/transition-dialog.tsx` refactored onto the same shared predicate, with no behaviour change of its own from the EXTRACTION (21/21 unchanged) — its blank-field rendering DOES change from the trim, and that change is intended.
- ✅ **Board move arrows — the first write path in this port (board-prototype-port Task 13, 2026-09-16)** — per-card `‹ ›` buttons that move a ticket between the columns its workflow actually DECLARES, never by column order. `MoveArrows` (`board.tsx`) resolves each arrow's targets via `arrowTargets` (`board-arrows.ts`; `arrowTarget`, the singular, is its head): every state in that direction for which `transitionOptions` declares a real edge, nearest first, walking past every column that does not — one declared target moves, several open a picker (the 2026-09-17 bullet below) — a workflow can declare `todo -> done` while `doing` sits visually between them, and `›` from `todo` lands on `done`, never `doing`. Both arrows always render, one per direction; the direction with nothing declared is a genuinely DISABLED button (native `disabled`, `opacity:0.4; cursor:not-allowed`), not a missing one — the move is absent, not the control. Every click routes through `moveOutcome` (immediately above) and never re-derives its verdict: `direct` submits the SHIPPED `{to}` `ticket.transitioned` payload with no dialog; `needs-dialog` opens the EXISTING `TransitionDialog`, aimed at the identical `(workflow, fromStateId)`; `refused` renders `MoveRefusalNotice`, naming the real alternatives BY NAME (`Can't move there — try Doing.`), never a bare "you can't do that" — `refusalCopy` is exported and pinned by a test that feeds it `moveOutcome`'s OWN `available` output, not a hand-typed string. **`ticketFields: {}` at every call site, by design, not a gap** — `BoardCard` carries no field claims (unlike `ListRow`, which does; the port's own design spec says so of this exact gap, in these words: "the dialog needs `ticketFields`... and `BoardCard` does not carry them"), so `{}` is the conservative reading: every `require-field` rule reads as unmet, meaning the failure mode is a needless dialog open on an already-satisfied field, never a `direct` submit the server then refuses with nothing on screen. **A live, ENABLED arrow click cannot itself land on `moveOutcome`'s `refused` branch, and this is proven rather than assumed** (`board-arrows.test.ts`'s own mutation witness: forcing the scan to the literal adjacent column reddens exactly the two skip-column cases and nothing else) — the arrow's own target and `moveOutcome`'s own check read `transitionOptions` off the identical `(workflow, fromStateId)`, so a target this component ever actually submits is, by construction, always declared. The branch stays real and is exercised at the level that IS reachable — the pure `moveOutcome`/`refusalCopy`/`MoveRefusalNotice` pipeline, fed real gate output — and stays load-bearing for Task 14's drag-and-drop (the next bullet below), whose drop target is NOT filtered this way; the SAME refusal copy now DOES fire for real there, proven end to end by a real `dragstart`/`drop` sequence rather than only at this pure-gate seam. **44×44px tap targets, not the metrics table's own 32×36** — a control at the prototype's number fails this repo's already-measured 44px WCAG 2.5.5 floor (`ui.css:2424-2430`; the tab rail's own identical, already-decided divergence for the identical reason, `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-16-board-prototype-port.md:56`, applied here rather than re-litigated) — the visual treatment (`ctlBg`, accent text, 15px/600) is kept exactly as specified; only the tap target is raised. `ctlShadow` omitted, the SAME repo-wide open decision `.gn-button` and every other ported board control already states rather than re-deciding piecemeal. Wired into the real page (`apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/p/[projectId]/page.tsx`), gated on `session.kind === 'signed-in'` — the SAME precedent `CreateTicketFlow` already sets on this page and for the identical reason: an ungated click in the session-loading window, or from a signed-out viewer, would post an event with an empty actor and read back as a permission refusal rather than "not signed in yet". **`needs-dialog` does NOT pre-aim `TransitionDialog` at the arrow's own computed target** — only `(workflow, fromStateId)` are threaded through, and the person picks a target from the dialog's own dropdown exactly as they would opening `TicketSheet`'s "Move…" button; said plainly here because an earlier draft of the test suite and this task's own report claimed otherwise before review caught it. **A REJECTED `ingest` (transport failure, not a server answer) does not brick the card** — `submitDirect`'s `submitting` latch, which has no precedent in `TicketSheet.submitTransition`, is reset in a `try/catch/finally` rather than only after a successful `await`; found in review, mutation-witnessed both directions (`13.504`). **Both submit paths guard every local `setState` against firing after this card has unmounted** — a `mountedRef` (REMOVED 2026-10-01: the session now lives in `Board`'s move-state, keyed by ticket id, so nothing card-local can be set after unmount; same idiom as `use-live-query.ts`'s `isCurrent()` and `TransitionDialog`'s own precheck `cancelled` flag), gating `setServerRefusal`/`setSubmitting`/`setDialogOpen` in `submitDirect` and `submitFromDialog`, but never `moves.onMoved()` itself, which reaches the PARENT (`board.reload()`) and stays safe to call regardless — found in review (a successful move on ANY card, this one or a sibling, can restructure the board and unmount a card whose own `ingest` is still in flight; React 18 drops the console warning for this, so no test in this file could ever have surfaced it, and none was added — the same structural, untested-by-design shape as its two cited precedents). **`submitFromDialog` GAINED a `try/catch` of its own (case `13.505`)** — found in the same review round: `TransitionDialog`'s `onSubmit` prop is `void`-typed and `MoveArrows`' own call site is fire-and-forget, so a transport failure inside the dialog's own submit used to become an unhandled promise rejection, leaving the dialog open with nothing on screen saying it failed. At the time this landed the fix reused `TransitionDialog`'s existing `serverRefusal` display — corrected below by Ruling 27, which found that reuse was itself the defect. Unlike the `mountedRef` guard immediately above, this fix IS independently mutation-witnessed, since a missing catch is a real behavioural gap rather than an unmount race React 18 hides. **RULING 27 (coordinator, 2026-09-16) — the client was minting refusals, and the rule engine forbids it in as many words.** `board.tsx` built `{ rule: 'no-response'|'transport', reason }` objects by hand (never through `refuse()`/`ACCEPT`, deliberately unexported by `rule-engine/src/index.ts:32-41` for exactly this reason) and fed them into `serverRefusal` — the same channel `TransitionDialog`'s own docblock calls "the authority's answer, shown VERBATIM". Neither value exists in `REFUSAL_RULES` (`rule-engine/src/refusal-rules.ts:9-25`); both rendered through the identical `Refused by the server — …` sentence a real refusal uses, so a dropped connection or an empty `ingest` response read as though the server had adjudicated and declined the move. **Fixed with a wholly separate, plain-sentence channel — never a `{rule, reason}` pair, never `refuse()`/`ACCEPT`.** `MoveArrows` gained `transportError: string | null`, kept apart from `serverRefusal` rather than tagged onto it; `TransitionDialog` gained the identical `transportError` prop (now REQUIRED, matching `serverRefusal`'s own required shape), rendered in its own `<p role="alert" className="gn-refusal gn-refusal--transport">`, never beside the words "Refused by the server". `ui.css` gained `.gn-refusal--transport`, reusing the `warning` role `.gn-refusal--preview` already uses (amber, not `--server`'s danger-red) rather than inventing a new token role. `ticket-sheet.tsx`'s own `TransitionDialog` mount passes `transportError={null}` with a comment explaining why: `TicketSheet.submitTransition` stays unguarded, untouched, and never fabricated a refusal either — it just never caught the rejection. **`13.504`/`13.505` amended, not silently rewritten** — quoted verbatim, before and after, in `test-cases/13-deployment-dogfooding.md`'s Ruling 27 section: the OLD assertion (`toHaveTextContent('network unreachable')`, a substring check) is proven, by an actual suite run against the fix, to have STILL PASSED under the fix (`PASS (29) FAIL (0)`) because the new sentence also contains that substring — the coordinator's own expectation that the fix would redden this case was measured false, reported rather than assumed. The NEW assertions check the corrected sentence, the `gn-refusal--transport` class, and the ABSENCE of both the refusal-shaped sentence and its class. **Case `13.506`** covers the sibling "silence" path (`results[0] === undefined`) that had zero prior coverage. **Mutation witness**: `board.tsx`/`transition-dialog.tsx`/`ticket-sheet.tsx` reverted in place to the exact pre-ruling commit (`git show f5041052:<path>`), the two affected test files re-run — `PASS (27) FAIL (3)`, exactly the three touched cases, each failing with the ruling's own defect text verbatim (`"Refused by the server — transport: network unreachable"`, `"Refused by the server — no-response: The server did not answer this move."`) — then restored byte-identical (`diff` confirmed clean) and the full suite re-confirmed green. **FLAGGED, not fixed: `MoveRefusalNotice` (the CLIENT-side refusal — `moveOutcome`'s `refused` verdict, never touched by a server) still wears `.gn-refusal--server`**, the same danger-red class this ruling just reserved for a real server verdict — its own docblock says so explicitly ("Shares `.gn-refusal.gn-refusal--server`'s existing danger-tinted style"). Milder than the fabrication this ruling fixed (the SENTENCE, `Can't move there — try Doing.`, never claims server authority — only the CLASS does), and pre-dating this ruling (Task 13's own first commit, `8e0f747a`, with its own considered reasoning), so left as a named, escalated question rather than changed unilaterally: `--preview` (`.gn-refusal--preview`, amber) is the closer analogue used by `TransitionDialog`'s own client-computed precheck refusal — but that class's own docblock calls its refusal "advisory, not authoritative", where `moveOutcome`'s refusal is a certain structural fact (an undeclared edge), not an uncertain guess, so the swap is not obviously correct either. No test pins the class today (`grep` confirmed), so a future change is mechanical whichever way the coordinator rules. `packages/app-core/src/views/board-arrows.ts`, `packages/app-core/src/views/board.tsx`, `packages/app-core/src/views/transition-dialog.tsx`, `packages/app-core/src/views/ticket-sheet.tsx`, `packages/ui/src/ui.css`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/p/[projectId]/page.tsx`
- ✅ **Board drag-and-drop (board-prototype-port Task 14, 2026-09-16, the plan's final task)** — dragging a card from one board column and dropping it on another. **Ships no second decision point.** A drop's target (`toStateId`) comes from whichever column it lands on; rather than re-deriving `moveOutcome`/refusal/dialog/transport-error handling a second time, the dragged card's OWN `MoveArrows` instance (Task 13, immediately above) registers its real `attemptMove` closure into a shared registry (`MoveRegistry`, `board.tsx`) on every render, keyed by ticket id, and the target column's drop handler looks it up and calls it — the IDENTICAL function an arrow click on that same card would call, with the identical state (`refusal`/`serverRefusal`/`transportError`/`dialog` — since 2026-10-01 held in `Board`'s move session keyed by ticket id, not in the card) rendering in the identical place, under that same card. A drop and an arrow cannot disagree: they are one code path, reached from two input events, never two products. The registry is held by `Board`, not by each per-workflow group, so a drag starting in one workflow group and landing on a DIFFERENT group's column (a mixed-workflow board) still finds the dragged card's real registration and correctly names alternatives from the ticket's OWN workflow rather than doing nothing. **All three outcomes proven end to end, by a real `dragstart`/`dragover`/`drop` sequence, matching the design spec's own enumeration of the three drop cases**: a drop on a declared, rules-free column actually transitions the ticket — the SHIPPED `{to}` payload, `onMoved` called, no alert (`13.507`, the positive control the brief demands, mirroring `13.498`'s role for the arrows); a drop on an undeclared column refuses, naming the real alternative BY NAME rather than merely showing some alert (`13.508` — the case an arrow can never organically reach, since an arrow's own target is always declared by construction, so this is the first END-TO-END exercise of the refusal pipeline this port has); a drop on a declared, rules-bearing column opens `TransitionDialog`, unchanged from how an arrow would open it (`13.509`, reusing `13.501`'s gated-edge fixture verbatim — not re-proving the dialog's own submit mechanics, which `13.501`/`13.504`/`13.505` already do over the identical function this drop reaches). **`preventDefault()` on `dragover` is separately pinned (`13.510`)** because it is invisible to every outcome test above — `fireEvent.drop` in a test dispatches straight to the React handler regardless of what `dragover` did, so a suite built only from the three outcome cases could pass in full against an implementation where a real browser's default (disallow dropping) would silently defeat every drop; asserted directly via `fireEvent.dragOver(...)` returning `false` (the `dispatchEvent` return value when a cancelable event's default was prevented), not inferred from a drop succeeding. **A drop with no real `dragstart` behind it is a silent, inert no-op** (`13.511`) — an empty `DataTransfer` answers `''` from `getData`, which the registry has never seen, so `Map.get` answers `undefined` and nothing further happens; no ingest, no alert, distinguishing "the gate ran and refused" from "the handler found nothing to act on". **Every outcome-dispatch case (`13.507`–`13.509`) and the `dragover` mechanism case (`13.510`) is MUTATION-WITNESSED, not merely passing once**: disabling the registry's `attempt(toStateId)` call reddened exactly `13.507`/`13.508`/`13.509` and nothing else (`PASS (3) FAIL (3)`); removing `preventDefault()` from the `dragover` handler reddened exactly `13.510` and nothing else (`PASS (5) FAIL (1)`) — both mutations reverted and the full 6-test file re-confirmed green afterward. **`13.514` closes the one behavioural gap every other case leaves open: it drags and drops the SAME card TWICE in sequence**, proving the registry's `useEffect` re-registration publishes the FRESH `attemptMove` closure on every render — the one that sees `submitDirect`'s own `finally`-reset `submitting` flip back to `false` — rather than one frozen at first render, which would either brick a card after its first move or silently bypass the double-submit latch; neither bug touches any line the other six cases exercise. **`cursor: grab` is added in this same commit, beside the behaviour that makes it true** (Ruling 15's own instruction, `ui.css` Task 6 comment) — deliberately NOT declared on `.gn-board-card` itself, for two independent reasons stated at length in `ui.css`'s own comment: (1) `.gn-board-card` still renders on the READ-ONLY path (`moves` absent — session loading, signed out, or no capability wired), where the card genuinely cannot be dragged, and a grab cursor there would be exactly the "control that lies" shape Ruling 15 already named; (2) case `13.464`'s own `rule()` helper matches the FIRST literal substring `.gn-board-card {` it finds via a plain regex with no selector parser, so any new rule whose selector text happened to END in that substring — even a compound one — would silently hijack that case's match. The rule lives on `.gn-board__card-slot[draggable="true"]` instead (`13.513`, a CSS-binding gate proving the rule exists with the right body, the same shape `inbox-css-binding.test.tsx` already uses for `gn-timeline__bar`) — a selector containing no `.gn-board-card` substring at all (`__card-slot`, not `-card`), so it cannot collide, and keyed off the REAL `draggable` attribute rather than a second, parallel boolean class. `draggable` itself is set on the card's `<li class="gn-board__card-slot">` wrapper, gated on the SAME `arrows !== null` check that already gates the move arrows — never a second, independently-maintained boolean — so a card with no `MoveArrows` instance behind it (no `moves` capability wired, or this group's workflow still loading) is provably not draggable at all: `13.512` asserts `draggable="false"` on that path, mirroring `13.500`'s identical "no arrows at all" proof for the arrows themselves, and confirms a drop aimed at it anyway is still inert since `onDropCard` itself is `null` on that path (the column never even receives an `onDrop` handler). **Keyboard is unaffected, and this is proven rather than assumed**: `board-moves-ui.test.tsx` — the arrows' own 8-case suite, `13.498`–`13.506` — runs UNCHANGED, byte-identical, and stays green (this task edited no assertion, no aria-label, no disabled logic in it); `draggable` is a plain HTML attribute that adds no tabstop, no ARIA role and no accessible-name change, so the `‹ ›` buttons remain the complete keyboard path they were before this task, with drag-and-drop as a pure addition, never a replacement. **Two decisions stated rather than left for a reviewer to find**: a drop onto the SAME column a card is already in is refused like any other undeclared target (`transitionOptions` already excludes a self-loop, so `moveOutcome` treats it identically to any other wrong target) — no special case, consistent with the plan's own "same four outcomes" instruction; and a refusal renders where `MoveArrows` already renders it — under the SOURCE card, in its origin column — never a second rendering site near the drop point, which would be exactly the fork ("two products") this task was written to avoid. **RULING 28 (coordinator, 2026-09-16) resolved the tension this created rather than leaving it as a named risk**: the origin column CAN scroll out of view (the rail is `overflow-x: auto`), which is functionally the "silent snap-back" the design spec forbids for sighted users — `role="alert"` already covers assistive technology regardless of scroll position. Fix, keeping the single rendering site: `attemptMove` gained an optional `source: 'arrow' | 'drop'` parameter (default `'arrow'`, every arrow `onClick` unchanged) that a new `source` field (first a `lastAttemptSourceRef`, since 2026-10-01 part of `Board`'s move session) records; the registry wrapper `registerAttempt` registers now passes `'drop'` explicitly. The three mutually-exclusive notices are wrapped in one `<div className="gn-board-card__notice" ref={noticeRef}>` (`display: contents` in `ui.css`, invisible to `.gn-board-card__moves`'s own flex layout, so no visual change), and a `useEffect` calls `noticeRef.current?.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest', inline: 'nearest' })` exactly when a notice is about to render AND the triggering attempt came from a drop (`13.515`, mutation-witnessed; `13.516` is the paired negative proving an arrow-reached notice never scrolls, also mutation-witnessed — `13.515` alone would still pass an implementation that scrolled unconditionally). **RULING 29 (same day) corrected `13.512`'s own assertion**: it pinned the literal `draggable="false"`, which is STRICTER than the CSS contract it guards (`[draggable="true"]` is equally unmatched by an ABSENT attribute) — a future refactor that omits the attribute instead of setting it `false` would have reddened it with no real regression behind it. Amended to `card.matches('[draggable="true"]')`, the literal selector string, verified both directions: a real regression (`draggable={true}` unconditionally) still reddens it, and the OLD assertion text, re-run against the phantom mutation for real rather than reasoned about, DOES fail where the amended one correctly stays green. `packages/app-core/src/views/board.tsx`, `packages/app-core/src/views/board-arrows.ts` (docblock correction — no second module ships), `packages/ui/src/ui.css`
- ✅ **Board moves are optimistic, animated and followed by the scroll (owner, 2026-10-01; cases 20.125–20.148, 20.160–20.161, 20.162–20.179)** — a drop or a `‹ ›` press draws the card in its target column AT ONCE, at the landing index the drop placeholder showed, and the write happens behind it; if the write is refused, fails, is offline, errors or answers nothing, the card glides back to its source slot and the existing refusal copy shows. `Board` holds a pending-move overlay keyed by ticket id (`board-move-state.ts`: `useMoveState`, the pure `applyPendingMoves` and `retireAgreed`); it is view state laid over the read, never an optimistic write to the live query, and it retires only when a refreshed read shows the card in its target (a stale refetch never flashes the card back) or, for a committed entry, after 20s. The per-card move session (refusal, dialog, `submitting` latch) lives in that overlay's context because the card is a different `<li>` in its new column. A move that needs a comment waits in the landing slot behind a wash (`--waiting`) while its dialog is open; Confirm settles it, Cancel sends it back. The card FLIPs from the drop point to its slot (`gn-board__card-slot--flight`, `gnCardFlight` on the move token, transform only; `ui.css`), and glides back the same way; `prefers-reduced-motion` places it instantly. During a card drag the edge scroller (`board-motion.ts`, `createEdgeScroller`) scrolls the page within 64px of the window's top/bottom and the rail within 64px of its left/right edge, faster nearer the edge and capped; it runs only while the pointer is in a zone and stops on leave, drop, dragend and unmount. After a drop, an off-screen landing slot is scrolled into view (`scrollIntoView` nearest, smooth). Spring-loaded columns: a drag held ~600ms over a collapsed column where the drop is legal opens it (without touching the collapse memory), leaving or Esc collapses it again, and a drop there keeps it open and remembers that; an illegal column never springs. (`board.tsx`, `board-move-state.ts`, `board-motion.ts`, `ui.css`) The landing slot carries `scroll-margin: var(--gn-space-2)` (`.gn-board__card-slot`, `packages/ui/src/ui.css`), so the settle scroll stops 16px clear of the window and rail edges, not flush (20.160); at code level Confirm on a gated move lays the `writing` entry in the same tick as the click (20.161 guards it against drifting behind an `await`). The browser pass's B4 finding 3 (the `--waiting` wash seen for ~2 s after Confirm) is NOT reproduced in jsdom and stays open; the dialog itself stays open until the write answers (`setDialog(null)` runs on commit), which is the other thing on screen in that window. **The source column closes up with a glide too (owner, 2026-10-01):** the cards BELOW a card that leaves (by drag or arrows) slide up into the gap — and back down on a refusal — on the same FLIP as the landing (`board-move-state.ts` `recordSiblings` notes them into the shared `flights` map flagged `sibling`; `BoardCardSlot` claims the flight after the render that moved it and sets the same `--gn-flip-x/-y` and `gn-board__card-slot--flight`), so the timing is the move token's and reduced motion switches it off; a card with its dialog open and the cards above the mover are not glided. On an ARROW move (a `‹ ›` press, or the picker's confirm) nothing has opened a slot in the target column, so the cards that sort after the mover (below its landing index) slide DOWN on the same sibling flight (`recordBelow`, `board-move-state.ts`); a DRAG records none at the drop, because its drop placeholder already opened the slot. Either way, a refusal or a cancelled dialog slides those cards back UP (the drag remembers its target column so the release can close the slot smoothly — owner, 2026-10-01; 20.162–20.173, 20.175 for the dialog-awaiting arrow move, 20.176–20.178 for the drag release; a sibling that also reflows sideways flies from its old x as well, 20.168). The placeholder and every glide follow each card's OWN measured height (`board-variable-heights.test.tsx`, cases 20.410–20.414 and 20.416; a tall card among short ones in a real browser is 🧪 20.415) — a test-only proof on a mixed-height fixture: no product code changed.
- ✅ **The whole board card opens the ticket (owner request, 2026-09-17)** — a click anywhere on `.gn-board-card`, not only its title, opens the ticket sheet. The listener lives on the `<li class="gn-board__card-slot">` wrapper, extracted into `BoardCardSlot` (`board.tsx`) so it can hold a ref — never on `Card` (`packages/ui`, documented "never itself interactive") and never as a `role="button"` (the card already contains buttons; the title stays a real `<button>` and remains the keyboard path and the accessible name). Three bail-outs: a click whose target is not a DOM descendant of the slot at all (`currentTarget.contains` — `Select` portals its dropdown to `document.body`, and React bubbles the synthetic click up the REACT tree regardless; `13.535`–`13.537`, found in review); a click whose target sits inside a control or inside the `TransitionDialog` subtree (`CARD_CLICK_BAIL_SELECTOR` — the dialog renders INSIDE the card and its scrim closes it without stopping propagation, so without this a close-by-clicking-outside would open the sheet in the same gesture) is that thing's click; and a click that follows `dragstart` is the tail of a drag (`draggedRef`, set on `dragstart`, cleared on the NEXT `mousedown` — not on `dragend`, not on a timer). `.gn-board__card-slot { cursor: pointer }` for the read-only path; the `[draggable="true"]` rule keeps `grab`. Cases `13.518`–`13.523` and `13.535`–`13.537` (`packages/app-core/test/views/board-card-click.test.tsx`, `packages/ui/test/components.test.tsx`), every guard proven by deletion.

The shared confirm both bulk surfaces open (`BulkCloseDialog({ open, tickets, dataSource, workspaceId, currentUserId, onClose, onClosed })`): title and confirm both read `Close N tickets` (singular `Close 1 ticket`), the body lists every title, and confirming submits **ONE `ingest` batch of N plain `ticket.closed`** — `payload: {}`, one `make` per ticket, in the listed order — rather than N calls. **Marked ⚙️ rather than ✅ deliberately: the MECHANISM ships here, and only one of its two surfaces exists.** **CORRECTED IN TASK 10 (2026-09-18): this bullet said "no surface calls it yet — Task 10's board column action and Task 11's list selection are the callers, and until one of them wires it nothing a user can see has changed."** That sentence is now half false and was rewritten in the same change set that made it false, per the no-silent-drift rule: Task 10 wires the BOARD surface, so the dialog IS user-visible there and the ✅ belongs to that feature (the bullet on the next line). Committed ids go to `onClosed`; refused ones stay listed under `Could not close` as `<title> — <reason>` (an `invalid` answer contributes its `message`, a `refused` one its `reason`), which is what makes the dialog stay open on a partial outcome rather than closing over the evidence. **The two sentences are the CLIENT's**: `We could not reach the server for this close — <message>` for a rejected promise and `The server did not answer this close.` for the short array, through `.gn-refusal--transport`, the same split `board.tsx`'s `closeCard` and `ticket-sheet.tsx`'s `closeOrReopen` already made — a person reading "Refused by the server" is reading the server's words and neither of these is one. **The dialog never closes itself:** `onClose` fires from Cancel, Escape and the scrim only, matching `NewTicketDialog` and `TransitionDialog`, and the parent owns the reload through `onClosed`; the shipped clear is `closedIds.length === tickets.length`, and the board surface's own ✅ bullet below carries the reasoning and the mutation that proves it. The sentence is left standing rather than rewritten because it is this component's own contract and the qualifier is the board's business; Task 11 must snapshot its tickets at click time and keep its own open flag, because its plan text wires `onClosed` → `list.reload()` with the selection cleared on reload — which would set `open` false and unmount the dialog the moment a PARTIAL close reports, destroying the `Could not close` rows spec §8.3 requires it to keep on screen. **DONE IN TASK 11 (2026-09-18), exactly as required and with the same conditional-clear/unconditional-reload shape the Board uses: the List's `pendingClose` is the click-time snapshot and its own open flag, released only on a complete close. - ✅ **`Close all (N)` on a terminal board column** — backlog/closed spec §8.3, second wave, 2026-09-18 (Task 10, executor 2). A column whose `category === 'terminal'` and which holds at least one card gains one action in its header: visible text exactly the spec's `Close all (N)`, accessible name `Close all N in <column name>` — the column is in the NAME because a board draws several columns at once and a page-level duplicate would make the control unaddressable by role and name. It opens the shared `BulkCloseDialog` on that column's cards, snapshotted at click time so a later reload cannot rewrite a dialog already on screen. **Three separate terms gate the button, and each excludes a different way of rendering a control that cannot work:** `bulkCloseFor !== null` (no `moves`, so no `dataSource`/`workspaceId`/`currentUserId` to open a dialog with — the whole control is ABSENT on the read-only path, not disabled); `category === 'terminal'` (anywhere else `ticket.closed` is refused by `close-requires-terminal`, so offering it would be offering a write the engine rejects — and the negative case holds a card, so it discriminates on the category rather than on the column being empty); and `cards.length > 0` (spec: "N = cards in the column", so `Close all (0)` is not a thing this action has to say). **★ THE CORRECTION THIS TASK CARRIES — the plan's text and the task's own dispatch were both insufficient, and the gap was a SPEC requirement.** The plan wires `onClosed` → `moves.onMoved()` and says nothing about dismissal; the dispatch then said to clear the board's `bulkClose` state in `onClosed`. Taken literally and unconditionally, that satisfies both documents and silently deletes half of spec §8.3's Board bullet, whose single sentence carries **both** halves: *"Per-ticket refusals … **stay listed**; the rest close and the board reloads."* `onClosed` fires on a PARTIAL close too (the dialog calls it whenever at least one ticket committed), so an unconditional clear unmounts the dialog and destroys the `Could not close` rows the same sentence requires it to keep on screen. **The clear is therefore CONDITIONAL — `closedIds.length === tickets.length`, i.e. everything this opening listed came back committed — and the reload is UNCONDITIONAL**, because "the rest close and the board reloads" holds on both outcomes: the committed tickets are gone from the server's board whether or not their siblings refused. Full success → the dialog LEAVES, which is the defect the dispatch was written to fix (`moves.onMoved()` alone reloads the board and leaves the dialog mounted and empty — every ticket closed, nothing but a Cancel left to press). Partial → the board still reloads, and the dialog STAYS with the refusal listed. **Witnessed, not reasoned, and the witness is mutation-proven:** case 13.792 drives a two-ticket column where the second is refused and asserts the reload AND the surviving `Could not close` row; the mutation that reinstates the dispatch's literal reading (clear unconditionally) reddens **13.792** (and 13.793, whose partial-close setup cannot reach its own subject without it). The plan's own mutation (render the button regardless of category) reddens 13.789's non-terminal negative; dropping the `cards.length > 0` term reddens 13.790. **★ AN INDEPENDENT REVIEW FOUND A REACHABLE PATH THIS TASK'S FIRST DRAFT HAD, AND THE FIX IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE.** `BulkCloseDialog`'s docblock states that a parent swapping `tickets` while the dialog stays OPEN is not covered by its reset and declares that this cannot arise for its two consumers — and that was **false for this one**: `open` is `bulkClose !== null`, so writing a second column's tickets into a non-null `bulkClose` swapped the list with no `open` transition, leaving the previous opening's `closedIds`/`failures` describing a list they were not about. The concrete failure is a FULL success that does not clear (stale ids subtracted from the new list's `pending`, so `committed.length < tickets.length`) with a `Could not close` row naming the OTHER column's ticket. **`openBulkClose` now refuses the swap, and the two alternatives were measured rather than not chosen: a `key`/remount DOES reset that stale state and is WORSE**, because the attempt token lives on the INSTANCE, nothing bumps a destroyed instance's token, and an in-flight answer then passes its own check and calls the old closure's `onClosed` — exactly the defect 13.787 exists to prevent. **The path is a keyboard one** (`Dialog` ships no focus trap and no portal, so focus can escape the modal; recorded below as a named follow-on on the SHARED component), and jsdom does not hit-test the scrim, which is why the invariant is testable here at all. Case 13.793; the guard-removal mutation reddens it and nothing else. `.gn-board__column-action` is added to the SAME rule body as `.gn-board-card__close`/`.gn-row-action` — a third class in one body rather than a copy, so the shared metrics cannot drift from themselves; like `.gn-row-action` it is a distinct class because the DOM is distinct (this button sits in `.gn-board__column-header`, not in a card) and only the metrics are shared. The dialog is rendered ONCE for the whole board (`open={bulkClose !== null}`), which is the mounting shape the component's own attempt-token guard assumes. **TWO OBSERVATIONS FROM THE SAME REVIEW ARE RECORDED WITH NAMED OWNERS RATHER THAN FIXED HERE, because each belongs to something larger than this task:**

The plan mandates that exact attribute string verbatim and the spec's copy verbatim, so this is a plan-text defect shipped as written rather than an implementer's slip; and it is NOT a new house pattern — the shipped, reviewed `apps/web/src/backlog-rank-controls.tsx:291` carries `aria-label="Move ${row.title} up"` over visible `Move up`, which breaks containment identically. `Close all (${n}) in ${column.name}` would satisfy it at no cost. **Owner: whoever next touches accessible names across the bulk-close and rank controls — fix BOTH controls together, since fixing one alone makes the pair inconsistent.** (Containment IS asserted where the house has chosen to hold it — the `/privacy` Back control, WCAG 2.5.3 — so this is a case-by-case standard rather than a gap nobody knows about.)

- ✅ **Backlog ranking: drag to reorder, and Move up / Move down** — backlog/closed spec §8.1, second wave, 2026-09-18 (Task 5). The Backlog tab now draws its rows in RANK ORDER — ranked first by key, unranked last by ticket id — instead of the server's arrival order, and a row can be moved by dragging it or by a pair of per-row buttons. **The three pieces of rank arithmetic are pure and headless** (`packages/app-core/src/views/backlog-rank.ts`, 19 cases at 13.707): `sortByRank` (which delegates to the domain's `compareByRank` rather than restating "where do unranked rows go" — a second copy of that rule is exactly the drift this series keeps finding), `neighboursFor(sorted, movedId, beforeId)` → the `{before, after}` pair `rankBetween` is handed, and `moveTarget(sorted, movedId, 'up'|'down')` → the `beforeId` a button should use. They are separate from the component because `rankBetween` only throws on an INVERTED pair, so a neighbour pair that is merely off by one ROW yields a perfectly valid key in the wrong place and the tab renders it happily. **Two rules in there are the ones nobody guesses, and both are stated in the docblocks:** (1) the moved row is excluded from its own neighbour search — otherwise "move to the end" reads the last ranked row as the row being moved and builds the new key from its own old one; (2) when the row is placed last and the last row is UNRANKED, `before` is the last **ranked** row's key, because an unranked row has no key to sit after — reading `.rank` off the immediately preceding row answers `null`, and `rankBetween(null, null)` is the midpoint, so the row lands wherever the midpoint sorts rather than where the pointer was. `moveTarget`'s `down` points TWO rows below, not one, and that is not an off-by-one: the target is a `beforeId`, so "move down past the next row" means "place before the row after it" — pointing at the row directly below is a NO-OP that spends a round trip to move nothing. **`submitRank` is ONE path** (`apps/web/src/backlog-rank-controls.tsx`): both the buttons and the page's `rowDrag.onReorder` call the same exported function, which is the plan's own requirement and is measured rather than asserted — mutation M2 (ingest `before ?? 'i'` instead of the computed key) reddens both 13.709 drag cases *together with* 13.708's between-assertion, which a second independent neighbour calculation could not do. It computes the key, applies the optimistic override, ingests one `ticket.ranked`, and splits failures the way Ruling 27 requires (refusal / silence / transport failure, three different sentences, the same shape `BacklogStartButton` established). **The optimistic order is real:** the page holds `rankOverrides: Map<ticketId, rank>` which `sortByRank` reads over the server's rows, so the row moves under the pointer before the answer lands; it is cleared when the server's ANSWER identity changes rather than when the reload is CALLED — keying it on the call would drop the override the moment the request goes out and the row would snap back then jump forward again, two moves for one gesture. A non-committed answer clears the override too (the snap-back), via a `finally` that deliberately does not fire on `committed`. The two buttons carry `aria-label` `Move <title> up` / `Move <title> down` and are disabled at the edges — but only the genuinely last row's `Move down`, since the second-to-last row's means "place last" and must stay enabled. **The drag is gated on the same `session.kind === 'signed-in'` check as Start**, because a drag ends in an event carrying an `actorId`; the buttons appear and disappear with it. **THE UNRANKED TAIL — A DEFECT FOUND BY REVIEW, HELD RATHER THAN SHIPPED, AND FIXED UNDER AN OWNER RULING (2026-09-18, option B).** In a backlog where **nothing is ranked yet — the default state of every project, since `rank` starts `NULL` (13.702) — "place last" moved the row to the TOP.** Measured against the built module, not inferred: `[t1,t2,t3,t4]` all unranked, drag `t4` to the tail → `{before:null, after:null}` → key `'i'` → drawn order `t4 t1 t2 t3`. The cause is structural — `compareByRank` sorts every ranked row above every unranked one, so no rank key can place a row *after* an unranked row — and the same fact made an enabled `Move down` a no-op whenever it would step over one (`[A('g'),B('n'),C(null)]`, `Move B down` → key `'q'`, order unchanged `A B C`). It was the plan's §8 rule implemented faithfully, so it was recorded with a named owner rather than repaired by guess, and **the PR was held** — the controller's ruling that a short hold is cheaper than shipping it and correcting it in a second PR. **The fix, now shipped: `planRankMove` ranks the rows that have no key FIRST, in their drawn order, then applies the move, in ONE ingest** (N+1 `ticket.ranked` events, existing vocabulary, no schema change); `submitRank` publishes those keys optimistically too, without which the moved row would be the only ranked row on screen and would draw above the rows it was dragged past. **The accepted cost is handled explicitly rather than left implicit:** the results are read BY INDEX, and a batch that only partly commits reports its own `partial` outcome — on the transport channel, because part of it committed and it is not a verdict — drops every optimistic key and **reloads so the tab shows the server's state, not the requested one**. Cases 13.707–13.712. **KNOWN LIMITATION, MEASURED, NOT FIXED:** `DEFAULT_GROUPING` is `'epic'`, so with backlog rows under more than one epic the tab draws them grouped while the handlers compute from rank order — rank order `A('e1') B('e2') C('e1')` draws `A C B` under `epic` and `A B C` under `flat`. A move therefore lands where rank order says rather than where the screen says. Same class as the defect above and **not covered by its remedy**; owner: the ruling that priced both. `packages/app-core/src/views/backlog-rank.ts`, `packages/app-core/src/index.ts`, `apps/web/src/backlog-rank-controls.tsx`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/p/[projectId]/page.tsx`, `packages/app-core/test/views/backlog-rank.test.ts`, `apps/web/test/backlog-tab.test.tsx`

- ⚙️ **Preferences document hook** — `usePreferences(source, workspaceId)` → `{document, error, save}` (the exported `PreferencesResult`). **There is deliberately no `reload`:** an earlier shape returned one, nothing called it, and a reload bumps the generation counter without clearing `document` — so between the bump and the resolve `useTicketList` still reports `canSetPrefs: true` and a `setPrefs` landing there merges into a document the counter has abandoned. That the write wins anyway is an argument, not a measurement, and an export whose safety has not been measured is a liability. Deliberately NOT `useLiveQuery`: preferences are server-owned per-user rows (amendment 14) and no stream frame can carry one, so subscribing them to the ledger stream both wastes a refetch per ticket event and makes `use-live-query.ts`'s recorded F6 reachable — a debounced GET in flight when a `putPreferences` lands resolves afterwards under the same key with the PRE-WRITE document, and the arrangement the user just chose snaps back on screen while the server holds the new one. One generation counter orders loads against saves. `document` is `null` until it loads, never an empty document, because a whole-document PUT composed from a document this client has not read would erase every saved filter and every other project's arrangement — `useTicketList` refuses the write in that window and `TicketList` disables the controls so the refusal is visible. **Ruling P24 at the surface, BOTH of its asymmetries.** A project absent from the document reports `prefsOrigin: 'default'` and the view SAYS so, rather than presenting this client's stock arrangement as the user's own choice. The ruling's other asymmetry — a project present in the server's `listColumns` and absent from its `grouping`, or the reverse — used to be *erased* by a `DEFAULT_VIEW_PREFS` fill inside `mapPreferences` before any view was handed the document, which is what P24 forbids in as many words (*"reaching for `DEFAULT_VIEW_PREFS` there invents a preference the user never set … a project missing from `grouping` surfaces as **not set**, never as a default wearing a user's authority"*). **It is now represented rather than erased:** `ProjectViewPrefs`' two halves are each a `Chosen<T>` = `{origin: 'stored'; value: T} | {origin: 'default'}`, and the `default` arm carries NO value, so reading a value without first narrowing on `origin` does not compile — the ruling is enforced by the type checker rather than by convention. The stock values live in their own constants (`DEFAULT_LIST_COLUMNS`, `DEFAULT_GROUPING`); `DEFAULT_VIEW_PREFS` is now the statement that *neither half is set*, and fusing those two facts in one constant is what let a default be read as a choice. `mapPreferences` reports an absent half `{origin: 'default'}`; `toServerPreferences` contributes no key for such a half, so a grouping chosen alone is stored alone and a stock value is never PUT under the user's name; the pair round-trips a half-set project as half-set. One vocabulary for both scopes: `PrefsOrigin` is declared in `view-types.ts` and re-exported by `ticket-list.tsx`, and the project-level origin is derived from the halves by the single exported `prefsOriginOf` rather than stored beside them. `packages/app-core/src/views/use-preferences.ts`
