A selector is therefore not a control to add but a question to answer: **which type is the default, and what happens to the derived-type guarantee** — exactly the design question the controller's override said to stop and report rather than decide alone. **This sentence is that report, and the owner decides.** It went unnoticed because the dispatch that carried the request also required a mutation *"that an illegal type is absent from the selector"* — an assertion that cannot exist while there is no selector. **THE ROWS ARE CARDS NOW, THE HEADING WEARS THE SHEET'S CAPTION, AND THE ADD ROW IS ONE LINE (sheet prototype parity, Task 6, 2026-09-22).** Each child draws a tinted card (`desktop.dc.html:3629`): its title, then a meta row carrying its state as a `Chip` and a `type · Due <day>` detail. **⚠ NO TICK BOX** — the prototype's box advances the child's state on click; drawing one that does nothing would be a control that lies, and wiring it is functionality this plan does not add. **The heading gains `.gn-ticket-sheet__caption`** (the same eyebrow `Comments · N` wears) and its words are NOT retyped — the caps come from `text-transform`, which is paint, so every existing text query still matches. **The add row's visible `New subtask title` label is gone**; its words live on the input as `placeholder` AND `aria-label`, because a placeholder alone is not an accessible name, and every pre-existing `getByLabelText('New subtask title')` keeps resolving. **The ` · ` separator between the state chip and the type detail is a real character, not the flex gap** — the same 'one run of glyphs' property this section's 2026-09-20 defect was about, one element to the right, and mutation M8 reddens three cases if it is removed. Cases `16.123`–`16.125`, `16.15` (amended). `packages/app-core/src/views/ticket-sheet.tsx`, `packages/ui/src/ui.css`
- ✅ **Add subtask under a TERMINAL parent offers the reopen** (executor lane 4, 2026-09-30) — the sheet's Add subtask used to show the `hierarchy.parent-terminal` refusal ("Adding live work reopens it — choose a state to reopen it to…") with no chooser. It now takes the create flow's guarded path (`submitChildEvent` → `ReopenDialog` → `reopenAndProceed`): the dialog offers the parent's own reopen states, and a chosen state reopens the parent and adds the subtask in that one guarded sequence; Cancel adds nothing and the parent stays terminal. The offer/outcome logic is shared with the create flow (`reopenOfferFor`, `parentNoLongerClosed`). A CLOSED parent's accept batch is `[ticket.reopened, ticket.transitioned]`, and a refused reopen keeps the dialog open and retries without resending `ticket.reopened`. Cases `16.130`–`16.134`. `packages/app-core/src/views/ticket-sheet.tsx`, `packages/app-core/src/flows/guarded-child-event.ts`
- ⚙️ **Fixture harness folds the ticket-type ladder and reparenting** — `buildInMemoryContext` folds `ticket-type.defined` (last definition wins, which is what makes a rank re-definition and the loop it enables reachable) and `ticket.reparented` (parentId and nothing else), and its `getTicketTypeDef` answers from the folded ladder instead of throwing. Both folds mirror `buildMemoryContext` deliberately: these fixtures do not traverse the shared reducer, so nothing but the mirroring keeps the two folds honest about what a rule sees. `workflow.defined` stays out of the dialect — admitting it would oblige this fold to carry the refresh-on-publish walk too, and a harness that took the event without the walk would split from the memory context at the seam the shared suite exists to weld. `packages/rule-engine/src/fixtures/harness.ts`

## 6. Server core — auth, membership & visibility

*(Plan 4, Tasks 4–13. The identity surface of Tasks 1–3 shipped on `main` before this section existed and stayed uncatalogued until now — Task 12 is the catalogue task that owns its bullets, and its own bullet is the first below. What follows after it is what Tasks 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 added. Task 6 brought the table that resolves every ticket's audience; Task 7 brought the decision that reads it; Task 8 is the first surface that ASKS it before serving; Task 9 is the first that asks it before COMMITTING. Task 10 is the first that tells a viewer the size of what they CANNOT see; Task 11 is the first that decides what leaves the server for a device it does not control; Task 12 is the first that proves the role, visibility and session properties hold at the real HTTP surface rather than at the gate or projection alone; Task 13 is the first door the product has for making a workspace at all, and the directory that tells a person which ones they are in. What is still absent rather than missing: the ROUTE that carries sync-down and the backfill on newly granted visibility, both Plan 10's; the narrowing of a guest's definition stream to the definitions their own tickets use, which needs `proj_tickets`; `invite.sent`'s owner/admin slice, Task 14's (`POST /v1/workspaces` was Task 13's and has now landed); HTTP-Origin checking on product routes, a decided non-gap rather than an absence (case 6.54) — `SameSite=Lax` already withholds the cookie cross-site, so a forged-origin request meets `requireSession`'s 401, and the residual a non-browser replaying a stolen cookie sets any header it likes; the per-category half of a rollup ("5 of 8 **done**"), which needs `proj_rollups`, Plan 3 Task 11's; and no ticket titles exist to serve, because `proj_tickets` is Plan 3 Task 12's. Named as open rather than closed: nothing anywhere asks who may emit a **workspace-entity** event other than `workspace.created` — a guest is still admitted for `workspace.renamed`, and which roles may rename a workspace is a product decision no plan has taken.)*

- ⚙️ **Identity & sessions** — better-auth on Fastify (`/api/auth/*`, mounted whole): phone OTP, email magic link, Google OAuth (registered, unusable without credentials), and passkeys — no passwords, `emailAndPassword` is disabled outright. Every id better-auth mints, including a user's, is a ULID (`advanced.database.generateId`), because a user's id becomes `actorId` on the events they author and the envelope schema refuses anything else. httpOnly cookie sessions carry the web client; `bearer()` issues a token for the apps and for every later task's route test, because a bearer request sends no cookie and needs no trusted `Origin`. Identity is server-owned infrastructure — `user`, `session`, `account`, `verification`, `passkey` — never events; membership, which IS history, lives in the ledger and is what the rest of this section resolves. `apps/server/src/auth/`
- ✅ **Session hygiene** — sign-out deletes the session row, not just the cookie, so a signed-out bearer token stops opening `requireSession`-guarded routes even though its signature still verifies: the guard asks the database on every request rather than trusting the signature alone, which is the only way a revoked session can be told from a merely-old one. Verifying an OTP or magic link while carrying an attacker-chosen `better-auth.session_token` cookie never adopts that value — sign-in always mints and sets a fresh token, so there is no fixation window. `SameSite=Lax` and `HttpOnly` are pinned as SETTINGS rather than inherited vendor defaults (`defaultCookieAttributes`), and `crossSubDomainCookies` stays off so the session cookie never grows a `Domain` attribute that would hand it to every subdomain of the zone. `apps/server/src/auth/auth.ts`, `apps/server/src/auth/require-session.ts`
- ⚙️ **Membership history becomes effective roles (`proj_memberships`)** — a projection of `membership.granted`/`revoked` and `project.member_added`/`removed`, keyed `(workspace_id, user_id, scope_kind, project_id)` so that **each key has exactly one totally-ordered writer**: the workspace-scope row is written only by the membership entity's stream, each project-scope row only by that project's. That is not a tidiness choice — the plan text's revoke handler deleted project rows too, and because `readLedger` replays in `(entity_kind, entity_id, seq)` order every membership event precedes every roster event, so live application and a rebuild disagreed and `verify-projections` would have reported drift on a table nobody corrupted. `apps/server/src/projections/proj-memberships.ts`
- ⚙️ **Effective role resolution (`resolveEffectiveRole`, `hasProjectAdminRights`)** — the one safe reader of `proj_memberships`: given `(workspaceId, userId)` it answers the workspace role and the projects the user is on. **A null workspace role always yields an empty project set**, which is where the safety the revoke handler used to provide now lives — and it is stronger there, because it also covers the roster row a legitimate rebuild leaves standing. A bare project-scope `SELECT` can return a row for someone no longer in the workspace; this function cannot. **The rule engine now reads memberships through it too** — the server `EngineContext`'s `getEntityState('membership')`, wired by ruling P18, which is what makes `restrict-to`'s role criterion decide anything on the server path; it takes a `Queryable`, so the ingest transaction's own client goes in unchanged and the answer is the world as of the events committed before the one under judgement. `apps/server/src/permissions/effective-role.ts`, `apps/server/src/engine-context.ts`
  - ⚙️ **Rule A — owners, admins and members are on every project of their workspace** (owner ruling 2026-09-29; access plan Task 1; `apps/server/src/permissions/effective-role.ts` `RULE_A_ROLES`) — the project set gains every founded project (`proj_projects`) with `projectAdmin: false`, explicit roster rows applied after so a project admin keeps their flag. Read-time, no data written: the members who joined through "All projects" invitations with zero roster rows see everything with no migration. Guests are unchanged. A DELETED project is not added (the canSee-only doors carry no deletion predicate), so only its explicit members keep reaching it, as before rule A. Cases 6.180–6.186, 6.217.
- ⚙️ **Pre-engine permission gate** — `checkRolePermission` (pure) and `checkPermission` (async, reading roles only through `resolveEffectiveRole`) refuse under-privileged claims **before the rule engine sees them**, in a pinned order: a claim attributed to someone other than the session user, a client-submitted event wearing the server's envelope-origin, a non-member of the workspace, an admin-only event type from below admin, project-roster changes without project-admin rights, and a **guest creating a ticket**. The gate is handed the **ingest transaction's own connection**, never a second one from the pool. Its docblock carries the register of what it does NOT ask — absences stated as questions nobody asks, never as degrees of doneness. **A member or guest can now LEAVE a workspace (E6-21):** `membership.revoked` used to gate on `isWorkspaceAdmin` for every submission, including one's own — refusing self-revocation with the same `WORKSPACE_MEMBERSHIP_REASON` aimed at someone trying to manage a DIFFERENT person's membership, even though `http-origin.ts`'s CSRF docblock and the export's privacy copy both already assumed leaving was possible. Any role may now revoke their own membership; revoking someone else's is unchanged. The sole-owner exception is not re-guarded at this gate — the engine's own last-owner guard (`rule-engine/checks/membership.ts`, the bullet above) already refuses that shape for every door, by counting owners in the world rather than trusting an actor check. A `Leave` CONTROL on the workspace home and account page is not built here — this closes the door only, per the finding's own split. `apps/server/src/permissions/check-permission.ts` — `checkRolePermission` (pure) and `checkPermission` (async, reading roles only through `resolveEffectiveRole`) refuse under-privileged claims **before the rule engine sees them**, in a pinned order: a claim attributed to someone other than the session user, a client-submitted event wearing the server's envelope-origin, a non-member of the workspace, an admin-only event type from below admin, project-roster changes without project-admin rights, a **guest creating a ticket**, and — after the audience check, so nothing about the ticket is disclosed by it — a `ticket.assigned` or `ticket.collaborator_added` **naming someone with no role in the workspace** (*"That person is not in this workspace."*; a guest may be named, `assigneeId: null` and `collaborator_removed` pass; E6-17, cases 6.151–6.152). The gate is handed the **ingest transaction's own connection**, never a second one from the pool. Its docblock carries the register of what it does NOT ask — absences stated as questions nobody asks, never as degrees of doneness. `apps/server/src/permissions/check-permission.ts`
- ✅ **The last-owner guard — a workspace cannot be emptied of its owners** (the WORLD half; its ACTOR half is the bullet below, and they are one guard) — `checkMembershipGranted` and `checkMembershipRevoked` refuse `last-owner` when a change would move the workspace's last remaining owner out of the role, through **either** door: a demotion (`membership.granted { role: 'member' }`) and a `membership.revoked` of the sole owner both refuse, each carrying the remedy in the sentence (*"Grant the owner role to somebody else first."*). The rule is deliberately NARROWER than "an owner is involved", and that narrowing is what the tests pin: a grant that leaves an owner an owner — re-stating the same role, or promoting somebody who is not an owner — is accepted however few owners the workspace has, and demoting one of **two** owners is accepted BY THE ENGINE because the workspace is not emptied — **but no longer on the client door: an admin's demotion of ANY owner, last or not, is now refused there by the ACTOR rule, before the engine runs. See the mirror bullet above.** It **counts** rather than lists, through a new OPTIONAL `EngineContext.countWorkspaceOwners(scope, excludingUserId)`, implemented by the server over `proj_memberships`; the subject of the change is excluded from the count, and that exclusion is load-bearing in the other direction — without it the sole owner counts himself and the guard never fires. **Batching is not a way around it:** two events in one submission are judged one at a time and the context reads through the ingest transaction's client, so demoting one owner and then the last in a single batch commits the first and is refused `last-owner` on the second. **The actor must be an OWNER, and this sentence said `an admin` until 2026-09-18's second sitting: an admin is now refused on the FIRST event by the actor rule above, so an admin-driven batch pins nothing here.** A context that cannot supply the count **THROWS rather than refusing**, following the contest evaluators' rule and for a sharper reason: `last-owner` is a sentence about the WORLD, and a context that never counted has made no claim about it. An event about a ticket the viewer cannot see now is never yielded — **not the payload and not the id**, because an envelope naming a ticket while withholding its body still discloses that the ticket exists, which is the oracle the read door spent a whole task closing. What a SCOPE REVOCATION inside the window took away comes back as a tombstone instead, since an event that merely stops arriving leaves the data on the device forever: losing a project purges that project's now-invisible tickets, and a revoke-and-re-grant purges what the new role no longer reaches. **A purge is a per-BOUNDARY instruction and only a per-boundary one.** There was a second emitter — a per-EVENT walk that ran on every `visibility.set` and `ticket.reparented`, purging that ticket and every inheriting descendant the viewer cannot see NOW — and a controller ruling struck it. A purge names "cannot see NOW", which is true of a ticket taken away and equally true of one never held; the module cannot tell them apart, because `proj_visibility` keeps no prior audience and neither payload carries a before-image, and re-deriving the projection's `resolve()` rule here against a ledger lookback would be a second definition of visibility that can disagree with the table every other door reads. **What makes an id tolerable is RELATIONSHIP, not size.** The read door's restricted-parent disclosure is acceptable because the viewer already HOLDS the child whose parent id it names; the walk had no such axis — its own test seeded a ticket in a project the viewer was never on and watched the walk purge it — so it was the guest disclosure at a smaller radius, and the cardinality defence for it compared a per-emission quantity against a per-boundary one. A `req` serializer redacts that one segment and leaves every other path alone, so log access does not become workspace access. **A sign-in credential in the query is redacted too** — `redactRequestUrl` replaces the VALUE of `token`, `code`, `state`, `access_token`, `refresh_token` and `id_token` with `[redacted]` (key and the other parameters kept), because the production log held `GET /api/auth/magic-link/verify?token=…` in plain text (2026-09-29); the same function feeds the request serializer and the 5xx alert context. `apps/server/src/app.ts`, `apps/server/src/http/redact-url.ts`, `apps/server/src/routes/invites.ts`
- ✅ **Inviting an address twice does not make two invitations, and a changed role or project set UPDATES the pending one** (fix-now S4, owner ruling 2026-09-29; invite update, owner ruling 2026-09-30) — a repeat `POST /v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/invites` for an address with a PENDING invitation in the same workspace and channel (email compared case-insensitively; matched on the address only, newest first) either (a) **repeats** it — the newest pending invitation has this very role and project set (the set in any order): its token is rotated (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT (invite_id) DO UPDATE` on `invite_tokens`; the old link stops opening), the same `inviteId` returns with a fresh link and letter and no second `invite.sent` is appended — or (b) **updates** it — the role or project set differs: the pending invitation (and any older pending duplicates minted before S4) is revoked and a fresh invitation for the new role and projects is sent, with a new `inviteId`, a new link and a letter naming the new role, so the pending list shows ONE invitation and the old link is dead. There is no `invite.updated` event: the update is `invite.revoked` then `invite.sent`, both through the gated client door as the caller, so it is two commits, not one transaction (a `invite.sent` refused after the revokes committed leaves the address with no pending invitation; the admin invites again). The authorisation runs first and changes nothing on refusal — the parsed `invite.sent` and every `invite.revoked` go through `checkPermission` dry before the first revoke commits, and any refusal or parse failure falls through to ingest (or answers the dry-run's own refusal) for a 422 with the pending invitation untouched — and the check-and-mint holds a per-(workspace, channel, address) advisory transaction lock on a dedicated pool client, released before the letter is sent, so two simultaneous updates end with one pending invitation carrying the later request's role. The `invite mint timing` line carries `deduped` (repeat or update) and `updated`. `apps/server/src/routes/invites.ts` (`withMintLock`, `findPendingInvites`, `isRepeat`); cases 6.222–6.226, 6.230–6.234.
- ✅ **Remove from workspace** (R5, owner ruling 2026-09-29) — an owner or admin removes a member: `POST /v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/members/:userId/remove` submits `membership.revoked` and then `invite.revoked` for each pending invitation addressed to the person (verified email, case-insensitive; verified phone, digits) in that workspace, all through the gated client door as the caller, so the last-owner guard and the owner-only-removal rule answer in their own words (409 `{rule, reason}`). Separate transactions: the membership goes first, an invitation refused afterwards is reported in `invitesNotWithdrawn`. History is kept, assigned tickets stay with a `(removed)` label, the person keeps their account and reads the workspace as a non-member. A plain member, guest or non-member gets the shared 404. `apps/server/src/routes/members.ts`, Members page (a per-row "More actions for <name>" overflow holding the action — UX fixes T2, 23.023 — then the confirm dialog).
- ⚙️ **One pooled SMTP transport for both mail senders, and a connection-only mail log** (fix-now S2 + S1, owner ruling 2026-09-29) — `smtpTransportOptions` (`apps/server/src/auth/smtp-magic-link-sender.ts`) is the one place the invitation mailer and the sign-in sender get their nodemailer options: the `url`-carrying object, the bounded timeouts and `pool: true`, so sends reuse a connection instead of paying a fresh TCP + TLS + AUTH each time. **Measured on Mailpit: reuse holds for sends within the 20 s socket timeout of each other; a send 25 s after the last opens a new connection** — keeping it warm longer would loosen the hung-send bound, an open owner question. `connectionPhaseLogger` (allow-list) forwards nodemailer's DNS / connect / pool / handshake / failure records to the app log and drops everything that names the recipient, the AUTH user or the message; `debug` stays off, because the DATA phase carries the invitation link. Each mint also logs one `invite mint timing` line of per-phase milliseconds (`routes/invites.ts`, `phaseTimer`), durations and ids only. Cases 6.227–6.229.
- ✅ **A dead invitation link stops costing anything — the credential store is collected, not merely ignored** — a revoked or lapsed invitation's `invite_tokens` row opens nothing, but nothing was ever removing it either: acceptance deletes its own row and a dead link being presented does not clear it, because `openableInvite` refuses on status or expiry BEFORE the consume statement is reached. So the table was monotonic, holding password-equivalent hashes for credentials that had been withdrawn. `sweepInviteTokens` collects both kinds, and the revoked kind is the one that matters most: a withdrawal can land at any moment before natural expiry, so an expiry-only sweep would keep a cancelled workspace's credential for the rest of its fortnight. **One predicate string decides what a dry run reports AND what a live run deletes**, because two separately maintained `WHERE` clauses drift invisibly — both keep working, they just stop describing each other. The fragment is PARENTHESISED, because its top level is an `OR` and `AND` binds tighter: unwrapped, the first caller to append `AND workspace_id = $1` would silently sweep every lapsed token in every workspace, so "one predicate, safe in both callers" holds only under composition. Safe at any moment, safe twice; the scheduling surface is deliberately not here. `apps/server/src/tools/sweep-invite-tokens.ts`, `apps/server/test/tools/sweep-invite-tokens.test.ts`
- ✅ **Per-user data does not outlive the relationship that justified it** — `user_preferences` has no foreign keys and preferences are not events, so no purge tombstone reaches the table: a revoked member's arrangement survived forever, unreachable behind the door's 404 and collected by nothing. Storage was never the point; the statement was. `sweepUserPreferences` keeps such a row for one named window and then removes it, and the two hard parts are stated rather than assumed. **Who is a member is resolved through `resolveEffectiveRole` and never by reading `proj_memberships` directly** (ruling P22) — a revocation deletes only the workspace-scope row, so a direct read would report a departed person as current and keep their data forever, the very thing being fixed. The rule is pinned by the one fixture in which the two readers disagree — a revoked person whose PROJECT-scope roster row is still standing — because in every state built from workspace-scope facts alone the forbidden read returns the same answer and the rule tests as vacuous. **The DELETE re-states the membership condition rather than trusting the decision made three round-trips earlier**: the steps are separate statements with no enclosing transaction, and `user_preferences` is authored and rebuilt by nothing, so a grant committing mid-sweep would otherwise destroy a now-current member's row unrecoverably. **When they stopped being a member is read from the LEDGER**, because the revocation deletes the row that would otherwise have held the instant; a non-member with no `membership.revoked` event has no window start, so the sweep fails closed and NAMES the row in its report rather than skipping it silently. The window is one constant, disclosed as a default under uncertainty for the product owner to confirm or replace, and `now` is injected so the boundary is testable without sleeping through it. `apps/server/src/tools/sweep-user-preferences.ts`, `apps/server/test/tools/sweep-user-preferences.test.ts`
- ✅ **Find an account by its exact email, and pull an outsider in as a guest with the assignment** (owner rulings 2026-09-29; access plan Task 6; `apps/server/src/routes/people.ts`) — `POST /v1/workspaces/:id/people-lookup {email}` answers the ONE verified account whose email matches exactly (case-insensitive, trimmed; no prefix, no list; a synthetic phone address never matches) as `{userId, name, email, inWorkspace}` or `null` (carries no role, and refuses a guest caller with the shared 404 — R2, owner ruling 2026-09-29), to a workspace member, admin or owner. `POST /v1/workspaces/:id/assign-outsider {userId, event}` takes the caller's own `ticket.created`/`ticket.assigned` naming that person: the gate is run dry first (its own refusal is answered and nothing granted), then `membership.granted {role: 'guest'}` goes through the internal door and the claim through the gated door as the caller; a refusal after the grant is compensated with `membership.revoked`. Anyone who may assign may pull someone in, only as a guest, only with an assignment — a stand-alone grant is still admin-only. Both routes are HTTP-Origin protected; the lookup spends the invite rate-limit budget. Cases 6.202–6.216, 6.240–6.241.
- ⚙️ **Device identity on sign-in** (devices plan Task 1, 2026-10-01) — every sign-in method creates its better-auth session through one `databaseHooks.session.create.before` hook (`apps/server/src/auth/device-cookie.ts`, wired in `auth.ts`) that reads or mints an httpOnly `gn_device` cookie (SameSite=Lax, 1 year, Secure over https; a malformed value is replaced) and records its value in `session."deviceId"`. A context-less session gets NULL. The column is declared `returned: false, input: false`, so no better-auth response carries it; clients only ever see `sha256` key and a 4-character tag. Migration `1790900000000_devices-and-passkeys.sql` adds three NULLable columns (`session.deviceId`, `session.lastSeenAt`, `passkey.lastUsedAt`) and an index, safe for the old code. Cases 6.300–6.306.
- ⚙️ **`currentSessionId` and a throttled `lastSeenAt`** (devices plan Task 2, 2026-10-01) — `requireSession` (`apps/server/src/auth/require-session.ts`) sets `request.currentSessionId` (the session row id; `null` for an MCP token) and stamps `session."lastSeenAt"` at most once per 5 minutes per session (better-auth's own `updatedAt` moves only daily). The stamp is an observation, never an authorisation input, and a failed stamp is logged and never fails the request. Cases 6.307–6.310.
- ✅ **Your devices** (devices plan Task 3, 2026-10-01) — `GET /v1/me/devices` lists the caller's unexpired sessions grouped by `gn_device` (pre-cookie sessions group by user agent + address and read `legacy`): a one-way `key`, a 4-character `tag`, `isCurrent`, first/last seen and a session count, current device first. `POST /v1/me/devices/:key/sign-out` deletes that device's sessions of the caller only (404 for a key that is not theirs, 409 for the current device, 403 for an MCP token) and is in the Origin-checked POST set. The raw cookie value never leaves the server. `apps/server/src/routes/me-devices.ts`

## 7. API, realtime & search

*(**Plan 5, complete: Tasks 1–16.** Task 16 is this plan's catalogue task and has now run, so this
note is the replacement it owed rather than the placeholder that stood here. Every `/v1` surface Plan
5 promised is present: the board, the project list, the builder read surface and the one write that
belongs with it (the bulk workflow rebind), search, My Work, the attention strip, view preferences,
and the WebSocket route that mounts the hub. Plan 5 Task 1 (`docToPlainText`) keeps its bullet in §3,
beside the ledger material it belongs to, on the precedent §3 already records for Plan 6's and Plan
10's pulled-forward bullets; its test cases are **7.1, 7.2 and 7.159** in
`test-cases/07-api-realtime-search.md`. §8, §10 and §11 stay absent because the coordination doc
assigns `Features.md` sections one per implementation plan, so numbering is claimed from that table
rather than taken next-free.)*

*What this surface does **not** do — enumerated, because a partial surface that only calls itself
partial tells a reader nothing about which half they have. Every item below is a decision with a
reason on record, not an oversight:*

- ✅ **Your passkeys** (devices plan Task 5, 2026-10-01) — `GET /v1/me/passkeys` lists the caller's passkeys (oldest first) with the authenticator's NAME (`providerOf`, `apps/server/src/auth/passkey-providers.ts`: iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, Windows Hello, 1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane, Chrome on Mac; anything else, the all-zero AAGUID and null read "Security key or other" — never a UUID), `createdAt`, `lastUsedAt` and `notUsedRecently` (never used, or 90 days or more ago). Named columns only: no public key, credential id or counter leaves the server. Browser-only (403 for an MCP token). A successful passkey sign-in stamps that passkey's `lastUsedAt` (`apps/server/src/auth/passkey-last-used.ts`, a better-auth `hooks.after` on `/passkey/verify-authentication`; a failed verification stamps nothing). `apps/server/src/routes/me-passkeys.ts`.
- *Search answers the **top 50, unpaginated**, ordered by `ts_rank_cd` then ticket id, and its
  configuration is `FTS_CONFIG = 'simple'` — **nothing is stemmed, in any language**. Both were
  settled deliberately rather than deferred: stemming one language while not stemming the others
  would rank dishonestly for an audience that writes in more than one. Pagination stays additive
  (`hits` is already an array) and a language-aware configuration is a reindex, not a shape change.*
- *My Work is **per workspace** (`?workspaceId=`). There is no cross-workspace aggregation on the
  server; a client that wants one loops. A server-side join would need cross-workspace session
  scoping this series has not defined, and inventing it inside a view endpoint is how scoping rules
  end up owned by nobody.*
- *View preferences are **full-replace `PUT`** per (user, workspace). There is no per-key `PATCH` and
  no merge: last-write-wins on one person's own view arrangement can lose an arrangement, never
  truth.*
- *The board answers **`columns: []`** for a project with no visible tickets. Columns are derived from
  the workflows in use by tickets THIS CALLER may see, so inventing them from a default would show a
  viewer columns derived from tickets they cannot see. The first-run empty state is Plan 6's, as copy
  rather than as scaffolding.*
- *Attention reasons are **English template strings**, and there is no localisation. The structured
  fields (`stateName`, `thresholdDays`, `windowDays`, `due`) carry everything a later localisation
  needs to re-render without a server change; the standing rule is that no surface parses the English.*
- *The stream has **no load or soak coverage** — throughput, memory ceilings and reconnect storms are
  Plan 11's deployment concern (case 7.35, 🚫). The bounds this plan owns are proven as correctness
  instead: the per-user connection budget, the slow-consumer `1013` close, the payload bound on an
  oversized frame, and the heartbeat that terminates a silent peer.*
- *Two stream gaps are **recorded and unfixed**, each with a named owner, rather than quietly absent.
  A per-TICKET narrowing mid-stream sends **no purge frame at all** — the events simply stop and a
  replica keeps a subtree it may no longer see (case 7.158; owner Plan 4,
  `apps/server/src/visibility/visible-events-for.ts`, which records it as case 6.104). And the shared read world
  seeds fixed entity ids (`wf-errands`, `epic`, `task`) that reach the ledger past the door's ULID
  rule, so those envelopes fail the published frame schema (case 7.157; owner
  `apps/server/test/helpers/read-scenario.ts`).*
- *The **envelope** inside a stream frame is not `.strict()` — the outer frame object is, but an
  unknown ENVELOPE key is silently stripped by the published schema, and it is the test recorder
  rather than the schema that catches a hub leaking one. A Plan 6/9/10 mock importing only the schema
  must `.strict()` the envelope on its own side (case 7.142).*

- ⚙️ **FilterSpec compiler** — one strict zod shape (`@gisik-nokma/domain`) compiled to parameterized SQL; user bytes travel only as parameters, injection-proven against thirteen planted hostile inputs executed against a live database. The proof is that the emitted SQL is a CONSTANT, pinned clause by clause, rather than that a value fails to appear in it — a substring check reddens on a correct compiler the moment the value is `$1`, `t.`, `SELECT`, `->>` or `ESCAPE`, and a guard that fires on correct code gets deleted. A concatenating reference compiler stands beside it in the test, only to show what the bound one prevents: the same `fieldId` payload widens its answer past the caller's workspace scope to another tenant's ticket, which is a widened result set rather than the weaker kill a syntax error would be. **The door refuses exactly one byte on sight: U+0000**, in all seven free-form string slots, because Postgres `text` cannot carry it — every other control character, DEL and a lone surrogate included, round-trips and is admitted, so the rule is "what the store can hold" and not a taste for tidy input; the executed test shows each slot raising SQLSTATE 22021 past the door, which is what makes the refusal a 400 instead of a 500. A due bound is the shared `IST_DAY_REGEX`, imported rather than restated, and constrains day SHAPE, not calendar existence — fixed-width padding is what makes the compiled text comparison chronological. `fields[].value` deliberately carries no `.min(1)`: `eq: ''` is a real claim, so `contains: ''` is a declared field-PRESENCE predicate that still cannot widen a read. The two clauses that reach another table (`proj_search`, the blocked-states CTE) carry their own `workspace_id = t.workspace_id` correlation, so a filter term cannot answer out of a neighbouring tenant — executable because `proj_tickets.ticket_id` is globally unique, which makes a correctly-filed neighbouring row harmless and projection DRIFT (a search row filed under the wrong workspace) the thing the correlation actually refuses. `packages/domain/src/filter-spec.ts`, `apps/server/src/read/sql-params.ts`, `apps/server/src/read/compile-filter.ts`
- ⚙️ **`workspace.settings_set` v1** — the attention strip's two thresholds (`staleDays`,
  `dueSoonDays`, `DEFAULT_STALE_DAYS = 7`, `DEFAULT_DUE_SOON_DAYS = 7`), claimed as an attributed
  event against the workspace itself rather than assumed or hardcoded — a threshold is a claim about
  what deserves attention, so it gets provenance like everything else. Partial-update semantics:
  either knob alone or both together, at least one required, `.strict()` against unknown keys,
  integers only in `[1, 365]` for `staleDays` and `[0, 365]` for `dueSoonDays`. Registered with
  `entityKind: 'workspace'`, so `parseEvent`'s kind guard refuses a settings claim filed against
  anything else. Who may make the claim: workspace `owner` or `admin` only. A
  member or guest is refused `permission.role` naming the setting by name; a **non-member is
  refused earlier**, by the `role === null` branch that precedes every per-type case, so it carries
  the same rule id and a different reason — which is the better answer, since naming the setting
  would disclose it to someone holding nothing in this workspace. `packages/domain/src/events/workspace-settings.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/permissions/check-permission.ts`
- ⚙️ **`proj_workspace_settings` and `getWorkspaceSettings`** — the thresholds as a rebuildable
  projection with the last claim's provenance kept. A row exists only once somebody has CLAIMED
  something: the defaults are supplied at READ time and the answer carries `provenance: null`, because
  a default is not a claim and there is nobody to attribute it to. Both threshold columns are NULLable
  so a partial claim can say nothing about the other knob — the upsert's
  `COALESCE(EXCLUDED.x, existing.x)` is the partial-update semantics itself, not defensiveness, and a
  stored default would be indistinguishable from a deliberate claim of 7. The reader coalesces on NULL
  and never on falsiness, since `dueSoonDays: 0` is a legal claim. **`auto_close_after_days` (second
  wave, 2026-09-18, Task 6) is the one column here written with a `CASE` instead of that `COALESCE`,
  and the reason is the whole task:** `autoCloseAfterDays` is `number | null`, where `null` is a CLAIM
  ("turn auto-close off") and `undefined` is "this claim does not mention it". `COALESCE` cannot tell
  those apart — the explicit `null` binds as NULL, the COALESCE falls through to the stored value, and
  the claim is **silently ignored**: accepted by the door, committed to the ledger, its provenance
  even updated, with no effect on the setting. So the projection writes
  `auto_close_after_days = CASE WHEN $7 THEN $8 ELSE proj_workspace_settings.auto_close_after_days END`,
  where `$7` is `payload.autoCloseAfterDays !== undefined` — a PRESENCE boolean computed from the
  parsed payload, which is the only place the distinction still exists by the time SQL sees it (Zod
  preserves it; `.optional()` alone would erase it). On INSERT there is no prior value, so the column
  takes the value directly and a fresh row nobody mentioned stores NULL, which IS the default. **The
  regression proof is a mutation and it is exact:** swapping the CASE for a `COALESCE` reddens case
  13.714's clear-to-null assertion (`expected 30 to be null`) and **nothing else in the file** — 11 of
  12 cases stay green. An earlier, cruder version of that mutation (CASE removed but `$7` still bound)
  reddened 9 cases with `could not determine data type of parameter $7`, i.e. a plumbing error rather
  than the semantics; it was discarded as a mutant that does not isolate its property. Blind
  last-writer-wins is safe here
  for a stated reason rather than by luck: the table's key IS the workspace the events are filed
  against, so each key has exactly one totally-ordered writer and canonical replay order is that
  writer's own claim order. **Appended at registration — LAST until Task 6 put `proj_search` after it — and the append is a dependency decision rather than a
  §8 position** — coordination §8's canonical order stops at `proj_visibility` and `proj_contested` is
  already past its end, so "after `proj_visibility`" no longer picks a unique slot; this projection
  reads no other projection's table and none reads its table inside an ingest transaction
  (`getWorkspaceSettings` is a read-time function), so neither adjacency is load-bearing.
  `apps/server/src/projections/workspace-settings.ts`,
  `apps/server/migrations/1788272876259_proj-workspace-settings.sql`,
  `apps/server/migrations/1789400000000_workspace-settings-auto-close.sql`,
  `apps/server/src/projections/index.ts`
- ✅ **Workspace settings tab: stale / due-soon / auto-close days** — backlog/closed spec §8, plan
  ruling R5, second wave, 2026-09-18 (Task 6). A third tab on `/settings` (`?tab=workspace`, sidebar
  link `Workspace`) holding all THREE `workspace.settings_set` knobs in one form — `Stale after` and
  `Due soon within`, which had **no UI anywhere in the product** until now, beside the new
  `Auto-close after`. R5's own reason for one form rather than a lone auto-close field: one form for
  one event is smaller than a knob plus the settings tab it would need next. All three inputs are
  `days`; **the auto-close input carries a SWITCH** (an `Off` checkbox until the 2026-09-18 restyle
  below), because `null` is a claim a user has to be able to MAKE and a blank number box cannot
  distinguish "off" from "not typed yet" — switching it off disables the input and sends `null`. **ONE Save carrying ONLY the changed keys**, diffed against
  what the server answered: Save is disabled when nothing changed (the schema's `.strict().refine`
  refuses the empty claim, so an always-enabled Save would be a button whose only outcome is a
  refusal notice), and `null` is compared by VALUE rather than falsiness — a truthiness check would
  make "turn it off" invisible and the button would never fire, which is the same
  present-versus-null defect the projection's CASE prevents, one layer up. Failures split three ways
  per Ruling 27 (refusal in `gn-refusal--server` as `Refused by the server — <rule>: <reason>`,
  silence, transport failure), the same shape `BacklogStartButton` established. **Non-admins see the
  values read-only with `Only a workspace admin can change these.` and no Save control at all** —
  the server's own gate is `check-permission.ts:652`, and this flag only decides whether the controls
  are OFFERED; showing the values to someone who cannot change them is the honest rendering, a
  disabled control is not. **It reads through a new additive `DataSourceQuery.getWorkspaceSettings`**
  (see the next bullet). Cases 13.716. `apps/web/src/workspace-settings-form.tsx`,
  `apps/web/app/settings/page.tsx`, `apps/web/test/settings-page.test.tsx`
  **Fix round, after the independent review (2026-09-18).** The review found one **Important** defect
  and three mutations that survived the whole suite. **The Important one was real, not a false
  comment:** `onSaved`'s `settings.reload` gave the page new data, but the form's draft and `Off` box
  are `useState` **initialisers** — React runs them once — so the form kept rendering the SUBMITTED
  values, and the sentence promising that a clamped or engine-adjusted claim "becomes visible on this
  screen" was false. Case 13.718 reproduced it (a second read answering `30` left the field on the
  submitted `14`) and is its regression test; the fix, `adoptOnNextLoad`, re-derives the draft from
  the next `settings` the form sees after **its own** successful save — deliberately not "adopt on
  every change", since `useLiveQuery` refetches on every stream move and an unconditional adopt would
  clobber a draft mid-typing. The three survivors each got a case and each case was proved to kill its
  own mutant: **M9** (the `Off` branch claiming `null` unconditionally, live but unexercised because no
  fixture was in the already-off state) dies on **13.719**; **M12** (the `invalid` gate removed from
  both the guard and the button) dies on **13.720**; **M7** (the read door's non-object guard returning
  defaults instead of refusing) dies on **13.721**, whose reachability is stated as a guard rather than
  a witnessed behaviour because no production path to it was found. The same review measured that the
  `invalid` gate's promised signal does not exist — the user sees a greyed-out button and nothing else
  — so that docblock was **rewritten rather than left alone**, and a message naming the offending field
  is recorded as a follow-on instead of implied. Cases 13.718–13.721
  **The UI restyle, 2026-09-18 (owner).** The owner's instruction, verbatim: *"the settings ->
  workspace tab, needs to be a better UI. also have an info icon near the fiends to give a brief
  explanation (hover/focus/click - same witht the projects nav item). save button on a new row. auto
  close on/off -> make it a radio rather than checkbox (check the account page on the styling of the
  radio.) and be mindful of the spacings."* The control question was settled by the owner after two
  wrong guesses: what `/account` draws is a **switch** (`notifications-section.tsx:44-49`), so the
  `Off` box became one. Four things shipped: **(1)** the tab now wears its two siblings' shell —
  `section > header (h2 + summary) > Card`, the shape `ticket-type-list-screen.tsx:331-351` and
  `workflow-list-screen.tsx:183-204` already draw — rather than being a bare form in a bare div.
  (**Re-pointed from `:130-145` on 2026-09-19, while adding the count bullet below. `:130-145` was
  already off — it was the loading effect, not the shell — so this is a fix rather than a shift, and the
  same stale pointer in `apps/web/src/workspace-settings-form.tsx:94` and
  `docs/lanes/executor-2-state.md:807` is **recorded there untouched**, because neither file is in this
  change and the register's rule is that a citation into an untouched file is the controller's to sweep.**);
  **(2)** an **info icon beside each of the three fields**, opening on hover, focus and click and
  closing on Escape, blur, pointer-leave or an outside click — `InfoTip`, whose mechanism is
  `last-project-nav.tsx`'s disclosure reduced to one non-menu panel, deliberately **not** a `title=`
  attribute (`ui.css:322` records the ruling against those); **(3)** **Save moved to its own row**
  below the fields, over a `--gn-border` hairline, asserted as a relationship (the row is not inside
  the field column) rather than by class name; **(4)** deliberate spacing, stated in
  `globals.css`'s `.gn-workspace-settings` docblock with the sibling rule each number came from
  (`0.9rem` section gap, `1.25rem`/`1.5625rem`/`600` h2, `0.85rem` summary, `0.4375rem` label→control)
  plus the three this screen owns (group gap `1.25rem`, label→icon `0.375rem`, input→unit `0.625rem`).
  **The switch's polarity is INVERTED from the box it replaced** — `checked` means ON — which is the
  hazard of that swap: a binding carried across unchanged looks correct and saves the opposite claim,
  so both directions are pinned (**13.895**) and the blank third state is pinned as neither
  (**13.896**). The switch was **extracted, not copied**: the `/account` notification switch's CSS
  moved from `apps/web/app/globals.css` into `packages/ui/src/ui.css` as `.gn-switch`, and both call
  sites now render `@gisik-nokma/ui`'s one `Switch` component — the ruling on the task was *"if the
  notification switch is not factored into something reusable, extract it into a shared component and
  use it in both places rather than copying its CSS; two toggles that drift is the divergence this
  repo keeps paying for."* **None of the save semantics moved**: one `workspace.settings_set` carrying
  only the changed keys, the three refusal sentences, the read-only line, the `CASE`-vs-`COALESCE`
  behaviour and the three ranges are untouched. Cases 13.895–13.898 (web) and 13.899–13.901 (the
  shared primitives). The new `Switch` and `InfoTip` are recorded under their own bullets below.
  `apps/web/src/workspace-settings-form.tsx`, `packages/ui/src/components/switch.tsx`,

- ⚙️ **`reopenedAt`, and the reserved system actor `Auto-close`** — backlog/closed spec §8.2, second
  wave, 2026-09-18 (Task 7). **Two halves of one rule: "an explicit reopen wins"**, and neither half
  is a display fact. `TicketState.reopenedAt` is set by `ticket.reopened` to the ENVELOPE's
  `serverTime` (never the claim's `clientTime` — the sweep compares it against a server-clock cutoff)
  and cleared by ANY `ticket.transitioned`, **including one back into the same terminal state**: the
  sweep measures how long a ticket has sat in the state it is in, and a transition restarts that
  clock, so a flag that survived would exempt a ticket from auto-close forever after one reopen.
  Cleared on the transition rather than derived from the log at sweep time, so the sweep stays one
  column comparison instead of a per-candidate walk. Projected to `proj_tickets.reopened_at
  timestamptz NULL`, read unconditionally by `rowToTicketState`, and **deliberately absent from
  `TicketCard`/`ListRow`** — it is a SWEEP INPUT (Task 8's), not a card field, and putting it on the
  card would change the body of every card-serving route — FIVE route files call `assembleTicketCards`
  (`attention`, `board`, `list`, `my-work`, `search`) — for a value none of them renders.
  `SYSTEM_ACTOR_AUTO_CLOSE =
  '00000000000000000000SYS0AC'` is the id the sweep files its `ticket.closed` under: a ULID, because
  `submittedEventSchema` requires `actorId` to be one and a readable sentinel like `'system'` would be
  refused at the ingest door, so every auto-close would come back `refused` and the failure would
  present as a rules problem rather than as a malformed constant; and a RESERVED constant rather than
  a generated ULID, because "unlikely to collide" is weaker than "cannot", and this id is written to
  the ledger as an actor and read back by every provenance surface. **No user row ever carries it** —
  `newUlid()` cannot mint it and nothing in the product accepts an actor id from a client.
  `actorLabel` (`packages/app-core/src/provenance.ts`) consults `SYSTEM_ACTOR_NAMES` **before** the
  workspace roster, so the sheet reads `Closed by Auto-close on <date>` and **a roster row cannot
  rename a system actor** — a person's name printed over a decision no person made is the claim
  honesty contract 1 exists to refuse. **A RULED REMOVAL, and it is worth reading as one:** the plan's
  Task 7 `Files:` line asked for `t.reopened_at` in `read/ticket-cards.ts`'s `PROJ_TICKET_COLUMNS` and
  a matching `ProjTicketRow` member. Both were added, then measured, then **dropped on the controller's
  ruling** — that constant and that row type exist to feed `assembleTicketCards`, which builds CARDS,
  and this field is a SWEEP INPUT no card carries, so carrying it put one dead column into six routes'
  SELECTs and declared a member nothing dereferenced. The mutation deleting the entry **survived the
  entire server suite** (1,548 passed, byte-identical to baseline), which is what settled it; the
  plan's own Task 8 Step 3 gives the sweep its own SQL, so no reader was waiting for the list to have
  it. The value is not lost — `rowToTicketState` reads it off its own `TicketRow` in
  `projections/tickets.ts`, and the single-ticket route serves it. This is the "carried but never read"
  shape the mapper rule exists to prevent, one layer down: the closed flag was dead in production;
  this would have been dead in the query. Cases 13.722–13.726.
  `packages/domain/src/system-actors.ts`, `packages/domain/src/entity-state.ts`,
  `packages/domain/src/ticket-state.ts`,
  `apps/server/migrations/1789500000000_proj-tickets-reopened-at.sql`,
  `apps/server/src/projections/tickets.ts`,
  `packages/app-core/src/online/mappers.ts`, `packages/app-core/src/provenance.ts`
- ✅ **Auto-close after N days (daemon job `auto-close`, `AUTO_CLOSE_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS`)** —
  backlog/closed spec §8.2, second wave, 2026-09-18 (Task 8). A ticket that has SAT in a terminal state
  for the workspace's `autoCloseAfterDays` is closed by the reserved system actor, and the sweep runs
  on the existing backup daemon beside the notification sweep. **Three things it deliberately is not:**
  it reads "when did this enter its state?" from the LEDGER every run (the last
  `ticket.created`/`ticket.transitioned` event's `server_time`, the same LATERAL join the staleness
  sweep uses) rather than from a stored `entered_at` column that would be a second copy and would drift;
  its cutoff is IST-DAY arithmetic (`istDayBounds(isoDatePlusDays(todayIst, -N)).endUtc`, a strict `<`
  against a half-open interval) rather than `now - N * 86_400_000`, which would make a day count mean
  that many 24-hour spans from whenever the cron fired instead of the calendar a person reads; and it
  closes THROUGH THE INGEST DOOR, one `ticket.closed` per candidate with `origin: 'server'` and
  `actorId: SYSTEM_ACTOR_AUTO_CLOSE`, so the engine's refusals still apply and the ledger records who
  closed what — a direct projection write would be faster and would leave a closed row that no event
  explains, in a table that no longer rebuilds from the ledger. **A ticket somebody explicitly reopened
  is skipped** (`reopened_at IS NULL` in the SELECT, which is what makes Task 7's column earn its
  existence) and so is one already closed; a transition — **including back into the same terminal
  state** — re-arms the clock, so no reopen exempts a ticket forever. Refusals are COUNTED rather than
  assumed away: a candidate the engine refuses (the world moved between the sweep's SELECT and its
  close) stays open, and the run reports it. Idempotent by the ledger, not by a cursor — a ticket it
  closed no longer satisfies `closed_at IS NULL`, so a second run in the same hour selects nothing.
  **A parent with an open child is not a candidate** (E6-8, 2026-09-21, case 13.1167): a republish that
  promotes a kept state to terminal can put a parent there over open work without a transition, and the
  SELECT carries a `NOT EXISTS` over non-terminal children mirroring the engine's own new close refusal
  (4.55) — so no envelope is built and no nightly "refused" is logged for a world that did not move; the
  engine holds the ledger either way. Cases 13.727–13.731, 13.1167. `apps/server/src/auto-close/sweep.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/ops/backup-daemon-main.ts`
- ⚙️ **`proj_search` — the full-text projection** — one row per ticket holding its title,
  description and comments as PLAIN TEXT, plus a `tsvector` GENERATED from all three and weighted
  A/B/C so ranking can prefer a title hit. Fed by `ticket.created` (title), `ticket.field_set`
  (`title`, and `description` through `docToPlainText`) and `comment.added` (appended,
  newline-separated, in the ticket's own `seq` order, each rendered by `docToPlainText` so a mention
  indexes as `@label` and is findable by the name that was shown). A comment that renders to no text
  adds nothing — not even the separator, which would otherwise leave a trailing newline no comment
  accounts for; a title claim whose value is not a string is ignored rather than coerced, since the
  door admits any value and `SET title = $2` would otherwise write a number nobody typed. The text
  columns are kept beside the index because a `tsvector` cannot be read back into its words and the
  search response carries a snippet. **It stores EVERY ticket** — visibility is a read-time decision
  (`visibleTicketsWhere` against `proj_visibility`), because filtering at index time would put a
  permission decision inside a rebuildable table and go stale the moment an audience changed without
  a new ticket event. The configuration is `'simple'`, deliberately and at a stated cost: the
  audience writes in more than one language, so no English stemming, and `return` therefore does not
  match `returns` (flagged in the plan's Open questions; the query side names the same configuration
  and both must move together). Deterministic without a position guard: `apply` reads no table at all
  — not another projection's, not its own — and touches only the event's own ticket row, so
  per-entity `seq` order fully determines it, and the `tsv` column is generated by Postgres rather
  than written here. **`tsvector` is a new projection column-type class in this repo and was proven
  against the verifier by EXECUTION rather than argued from the type name**: `verifyProjections`
  diffs live against a shadow rebuild with `EXCEPT`, which needs an equality operator on every column
  — the whole reason `json` is banned as a projection column here. **Registered LAST, and the append
  is a dependency decision rather than a coordination §8 position**, on the same grounds as
  `proj_workspace_settings`: §8's order ends at `proj_visibility`. This projection does already have
  a reader — `compileFilterSpec`'s text clause — but it is a READ-TIME caller on a request path
  rather than a handler inside an ingest transaction, so it creates no adjacency.
  `apps/server/src/projections/search.ts`,
  `apps/server/migrations/1788278094725_proj-search.sql`,
  `apps/server/src/projections/index.ts`
- ⚙️ **Shared ledger-seeding test helpers** — `makeCommitted` / `applyCommitted` / `resetEntitySeqs`,
  the fixture every Plan 5 read-model task seeds through. `makeCommitted`'s per-entity `seq` restarts
  at 1 for each entity, exactly as `nextSeq` assigns it, with the per-workspace `workspaceSeq` cursor
  climbing beside it, exactly as `nextWorkspaceSeq` does — a process-monotonic counter in either place
  would still be unique, still satisfy both of the ledger's unique constraints, and still hide a
  handler that confused an entity's history with its workspace's stream. Both clocks default to a
  fresh instant per call so a test can tell WHICH claim last wrote a row. `applyCommitted` commits one
  transaction per event through the live registry, which is the unit ingest commits in.
  `apps/server/test/helpers/apply.ts`
- ⚙️ **`visibleTicketsWhere` — the read visibility table as one SQL predicate** — the clause every
  set-based read filters through (list, board, search, attention, My Work), against `proj_visibility`
  joined as `v`. It is an EXTRACTION, not a new expression: the SQL half of this table already sat
  inline inside `listVisibleTickets`, so the clause moved out and that function became a caller —
  there is no parallel SQL copy left beside it. Stated exactly, because the honest version is smaller
  than the tidy one: this removed a THIRD copy and did not produce a single source of truth. Two
  expressions of one rule remain — `canSeeResolved` in TypeScript, this one in SQL, kept because the
  SQL is what makes a list one round trip rather than a workspace-sized read filtered in memory — and
  what stops them drifting is an agreement test that compares an exact id set per viewer AND
  cross-checks `canSee` ticket by ticket. With one limit now stated rather than left implied: the
  cross-check is STRUCTURALLY BLIND wherever both implementations ignore the same input — for a
  guest, neither consults `eff.projects`, so they agree whatever the fixture holds — and there the
  only thing that discriminates is a fixture putting the viewer in the state the branch could get
  wrong. A guest on a project roster is that fixture, and it is what makes an over-permissive guest
  branch (one that gained the member clause's project disjunct) fail rather than pass the suite. A non-member compiles to `FALSE` and an owner to `TRUE`, so
  the predicate carries NO tenancy of its own and every caller must supply its own
  `workspace_id = $n`; the parameters are built inside the branches, since a value bound for a branch
  that returns a constant would have no `$n` to reference it. The role is walked by a bare `switch`
  with no `default`, which is measured rather than described: adding a fifth `WorkspaceRole` raises
  TS2366 here and in `can-see.ts`, while the if-chain it replaced reddened only `can-see.ts` and
  silently handed the new role the member branch. The mode side cannot have that guard — the modes are
  string literals inside SQL, invisible to tsc — so a fourth mode fails CLOSED and the agreement test
  is what would catch it. `apps/server/src/read/visible-where.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/visibility/visible-tickets.ts`

  role must be resolved in — so a route never trusts a workspace id the caller also supplied, which is

  planted hidden ticket the owner alone is named in (with a confidential comment and a due date), and
  a guest-shared ticket. Like `applyCommitted`, it ENUMERATES what it does not contain rather than
  calling itself simplified — no workspace-mode ticket, no admin, no second project, no revoked
  membership, no attachments or workspace settings, one workspace only — because those absences are
  the exact shape of what the tests built on it cannot catch, and each read task must seed for itself

- ⚙️ **Read-model view types** — the shapes every `/v1` read route serves and Plans 6/9/10 render
  through the `DataSource`: `TicketCard`, `StateProvenance`, `TransitionCause`, `TicketRollup`,
  `TicketDueDate`/`DueDateClaim`, and the response envelopes (`BoardResponse`, `ListResponse`,
  `SearchResponse`, `MyWorkResponse`, `AttentionResponse` and their parts). The standard they are held
  to is that **no field may collapse two different facts into one value** — never-claimed, claimed
  then withdrawn, and withheld-from-this-viewer all stay tellable apart, and where a type cannot tell
  two of them apart it SAYS so in the type rather than in a docblock. Two fields are that rule applied
  rather than described: `TicketDueDate` is a three-arm union (claimed / cleared / never-claimed) with
  **no null arm**, because `ticket.field_set` with `value: null` is an attributed clearing whose actor
  and clocks the reducer keeps on purpose, and a `DueDateClaim | null` would give that act the same
  value as a ticket nobody ever dated; and `TicketRollup.uncategorizedChildren` counts children whose
  state category nothing knows, so a "5 of 8 done" is never rendered off evidence for only six of
  them. `StateProvenance.cause` is `null` without such an arm, and the type says why: every state was
  claimed by exactly one event, so "the claim named no cause" is a complete statement about a claim
  that exists. `AttentionResponse.settings` is the third: it carries the whole `WorkspaceSettings`,
  provenance included, rather than a bare `{staleDays, dueSoonDays}` pair, because that pair gives
  "nobody has configured this workspace, so 7 is the default" and "somebody claimed 7" the same value
  — and `getWorkspaceSettings` had already kept them apart one layer down. `TicketCard.closed` (backlog/
  closed spec §3.3, 2026-09-17; Task 4) is the newest field held to the same standard: REQUIRED, unlike
  `TicketState.closed?`, because every card producer is this task's own code and there is no legacy
  literal predating the flag to spare — a reader spells `state.closed ?? null` at the boundary instead of
  the wire type inheriting the domain type's optionality.
  `packages/domain/src/read-models.ts`
- ⚙️ **`stateProvenanceFor` / `latestWorkflowDefs` / `blockedStateKeys` / `assembleTicketCards`** — the
  server-side readers that turn `proj_tickets` rows into cards. Provenance is the claim that produced
  each ticket's CURRENT state — the latest `ticket.transitioned`, or `ticket.created` if never
  transitioned — batched as one `DISTINCT ON … ORDER BY entity_id, seq DESC` over the ledger, carrying
  the actor, BOTH clocks and the reopen `cause`. An id with no claim is ABSENT from the map, never
  mapped to an anonymous one, and the assembler THROWS on the absence: a projected ticket whose state
  nobody claimed means `proj_tickets` and the ledger disagree. It throws on a missing or non-string
  title claim for the same reason — `''` would be a title nobody typed sitting exactly where a real
  one goes. `latestWorkflowDefs` is **workspace-scoped** (the shipped reader requires it, ruling P14)
  and `blockedStateKeys` keys on `` `${workflowId}:${stateId}` `` because a state id is unique only
  within its workflow. `assembleTicketCards` also folds `closed_at`/`closed_by` into `TicketCard.closed`
  (backlog/closed spec §3.1/§3.3, 2026-09-17; Task 4; case 13.573) — `PROJ_TICKET_COLUMNS` selects the
  pair, and both NULL maps to `null`, the same fold `rowToTicketState` makes over the same two columns.
  **`priority` is ALWAYS a claim (spec 2026-09-22, Task 3)** — `priorityOf(row)` beside `dueDateOf`, and a
  row with no `priority` key THROWS naming the ticket and the repair (`rebuild:projection proj_tickets`)
  rather than defaulting to P2: an absent claim after the built-in landed means the row's `proj_tickets`
  predates the reducer that writes it, not that nobody claimed one — the same reasoning `title`'s throw
  already follows. Cases 7.268–7.269.
  `apps/server/src/read/state-provenance.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/read/workflow-defs.ts`, `apps/server/src/read/ticket-cards.ts`

- ✅ **`GET /v1/projects/:projectId/board`** — one project's board. Columns are the states of the
  workflows **in use by the tickets this caller may see** — not every workflow the workspace has
  defined — with every state of a used workflow present whether or not anybody is in it, ordered by
  workflow id then by the order the publisher authored the states, cards by ticket id. Two workflows
  on one board sit side by side, so a state id they both use is two distinct columns and a card never
  appears under the other workflow's copy of its own state. The `blocked`
  flag is read off the definition, never derived from a category: the seeded `waiting` state is
  `active` AND blocked while a second workflow's `waiting` is `active` and not. Every column also
  names the **published definition version** its `name`, `category` and `blocked` were read out of
  (`workflowVersion`, Plan 6 Task 11 / ruling P25 clause 1) — the field the client keys its board
  groups on, and the one that stops two columns from different definitions being rendered as one
  group. A STRAGGLER column — a `(workflow, state)` no published definition names — carries
  `workflowVersion: 0`, which no publisher can mint (`workflowDefSchema` is `version ≥ 1`, and the
  only writer of `proj_workflows` on the product path parses every payload through it before
  inserting), because stamping it with the workflow's latest version would file a state under a
  definition it was never folded into — and would put it in the same group as that definition's real
  columns under the key `views/board.tsx:28` renders by, once an adapter regroups the server's flat
  `columns` into `BoardGroup`s. No such adapter exists yet (case 7.188), which is why the value is
  settled before one is written rather than after. Cards are `TicketCard`s, so each unfolds to
  who claimed its state and when by both clocks, and a parent carries its four-field rollup. The

  and not restated. **Never shows backlog or closed tickets (backlog/closed spec §3.2, 2026-09-17)** —

  NOT on the project passes the gate and gets **200 with an empty board** — the gate asks about the
  workspace, so a project's existence is not a secret from somebody already inside the tenancy, and
  the emptiness is the visibility predicate answering rather than the door.

- ✅ **`GET /v1/projects/:projectId/tickets` — the project list read** — one project's tickets as a
  filtered, grouped, keyset-paged flat list, behind the board's door and the same visibility
  predicate. It CONSUMES rather than re-expresses: `visibleTicketsWhere` for Plan 4's decision table,
  `compileFilterSpec` for every actor-supplied byte, `latestWorkflowDefs` (workspace-scoped, ruling
  P14) for state names. `filter` is URL-encoded JSON validated by `filterSpecSchema`; `groupBy`
  defaults to `flat`; `limit` defaults to 50 and caps at 200; pagination is keyset by `ticket_id`
  with `cursor` = the last id of the previous page. Hierarchy is children-by-parent-query:
  `parentId=<id>` answers direct children, `parentId=root` answers roots, absent answers the project;
  children are not inlined. Grouping is applied PER PAGE, so a key may recur on a later page and
  clients merge by `key` — the alternative would make a page boundary depend on the grouping, so one
  cursor would mean different things under different `groupBy` values. **Grouping by `epic` resolves
  on the epic RANK read from `BUILTIN_TICKET_TYPE_SEEDS`, never on the id `'epic'`**, so a workspace
  that renamed its top rung ("Initiative") gets its own headings (owner sign-off 2026-08-20).
  **The epic walk carries the visibility predicate and the tenancy clause**, which the plan's version
  did not: a group's key is a ticket id and its LABEL IS THAT TICKET'S TITLE, so a walk that climbed
  the parent chain without asking Plan 4's question would hand a caller who may see a child the title
  of an ancestor they may not — reachable rather than theoretical, because a child authors its own
  audience and stops inheriting. An invisible link STOPS the walk (the caller gets `no-epic`) rather
  than being climbed over, which would report a grouping whose reason the caller cannot see; the
  title is read inside the same walk rather than by a second unscoped query. Spec line 117's

  every live ticket in it vanished from the response with nothing thrown. `toString` was safe there

headline (`ts_headline(cfg, s.title || ' — ' || s.description || ' — ' || s.comments, …) AS snippet`), so **which field matched was not recoverable**, and the client REFUSED the answer rather than invent it (`mapSearchHits(_raw): never`, the last entry in `SERVING_GAPS`). **⚠ The distinction was in the data all along:** `proj_search` stores the three columns separately and its generated `tsv` already weights them apart (`setweight(… 'A') || setweight(… 'B') || setweight(… 'C')`). **No column, no migration — the SELECT was throwing away what the projection had kept, and the fix is the SELECT.** The route now computes `matchedIn` with **one `@@` per column** in a `CASE`: three `ts_headline` calls would answer the same question at three times the cost and give the snippet three ways to disagree with the field, and `setweight(…) @@ q` is equivalent to `to_tsvector(…) @@ q` — **weights affect RANKING, never MATCHING** — so the three predicates partition the very vector the `WHERE` already tested. **⚠ `matchedIn` is ONE value, so the precedence is a decision: title → description → comment**, the order the weights already imply (A, B, C), stated in the `CASE` so it is a rule rather than an accident of how the expression was written. **⚠ And the snippet stays COMBINED, deliberately:** narrowing the headline to the matched column was the easy way to make the field "obvious" and it strips a comment's words out of the window, which is the feature's reason to exist — a comment is where people put what they would not put in a title. **The un-refusal landed in the same change set**: `mapSearchHits` answers, `SERVING_GAPS` is now EMPTY (the entry is deleted, not emptied — *an entry claiming a method refuses ALWAYS is false the moment it maps*), and **the domain's own `SearchHit` gained the field**, which the compiler had not required because `rows.map(…)` is not a fresh object literal in that position. Cases `16.32`–`16.37`; two existing cases were **inverted rather than deleted** (7.189's rule) — app-core `3.39` and the server contract's *"DATA GAP — `matchedIn` is on no hit"*. `apps/server/src/routes/search.ts`, `packages/app-core/src/online/mappers.ts`, `packages/domain/src/read-models.ts`
