  round-tripped in the same case to hold the rule at "what the store can hold". An unset preference reads as `EMPTY_PREFERENCES` and the collapse is
  deliberate and typed: unlike `proj_workspace_settings`, "never saved" and "saved empty" are one
  answer, because there is nobody to attribute and no screen that could show the difference. The door
  is the shared one — 401 for no session and for a forged bearer, 400 `invalid_query` for a missing,
  empty or repeated `workspaceId`, the frozen `READ_NOT_FOUND_BODY` 404 for a non-member, and
  membership resolved BEFORE the body is parsed, so an unauthorised caller's payload is never read
  and their 404 does not depend on what they sent. There is no role gate above membership: a guest
  writes their own preferences like anyone else. Four malformed requests stay distinguishable — bad
  bytes are Fastify's `FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_JSON_BODY`, no content type is 415, a body past the 1 MiB
  limit is 413 (measured, and the ONLY bound on how much a caller may store — no second cap was
  invented), and a parsed-but-wrong document is this route's own `invalid_preferences`.
  `packages/domain/src/preferences.ts`, `apps/server/src/preferences/store.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/routes/preferences.ts`,
  `apps/server/migrations/1788295700000_user-preferences.sql`, `apps/server/src/app.ts`

- ⚙️ **The `WS /v1/stream` protocol** — `subscribeFrameSchema` (the only client frame: `{type:'subscribe', workspaceId, afterSeq}`, strict, the workspace a ULID rather than the plan's `min(1)` string because it is actor-supplied and becomes a lookup key), `ServerStreamFrame` (`event` / `purge` / `scope-revoked` / `caught-up` / `error`), `STREAM_ERROR_CODES`, `STREAM_CLOSE_CODES` (1008 / 1013 / 1011) and `ledgerEventSchema`. **The event frame carries a `LedgerEvent`, not the plan's `EventEnvelope`**: `EventEnvelope.seq` is the per-entity counter and restarts at 1 for every new entity, so a client resuming by it skips each new entity's early events, and `visibleEventsFor` selects on `workspace_seq` — the resume cursor is `workspaceSeq`, and a frame without it is one no client can resume from. It is a widening, so a consumer typed to `EventEnvelope` still compiles. `scope-revoked.projectId` is typed `?: never` because neither emitter produces one; the day one does, the hub's mapping stops compiling rather than silently widening a project's loss into a workspace's. `serverStreamFrameSchema` is published for the plans that will MOCK this protocol (6, 9, 10) rather than for safety — nothing here parses a server frame — so a fake that omits `workspaceSeq` or invents a `projectId` fails against the same shape the server is held to. **Where the strictness stops:** the outer frame object of every member is `.strict()`, but the ENVELOPE inside the event frame is not — `ledgerEventSchema` is `eventEnvelopeSchema.and(…)` over a non-strict `z.object` — so an unknown envelope key is silently STRIPPED rather than refused, and `payload` is `z.unknown()` by design. A consumer that needs the envelope closed must `.strict()` it on its own side; the server's own frames are held tighter than the schema by the recording socket in the stream tests, which compares the parse against the bytes. `packages/domain/src/stream-frames.ts`, `packages/domain/src/ledger-event.ts`
- ⚙️ **The subscription hub — the first fan-out, and therefore the first disclosure surface** — `createStreamHub`, one subscription per `(socket, workspace)`, several workspaces multiplexed on one socket. **Catch-up and the live tail are the SAME drain** of `visibleEventsFor(pool, sub.userId, …)`: nothing is broadcast to a workspace, every frame exists because Plan 4's filter yielded an item for that subscriber on that drain, and the hub holds no second opinion about who may see what — the two paths cannot disagree because they are one path. `onEventCommitted` reads and sends nothing; it marks the committed workspace's subscriptions dirty and wakes their pumps, and a subscription is registered BEFORE its first drain so a commit landing mid-catch-up is re-drained rather than lost — while a subscription its OWN drain ended is not re-drained, `dirty` or not, so a commit landing during the drain that revokes a scope costs no second full ledger scan. Narrowing is honoured by construction (every drain re-resolves the reader's role), and `scope-revoked` ENDS its subscription — the instruction means "empty this scope", there is no coherent resume cursor after it, and it is the only thing bounding the instruction for an ex-member whose cursor can never advance. A `scope-revoked` naming a project is refused rather than widened. A consumer past `maxBufferedBytes` is closed 1013 because the ledger, not the socket queue, is the durable buffer. `settled()` makes the fan-out awaitable without a clock (a heartbeat is Task 15's); `stats()` is the operational read and the leak detector — `dropSocket` empties the per-workspace index too, not only the per-socket one. The hub authorizes NOBODY: a stranger drains nothing and is handed back their own cursor, and the `not-a-member` error frame belongs to the route. `apps/server/src/stream/hub.ts`

- ✅ **`WS /v1/stream` — the route, and the only door the stream has** — `registerStreamRoute`, registered in `app.ts` beside the hub it fans out through (created there, next to the ingest service whose `onEventCommitted` it listens to, and released on the app's `onClose`). The hub authorizes nobody by design, so everything that keeps the wrong person off the stream is here. **The HTTP-Origin check now covers this handshake too (E6-15, cases 13.1077–13.1080):** `/v1/stream` is a `GET`, which every other read in this server is exempt from the check for, but a WebSocket upgrade is exempt from the same-origin policy that makes those reads safe — a foreign page could open one under the victim's ambient cookie and receive their live event stream (cross-site WebSocket hijacking, the round's most security-relevant finding). `httpOriginRefused` (`http-origin.ts`) now checks `STREAM_ROUTE_URL` by name, for any method, ahead of `requireSession`, so a forged-origin handshake never reaches the socket.
  - **The session is resolved at the UPGRADE, and a refusal happens before a socket exists.** MEASURED, not assumed (2026-09-02, `@fastify/websocket` 11.3.0): `preHandler` DOES run on a `websocket: true` route, and a reply from it refuses the handshake with an ordinary HTTP response — no socket is created at all. An anonymous caller and a forged bearer both draw the same `401 {"error":"unauthenticated"}`, byte-identical to each other down to `content-length`. That is the strong form of the refusal, so the plan's `close(1008)` fallback is deliberately NOT shipped: it is unreachable, and an unreachable guard is one no test can tell from its own deletion. A route registered without the preHandler still fails CLOSED — an undefined user resolves no membership and every subscribe is answered `not-a-member`.
  - **Membership is checked per SUBSCRIBE, not per connection**, because one socket multiplexes several workspaces. A null effective role draws one frozen `not-a-member` frame, and a workspace that does not exist draws the SAME one — the frames differ only in the workspace id the caller themselves sent, so there is no existence oracle, and the socket is not closed either way. A member with nothing visible gets a subscription and an empty catch-up, which is the stream's form of the read routes' *200 with an empty result*.
  - **A per-user connection budget** (`maxSocketsPerUser`, default 8), enforced as a second preHandler AFTER `requireSession` — the order is load-bearing, since a budget keyed before the session keys every caller on `undefined` and becomes one shared global bucket. Over budget is `429 {"error":"too_many_connections"}` at the handshake, and the budget is returned when the socket closes. **What the bound does not do is stated where it is written**: the count is read in the hook and incremented in the handler, so a burst of simultaneous handshakes can land a few over the cap — deliberately, because a preHandler-held reservation trades a coarse bound for a leak whose failure mode is a user locked out of their own stream. The other half of the same question: a connection's SUBSCRIPTION count is bounded by how many workspaces the caller actually belongs to, since the hub refuses a duplicate per workspace and this route refuses one for a workspace they are not in. **A 16 KiB `maxPayload`** bounds the client frame: the only legal frame is under a hundred bytes, `ws` defaults to 100 MB, and a frame is fully buffered before anything can call it malformed.
  - **A heartbeat driven by the INJECTED clock**, not by counting ticks: a peer is terminated after strictly more than two heartbeat intervals of measured silence, so two pings genuinely go unanswered first. Coalesced `setInterval` callbacks after an event-loop stall would otherwise kill a healthy peer whose pongs were queued behind them. This is the one and only caller of `StreamSocket.terminate()` — Task 14 declared it and named this task as its owner — and it is deliberately a terminate rather than a close: a peer that has answered nothing for three intervals is not going to read a close code. Both the tick (`schedule`) and the clock (`now`) are seams, so the two directions are tested without a sleep — and the PRODUCTION scheduler behind the seam (`realScheduler`, what every app that injects nothing runs on) is covered in its own right, on fake timers for the interval and the stop and on real ones for the `unref` that keeps a heartbeat from being the reason a process will not exit.
  - **`bad-message` and `not-a-member` are the route's frames**, produced by nothing in Task 14. Junk, a non-ULID workspace id, an unknown key, a negative cursor and a prototype-polluting body all draw `bad-message` and the socket keeps serving; a duplicate subscribe draws the hub's `already-subscribed` framed here. A refused frame subscribes **nothing** — the hub validates no workspace id of its own, so keeping an unvalidated actor-supplied string out of its Map keys is this route's job alone.
  - **A CLIENT fault and a SERVER fault get different answers, and the server fault gets the hub's.** A frame the route could not parse or validate is the client's, and is answered `bad-message` on an open socket. A THROW inside frame handling is not — it says nothing about what the client sent, and telling them otherwise leaves them with no recourse but to stop sending a frame they sent correctly — so it closes `1011 stream-error`, exactly as `hub.ts` closes a drain that threw. `STREAM_ERROR_CODES` is deliberately not extended for it: that enum is the protocol Plans 6, 9 and 10 mock, and a fourth code invented to avoid a close would be a protocol change.
  - **Resource lifecycle**: on close or error the heartbeat is stopped, the budget returned, and the socket dropped from the hub, so no subscription outlives its connection. `app.streamHub` is decorated onto the instance, which is both the operational read and the leak detector. **A subscribe whose socket left during the membership check is refused rather than registered**: frame handling suspends at exactly one point — the membership round trip — and a close delivered inside that window runs the teardown before the subscribe, so the subscription that followed could never be dropped by anything and the returned budget slot meant the leak was bounded at zero. Both a `torn` flag set by the teardown and the transport's own `readyState` are checked immediately before subscribing, because the socket reaches CLOSING when the close frame arrives and only reaches teardown later.
  - **A registration hazard worth knowing**: `app.register(websocket)` followed by a top-level `app.get(…, {websocket:true})` SILENTLY degrades to a plain HTTP route — the plugin's `onRoute` hook does not exist yet, `websocket: true` is never read, the handler is called with `(request, reply)`, and the upgrade dies in a 500 with no warning. The route is therefore declared inside its own `app.register(...)`.
  `apps/server/src/stream/routes.ts`, `apps/server/src/app.ts`, `apps/server/test/helpers/stream.ts`, `apps/server/test/stream/stream-route.test.ts`

- ⚙️ **The attention strip proved with `TZ` varied — the first such proof in this repository.** The
  strip is asked from `UTC`, `Asia/Kolkata` and `America/Los_Angeles` against a frozen clock thirty
  days after the ticket entered its state **and pinned to 20:00Z**, and the whole body must be
  identical in each. The pinned time of day is the load-bearing part: at 20:00Z the three zones
  disagree about which calendar page it is — 01:30 the next day in IST — which is the window
  `read-models.ts` names as "the whole Indian evening", and an instant inherited from the wall clock
  spends most of the day outside it. **Measured, not merely asserted:** making the strip's "today"
  process-timezone-dependent — `formatUtcDay` (`packages/domain/src/ist-day.ts`) reading
  `getDate()`/`getMonth()`/`getFullYear()` instead of their UTC forms — reddens this and nothing
  else, because the three zones then answer different `daysInFlight`. The expected count is
  **computed at run time rather than hard-coded**: pinning the frozen instant to 20:00Z makes the
  IST-correct answer 30 or 31 depending on where in the Indian evening the entry instant fell, so
  naming either as *the* answer would be a fixture that is right on some runs and wrong on others.
  Measured
  across all 48 test files on an earlier `main`: zero vary `TZ`, seven are clock-sensitive, all seven
  omit it — and both this machine and the product are `Asia/Kolkata`, so every day-boundary proof in
  the repo was consistent with the property being false. The zone switch carries its own control
  (`new Date(0).getHours()` is 0 under UTC and 5 under IST) so the three-way equality cannot pass on an
  inert knob, and the expected IST day is computed independently of `istDayOf` rather than imported
  from the code under test. `apps/server/test/integration/real-door-round-trip.test.ts`

Same `readList` as the project route, so visibility (`visibleTicketsWhere`), filters, `"me"` and groupings are identical; the one scope difference is that tickets of ARCHIVED projects are left out (a deleted project's already are). A non-member is the project route's 404, never an empty list. **It is `/ticket-list`, not `/tickets`:** `GET /v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/tickets` is the older Plan 4 visibility list (`{ tickets }`, 200-empty for an outsider) and is unchanged. `apps/server/src/routes/list.ts` (`readList`, `answerList`); cases `7.707`–`7.711`.


## 9. Editor, documents & attachments

*Plan 7's client half. §8 is reserved for Plan 6 and is deliberately absent — the coordination doc
assigns `Features.md` sections one per implementation plan, so numbering is claimed from that table
rather than taken next-free. (§6 and §7 were named here as absent too; both have since been opened,
by Plan 4 and by Plan 5 Task 2, and the reservation logic that kept them out is unchanged.)*

- ⚙️ **Document schema v2** — `DOC_SCHEMA_VERSION = 2`, `emptyDoc()`, `isDocJson()`, and
  `VersionedDocument`, a replacement for Tiptap's `Document` that carries `schemaVersion` on the doc
  node. The vocabulary is CLOSED: a set-equality test over node and mark types fails when an extension
  adds one, so a new vocabulary item cannot arrive unnoticed. A version-1 document contains none of
  v2's nodes and renders unchanged under v2. `packages/editor/src/doc.ts`,
  `packages/editor/src/schema/versioned-document.ts`
- ⚙️ **One extension set for every client** — `buildEditorExtensions(options)` / `EditorSchemaOptions`
  (`queryUsers`, `resolveAttachmentUrl`, `placeholder`, `readOnly`, `queryNotes`, `resolveNoteTitle`,
  `previewNote`, `onNavigateNote`). The single origin of schema v2:
  web, desktop, the RN webview bundle and every test build their list here, so the schema cannot drift
  between clients. Everything StarterKit contributes that v2 does not name is switched off by an
  explicit `false` rather than left to a default — `document` because it is replaced, `link` because it
  is reconfigured, `underline` because it is not this product's vocabulary.
  `packages/editor/src/schema/extensions.ts`
- ✅ **Task lists in every document** — `[ ] ` / `[x] ` at a line start; schema is version 2 **The checkbox is aligned and styled (owner screenshot 2026-09-29):** it centres on the item's FIRST text line (label `1lh` tall, the item's paragraph margins zeroed — measured 8.5px high before, 0.5px after), is a custom 1rem accent-on-check box inside a 24px hit area with hover, `:focus-visible` and a `neo` sunken coat instead of the native blue one, and a done item is muted, never struck through (owner). The comment body's read-only task item wears the same box (`apps/web/app/globals.css`). **A POSTED comment's task list draws like the composer's (owner screenshot 2026-09-29):** the item is `input + span > p`, one level deeper than the body's `> *` margin reset reached, so the paragraph kept 17px margins (row 56px, box 16.41px above the text, items far apart) — `ui.css` now zeroes the span's blocks, the row is 1.5rem tall at least and rows abut, and the box is nudged by (line-height − box) / 2; measured on a posted comment against the composer, heights 24/44/24 in both, gap 0 in both, alignment 0px vs the composer's +1px (`packages/ui/src/ui.css`, `apps/web/app/globals.css`). **Dark mode and the posted row (controller pass 2026-09-29):** a done item's colour is `--gn-text-subtle`, not `-muted` — `-muted` measures 1.01:1 from the body text in dark (1.28:1 in light), so a done item was not dimmer at all; `-subtle` is ≥ 2.16:1 from it and ≥ 5.28:1 on the surface in all six style × theme blocks — and `neo`'s unchecked box keeps `--gn-border-strong` (5.37:1 dark, 4.39:1 light; WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1), because neo's sunken surface IS its surface and the coat alone drew no edge. A posted row now starts where the composer's does (box 4px, text 32px; was 0 and 23.2), and each posted checkbox is named by its own text span (`aria-labelledby`, id unique per comment via `renderCommentBody`'s `idPrefix`) (`apps/web/app/globals.css`, `packages/app-core/src/views/comment-body.tsx`, `comments-thread.tsx`). Cases `9.360`–`9.362`, `9.365`–`9.366`, `9.480`–`9.484`.
- ✅ **A POSTED comment's bullet and numbered lists are tightened (owner, 2026-09-29):** a list item is `li > p`, one level deeper than the body's `> *` margin reset reached, so every paragraph kept 17px margins — items 17px apart (pitch 39px for one 22px line) plus a 2.4px `li + li` gap. `ui.css` now zeroes an item's blocks (a nested list, quote or second paragraph keeps the body's 0.4rem), zeroes a quote's paragraphs (their margins had collapsed through it), and sets items 0.25rem apart — the owner's choice, deliberately tighter than the composer's 0.5rem paragraph margin; the task list is excluded by `:not(.gn-comment__list--tasks)`. Measured in a real browser on a posted comment (item text 22px tall, wrapped item 88px): pitch 26px between single-line items in a bullet and a numbered list, gap 4px — was 39px / 17px before the list fix, and the composer draws 30px / 8px (`packages/ui/src/ui.css`). Case `9.367`.
  (`DOC_SCHEMA_VERSION`), version-1 documents render unchanged.

  clicks in one React batch both read a pre-commit `false` and both got through, measured as two

- ⚙️ **`ObjectStore`, and where attachment bytes actually live** — a three-verb interface
  (`put`/`getStream`/`delete`) behind which `LocalDiskStore` (dev/test) and `S3ObjectStore`
  (S3-compatible, path-style addressing default `true` so MinIO and R2 work unconfigured) are
  interchangeable; `createObjectStoreFromEnv` selects between them and, on a `local` misconfiguration or
  an unrecognised `OBJECT_STORE` value, names every missing S3 variable in one refusal rather than one
  per restart. Object keys are traversal-proof by CONSTRUCTION, not by blocklist: `w/<ulid>/a/<ulid>`
  segments admit only letters, digits, `_` and `-` — no dot is a legal character in any segment, so `.`
  and `..` are unrepresentable rather than merely refused. `LocalDiskStore.put` writes to a temp file and
  `rename`s into place, so a torn write can never surface as a readable half-object. A fourth verb,
  **`list(prefix?)`**, was added for Plan 11's orphan sweep: `LocalDiskStore.list` walks `rootDir`
  structurally rather than by a traversal check — `readdir(..., {withFileTypes:true})` reports a symlink's
  `Dirent` as neither `isDirectory()` nor `isFile()`, so the walk recurses into real directories and reports
  real files only, never following a symlink planted inside the root — and `S3ObjectStore.list` PAGINATES
  via `ContinuationToken` rather than trusting one response, since `ListObjectsV2` truncates at 1000 keys
  regardless of bucket size. `apps/server/src/attachments/object-store.ts`, `local-disk-store.ts`,
  `s3-store.ts`, `store-config.ts`
- ⚙️ **`ops:sweep-orphans` — the bytes an upload can leave behind with no row naming them** —
  `sweepOrphanObjects` walks the attachment store's own `list()` against a UNION of the two things that can
  name an attachment id: the `attachments` table row, and a ledger `attachment.added` event
  (`payload->>'attachmentId'`, the same shape `evidence-gate.ts` already reads). The union is deliberate and
  the more conservative of the two possible readings — **the web client does not currently post the ledger
  event at all** — ⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-09-21: this is no longer true, and this change set is what made it false.** The comment composer now posts `attachment.added` when an upload is attached to a comment (`TicketSheet.emitAttachmentAdded`, `packages/app-core/src/views/ticket-sheet.tsx`), so the event IS produced — though only on that one path, and the union below is still the right design for the reason it gives**, so treating it as the only survival signal would flag nearly every live attachment as an
  orphan, while treating the table row as the only signal risks the opposite the day some other path
  registers an attachment through the ledger alone. Keys are only ever considered if they have the exact
  shape `w/<workspaceId>/a/<id>`; anything else — including a torn-write `.tmp-<pid>-<ms>` leftover, which
  splits into four segments shaped exactly like a real key — is recorded as `unrecognizedShape` and NEVER
  touched, at any age, because handing such a key to `store.delete` would throw on the store's own key
  validator and take the whole sweep down. An unnamed, recognized object survives for
  `ORPHAN_OBJECT_RETENTION_MS` (30 days, matching the user-preferences sweep's constant) before a live run
  deletes it; a dry run reports the identical list with nothing actually removed. **Known ceiling, the same
  class 13.34 already names for `readLedger`:** `store.list()` is called unprefixed and materialises every
  object in memory before the loop starts, so peak memory scales with object COUNT rather than anything
  bounded — a constant-memory sweep needs a paged/streaming `list()`, a change to the `ObjectStore` contract
  itself, not fixed here. **KNOWN GAP, OWNED HERE
  RATHER THAN FIXED**: `deploy/do/app.yaml`'s `backup` worker env block does not yet include `OBJECT_STORE`
  or `OBJECT_STORE_S3_BUCKET` — it carries only the five `OBJECT_STORE_S3_*` variables the SEPARATE backup
  object-sink needs, under a different bucket variable. Without those two added to that worker's block,
  `createObjectStoreFromEnv` in the deployed worker silently falls back to a LOCAL DISK store no other
  process can see, and the scheduled sweep collects nothing real in production. Editing `deploy/do/app.yaml`
  is out of scope here (another lane's file at the time this shipped); this is the handoff for whoever next
  touches it. `apps/server/src/tools/sweep-orphans.ts`
- ⚙️ **`readAtMost` — the size ceiling enforced DURING the stream, not after buffering it** — an oversize
  upload is refused while its bytes are still arriving, so it cannot exhaust memory on the way to being
  refused; the refusal names the ceiling in the units a person reads (MB), and a sub-mebibyte ceiling
  changes units in its own message rather than reporting a misleading "0 MB". `apps/server/src/attachments/read-limited.ts`
- ⚙️ **Attachment metadata: repo, hashing, filenames, mime sniffing** — the `attachments` table and its
  repo functions (insert/get/list-by-ticket), with `sha256` nullable at the column level (`NULL` reads as
  unknown, never a substituted default) and CHECK-constrained to lowercase hex only — an uppercase
  duplicate of a real hash is refused by the database itself, not merely by application code.
  `sha256Hex` hashes exactly the bytes stored, over published test vectors. `sanitizeFilename` strips
  header-injection characters, path separators and control characters (NUL/DEL included) while keeping
  ordinary dots, and falls back to `"file"` for an empty or absent name. `sniffAllowedMime` decides mime
  by MAGIC BYTES alone — a renamed executable is refused for what it is regardless of its claimed name or
  content-type, unidentifiable bytes are refused without ever falling back to the extension, and the
  allow-list is closed: a real file outside it is still refused. Every embeddable-image mime is a subset
  of the uploadable allow-list, by test. `apps/server/src/attachments/attachment-repo.ts`, `content-hash.ts`, `filename.ts`, `sniff.ts`
- ✅ **`POST /v1/attachments` and `GET /v1/attachments/:id` — built, tested, and REGISTERED on the server this repo boots.**
  The route handlers are complete: upload answers `201 {attachmentId, url, mime, filename, size, sha256}`
  built from the server's own sniffed and hashed truth (never the client's claim about its file), refuses
  a session-less request 401, a malformed one 400, an oversize one 413 (the shipped ceiling is exactly
  26,214,400 bytes — 25 MiB), a mime the sniff refuses 415, and a guest without ticket visibility a 404
  BYTE-IDENTICAL to a nonexistent ticket; download streams the exact stored bytes under `canSee`, inline
  for images and as a sanitized-filename attachment otherwise, and answers that SAME 404 for an unshared
  guest, a nonexistent id, and metadata recorded with no bytes behind it — three different truths, one
  frozen body, so nothing about which of the three happened leaks. `apps/server/src/app.ts` registers
  both through `app.register(registerAttachmentRoutes, …)`, and `AppDeps.store` — required, like every
  other field but `now`/`stream` — carries the `ObjectStore` the pair writes to, built at the one boot
  path from `createObjectStoreFromEnv(process.env)`. **Until this landed the routes were reachable from
  nothing**, and the reason it survived so long is worth keeping: both attachment suites mount a bare
  `Fastify()` and register the routes BY HAND, so both were green against an empty composition root.
  `apps/server/test/routes/attachments-wired.test.ts` is the test that can fail on it — it registers
  nothing, goes through `buildApp`, and asserts the `attachments` ROW rather than the 201.
  `apps/server/src/routes/attachments.ts`, `apps/server/src/app.ts`

  is at the download door. **An empty list is a `200 {attachments: []}` and a refusal is a `404`** — the pair

- ⚙️ **Drive rule 3, enforced three ways** — a picked Drive file never becomes an image node: picking a
  Drive PNG produces an `attachment.added` claim and inserts no node; a `DriveReference` is not assignable
  to `insertTicketImage` at the TYPE level, and refused at RUNTIME too if the type is forced past; pasting
  a Drive share link (its URL as clipboard text, no file) uploads nothing and embeds nothing; and the
  drive module CANNOT reach the insert command at all, because it never imports it — a static-import scan
  over `packages/editor/src/drive/`, proven against a planted import. The server's own image-embed gate is
  the backstop should any of the above ever be bypassed (a reference has no bytes to embed, whatever mime

- ✅ **A contest cannot lie about which claim it is contesting** — `claim.contested` embeds the
  refused claim whole, and the embedded claim must name the **same workspace, the same entity kind
  and the same entity id** as the envelope carrying it. Before this, every layer validated one half
  and none compared the halves: a contest filed on a real ticket in its real workspace could embed a
  fabricated claim naming any other ticket in any other workspace, and it committed — a permanent,
  un-deletable ledger entry attributing a fabricated claim to any actor, since the ledger is
  append-only by trigger and can only ever be superseded. The check is **pure** (no database read, so
  it cannot go stale or be defeated by a missing row) and runs on **both ingest doors**, unconditionally
  — unlike the envelope-origin gate, which must distinguish doors because the server's own appends are
  legitimately server-origin. `apps/server/src/sync/contest-coherence.ts`
- ⚙️ **The server-side contest constructor** — `buildContestedClaim` reads the contest's workspace and
  entity **off the refused claim**, so it has no parameter through which they could disagree: coherence
  is structural there rather than checked. `checkContestCoherence` is the door that catches a contest
  built any other way. What neither can establish, and it is named rather than implied: that the
  embedded claim was **actually refused**, by the rule the contest names. Only the path that holds a
  real refusal can answer that, and now one does: **`POST /v1/sync` is the only production caller, and it
  passes the `Refusal` it is holding straight into `buildContestedClaim`** — so on that path the
  guarantee is structural in the PRODUCER while remaining, correctly, uncheckable at the consumer. The
  coherence check still cannot see whether a claim was refused and still says so; what changed is that
  every contest in the product is now built from a refusal the server made itself, rather than merely
  being well-formed. `apps/server/src/sync/contest-coherence.ts`, `apps/server/src/sync/sync-service.ts`
- ⚙️ **Contested-claims projection (`proj_contested`)** — one row per `claim.contested`, keyed by the
  contest event id and UNIQUE on the refused claim's id, so a sync retry finds the prior contest
  instead of filing a second one. `claimant_id` is the actor of the **refused claim**, not of the
  contest — the server files contests, so reading the contest's own actor would name the same person on
  every row and empty My Work for everyone. `original_event_id` is deliberately **not** a foreign key
  into `events`: a refused claim is never appended, so the row it would point at does not exist.
  `apps/server/src/projections/contested.ts`
- ⚙️ **Both writers of a contest row are one ticket's stream** — `claim.contested` and
  `claim.contested_resolved` are both filed against the ticket, and the engine refuses
  `contest.wrong-ticket` for a resolution aimed elsewhere, so canonical replay
  `(entity_kind, entity_id, seq)` always puts the contest before its resolution. A resolution reaching
  the handler with no contest row throws rather than silently doing nothing — the assertion of that
  premise, not defensiveness: a silent no-op would leave a resolved contest showing as open forever
  with no instrument saying so. The cost, named rather than left to be discovered: a rebuild replays the
  whole ledger in one transaction, so one inconsistent pair means `proj_contested` cannot be rebuilt at
  all until the ledger is superseded into consistency. `apps/server/src/projections/contested.ts`
- ⚙️ **The verifier runs over `proj_contested` with a real row in it** — `original_event` is the repo's
  first `jsonb` projection column, and the registry contract forbids `json` precisely because
  `verify-projections`'s `EXCEPT` diff needs an equality operator. That jsonb has one is an argument
  about the type; that a live `INSERT` and a shadow-schema rebuild agree through it byte for byte is an
  observation, and the verifier's seed now makes it. Its non-emptiness is asserted separately, because a
  clean verdict over an empty table is the check that cannot fail.
  `apps/server/test/verify-projections.test.ts`
- ⚙️ **`getContest` on the server engine context** — the engine's contest lookup, reading
  `proj_contested` through the ingest transaction's own client, which is what makes
  `contest.unknown` / `contest.wrong-ticket` / `contest.already-resolved` evaluable on this server at
  all. `null` here means "no such contest was ever recorded", which is TRUE of a projection rebuildable
  from the whole ledger — the reason the evaluator **throws** when the method is absent and **refuses**
  when it answers null. Asserted through the ENGINE — the three contest refusals `contest.unknown`,
  `contest.wrong-ticket` and `contest.already-resolved` are the whole reason the method exists, and a
  direct call would prove the SQL runs while proving nothing about the wiring that was missing.
  `apps/server/src/engine-context.ts`
- ✅ **`GET /v1/contests`** — the read surface the ticket banner and the attention strip share,
  filtered by workspace, ticket, claimant and open/resolved. Every row passes `canSee`, so a contest is

  **Each row carries the contested ticket's `title` and `projectId`**, joined from `proj_tickets` on
  `(ticket_id, workspace_id)` — LEFT, so a missing ticket row throws loudly instead of shortening the

- ⚙️ **Snapshot writer — the fold is the DOMAIN reducer, never `proj_tickets`** — Plan 1 shipped the
  `snapshots` table with no writer; this is the writer. `runSnapshotPass` snapshots every ticket whose
  head seq has run `SNAPSHOT_MIN_EVENTS` past its latest snapshot, and the stored `state` is
  `applyTicketEvent` folded over the ledger — the same reducer a replica runs. "Snapshot + tail is
  exactly full replay on every client" follows, but only JOINTLY with the serving side, and it was false
  until the fix round that added this clause: this writer skips every type outside `TICKET_EVENT_TYPES`
  while still advancing `seq` past it, so such an event reaches a replica only because
  `BOOTSTRAP_BACKFILL_TYPES` names it — and `visibility.set` was not named. Reading `proj_tickets`
  instead would look right indefinitely:
  that table is maintained by the same reducer today, so the two agree until the day they don't, and
  then a replica's bootstrap state differs from its own replay with nothing pointing at why. The
  equivalence is held by a test whose fixture leaves all three projections EMPTY and asserts it —
  under a fixture seeded through the full ingest path both implementations produce identical bytes and
  the assertion would distinguish nothing. `apps/server/src/sync/snapshot-writer.ts`
- ⚙️ **The snapshot's seq counts EVENTS, not folds** — `visibility.set`, `claim.contested` and
  `claim.contested_resolved` are all three filed against `kind: 'ticket'` and are deliberately absent
  from `TICKET_EVENT_TYPES`, so they
  move the cursor without moving the state. A writer that advanced the seq only on folded events would
  store a snapshot sitting behind events it had already passed, and a replica resuming from that cursor
  would be re-delivered them on every bootstrap. The cost of that design is paid on the serving side:
  those three exist in no snapshot, so bootstrap has to name every one of them or the ones it misses
  vanish below the cut. `TICKET_EVENT_TYPES` is TEN of the registry's thirteen `entityKind: 'ticket'`
  types, not all of them, and its own docblock used to say "the ten registered against
  `entityKind: 'ticket'`" — which is the most plausible reason `visibility.set` was missed.
  `apps/server/src/sync/snapshot-writer.ts`, `packages/domain/src/ticket-state.ts`
- ⚙️ **Reducer deps folded from the ledger's own definition events** — `buildLedgerDeps` builds
  `TicketStateDeps` from `workflow.defined` / `ticket-type.defined` rows, ordered by `workspace_seq`
  and NOT by `(entity_kind, entity_id, seq)`: a ticket type's key lives in its PAYLOAD and successive
  definitions of one key arrive on different entity streams (each event gets a fresh ULID entity id),
  so per-entity seq cannot order them against each other at all. Greatest `workspace_seq` wins for
  types and greatest `version` wins for workflows — the same two rules `proj_ticket_types`' guarded
  `DO UPDATE` and `proj_workflows`' `DO NOTHING` + `ORDER BY version DESC` already enforce, so the
  ledger fold and the projections cannot disagree about which definition is current — and neither can a
  replica, because `GET /v1/sync/bootstrap` serves `definitions` in this same `workspace_seq` order
  (12.117). It did not, for one task: the route shipped the plan text's `(entity_kind, entity_id, seq)`,
  so a workspace that had ever redefined a ticket-type key handed the replica the definitions in the one
  order this loader's docblock says cannot resolve them. Both rules are
  pinned by a fixture that defines one key TWICE, with the winning definition deliberately given the
  smaller ULID entity id so the plan text's ordering picks the loser, and the maps never cross a
  workspace. *That workspace filter is pinned by ONE case — dropping it reddens 12.93 and nothing else,
  974 of 975 green across all 88 server test files, re-measured; the "red in seven cases" this file's
  test-case entry used to claim was never run.* `apps/server/src/sync/ledger-deps.ts`
- ⚙️ **The writer's absences, named** — no locking (safe because the row is keyed by seq and the fold is
  pure below it, so a late arrival is the next pass's work, not a corruption), tickets only (there is no
  other reducer to fold), no visibility or tenancy gate (a background sweep has no caller identity — the
  route that SERVES a snapshot owes that), and no retention: the table grows one row per snapshot per
  entity forever. *Retention is unowned.* Retention is NOT how a stale snapshot is invalidated, and the
  distinction is worth keeping straight: `readLatestSnapshot` is `ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 1`, so a
  higher-seq row supersedes for every reader — a `DELETE` would buy nothing but a longer replay. The
  writer's deps also resolve the NEWEST definitions, which is safe only because the publish door below
  re-snapshots at head and so removes any tail that spans a version boundary; a ticket that door SKIPS
  is exactly one this pass can still throw on, and the interval wrapper logs and swallows that.
  `apps/server/src/sync/snapshot-writer.ts`
- ⚙️ **Refresh on publish, SNAPSHOT door — the repair is a snapshot ABOVE the offending event, not a
  deletion** — a `workflow.defined` re-snapshots every ticket standing on an older version of that
  workflow, at the ticket's own stream head, holding the state walked forward by the domain's
  `foldTicketToWorkflowVersion`. It runs inside the publish's transaction, before the projection loop,
  and it closes a gap that had no owner: until it, publishing invalidated no snapshot, so bootstrap
  could serve a snapshot plus a tail carrying a `ticket.transitioned` into a state the new version had
  dropped, and both the replica's `loadBootstrap` and the server's own `runSnapshotPass` threw
  `applyTicketEvent: workflow "…" has no state "…"` on it. Deleting or refusing to serve the stale
  snapshot makes it WORSE — both serve the ticket's full history instead, which holds the same event
  earlier — and no fold at the serving end can reach it, which is why the fix is on the writing side.
  Before the projection loop is not incidental: `proj_tickets`'s own refresh-on-publish sets exactly
  the rows this selects to the new version, so running second would match nothing. Not a projection
  either: `snapshots` has no shadow copy, so an unqualified write from inside one escapes
  `verify-projections.ts`'s `search_path` fence and writes LIVE during a verify. Each ticket folds
  inside a `SAVEPOINT`, so a fold that cannot be walked forward leaves that ticket's stale snapshot
  standing and the publish still commits — *a skip is silent on the live path; ingest has no logger to
  put the returned list in.* **"Every ticket" includes tickets that have never been snapshotted**, and
  the candidate query carries no snapshot-existence filter for that reason: below `SNAPSHOT_MIN_EVENTS`
  the background pass has written no row, bootstrap serves such a ticket its FULL history, and that
  history holds the offending event too — so it needs a snapshot above that event more than a
  snapshotted ticket does, not less. The publish therefore folds such a ticket from event 1 rather than
  from a tail, and writes a row below the threshold that the background pass would not; both are the
  price of the repair, and both are a FIRST-publish cost per ticket — the row this door leaves at the
  head is what its next publish resumes from. Narrowing the query to tickets that already hold a
  snapshot reopens the throw for everything under twenty events, permanently, since under that filter
  neither door ever writes them a first row (measured — 12.159 reds, 12.156–12.158 stay green).
  `apps/server/src/sync/snapshot-refresh.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/ingest/ingest-service.ts`
- ⚙️ **`SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL_MS` (300000) and `SNAPSHOT_MIN_EVENTS` (20)** — additive config, both

  pass on every tick of the event loop, and a zero `MIN_EVENTS` makes every ticket due on every pass,

  same state, only slower. `apps/server/src/config.ts`, `.env.example`

- ⚙️ **`EffectiveRole.projects` is a `Map`, and the wire shape is not** — `me.projectIds` is

  than enumerating the uncontestable rules is what closes it as a class. *The throw is KEPT for a
  contest-append that comes back `invalid` or is absent: a server-built envelope the server's own door

- ✅ **A re-widened ticket comes back even if the client read something else meanwhile — a bounded
  NOTICE on newly granted visibility, and the client pulls what it lacks** *(this bullet was ⚙️ and
  described the DEFECT; closure 5 closed it by PUSHING the history, and closure 5b re-shaped it under
  ruling P37.1 because pushing wedged)* — when an event widens a ticket's audience, everyone in the NEW
  audience is sent a `reach-granted` frame naming that ticket and every inheriting descendant, and each
  client fetches the ones it does not already hold through `GET /v1/sync/bootstrap/ticket`. The trigger
  is the visibility event itself and never a reconstructed prior audience — there is no before-image to
  reconstruct and re-deriving one is banned — and what makes that coarse trigger safe is an asymmetry
  rather than a check: a narrowing is invisible to the person it narrowed away, so it never becomes their
  trigger. A widening self-selects; a narrowing self-excludes.
  *Why it is a notice and not the history:* the pushed form was an atomic burst that advanced no cursor,
  so a slow-consumer close mid-burst left the client reconnecting into the identical burst for ever. A
  list of ids is a list of ids however long the histories behind it are. It also bounds an amplifier the
  permission check does not: a member may re-issue a visibility change that changes nothing, and a client
  that already holds the subtree now does no work for it at all. *And it is not a purge walk arriving
  from the other direction* — a purge names an entity to a device that may never have held it, which is
  news; a notice names ids the recipient may at that moment read in full.
  *The defect it replaces, kept because it is what the tests measure:* the sync cursor is the highest
  sequence DELIVERED, so one unrelated commit between a narrowing and a re-widening left the client
  holding two events where the server held four, permanently, with no purge, no backfill and no resync
  path. Cases 12.274-12.283. `apps/server/src/visibility/grant-backfill.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/sync/sync-routes.ts`, `packages/sync-client/src/replica/replica.ts`,
  `packages/sync-client/src/engine/sync-engine.ts`

  travel WHOLE rather than scoped to the ticket's own workflows because a scoped list missing one
  intermediate version fails silently at the fold and throws a step later. A ticket the caller may not
  see and a ticket that never existed get the identical 404: splitting them would make
  presence-versus-absence an oracle, the disclosure the reconcile door already refuses. The response
  carries no stream cursor, and the omission is load-bearing — a per-ticket pull that moved the workspace
  cursor would skip every intervening event for every other ticket and look exactly like convergence.

- ✅ **A pull that fails is remembered, not fatal and not forgotten** *(closure 5b(d))* — the ids a
  notice named are recorded in durable client storage, so a pull that fails or times out leaves the
  cursor free to advance while the id stays owed, and the next catch-up retries it. Both alternatives are
  wrong: throwing reaches the engine's stall, which is a one-way latch that only a process restart
  clears, so a brief network wobble would brick the device; swallowing and forgetting advances the cursor
  with the ids lost and no path back, because a fresh bootstrap is refused over an existing local
  baseline. Each pull is bounded by a timeout enforced in the ENGINE rather than the transport, because
  the transport has other implementors and a wait that never ends would stop the serial apply chain in
  total silence. Cases 12.292-12.298, 12.305-12.308.
  - ✅ **…and an id the server will never serve is dropped — keyed to the NOTICE, not to the status code**
    *(ruling P37.3)* — remembering without a bound was a quiet permanent leak: a revoked project left one
    HTTP request per catch-up, for ever. The drop cannot key on the 404, because the route answers "you may
    not see it" and "it never existed" identically **by design**, so the device cannot tell a phantom from a
    re-widening that raced the pull. Each pending entry instead carries the `workspaceSeq` of the notice that
    named it, and the 404 drops the entry only if that seq is still the one the pull was issued for — a later
    notice has already replaced it, so the entry survives and the next catch-up fetches it. **A 404 is never
    the last word; the next notice is.** Cases 12.317-12.318.

- ✅ **`POST /v1/sync/reconcile` — the client names what it holds and the server says what is no longer
  theirs** *(closure 5's other half; it closes case 6.104, the stale copy nobody takes away)* — a member
  un-shared by a plain visibility change used to keep the copy until a full resync, because a
  server-initiated purge would name an entity to a device that may never have held it. This inverts the
  direction instead: the device presents its ids, the server answers only about those, and existence is
  never consulted — a fabricated id comes back exactly as a genuine loss does, so the reply's SHAPE
  carries no oracle either. The engine deletes only what it itself presented, because a purge is
  destructive and local and this device does not need to trust the server to be safe from it.
  **The schedule is catch-up completion — which is once per RECONNECT, not once per catch-up**
  *(closure 5b, case 12.288)*, because the hub sends that frame once per subscription. The moment a
  device's cursor is current is the moment its holdings may be stale, because a narrowing sends the
  losing device nothing at all. Gating instead on "the catch-up delivered something" would skip the
  zero-frame catch-up, which is precisely the case reconcile exists for, so the bound is a minimum
  interval rather than activity: reconnects are on a fixed delay with no growth, and a flapping socket
  would otherwise reconcile every two seconds for ever. **Because that schedule is per-reconnect, a
  grant notice ALSO reconciles the ids it names, before deciding what to pull** *(closure 5c's minimal
  form)* — otherwise a device on a stable socket that was narrowed and re-widened would keep a stale
  partial copy indefinitely, the holdings filter being unable to tell it from a complete one. A failure there is swallowed — reconcile is idempotent and the
  next catch-up retries — and concurrent callers share one in-flight run. **A guest gets the same
  answers as a member**, which closes case 6.102: the door asks only `canSee`, and `canSee` resolves a
  guest through the explicit share list exactly as it resolves a member through a project, so nothing
  about it was ever role-aware — what was missing was the measurement.

  cannot make), real Postgres, real bearer-token auth on the handshake, the real unmodified sync-client

  truth after the reconnect. The chain has **two halves and one cut cannot see both**: while the notice is
  regenerated (its `backfilled` set is per-drain and a notice moves no cursor) the reconnect repairs the

- ⚙️ **The heartbeat is a PROTOCOL ping, and a peer that answers one as if it were an application frame

  client declares for its transport (`WebSocketLike`) has no ping event at all, so a client built against
  it cannot see one. That reasoning is what 12.328's deletion of a text `ping`/`pong` protocol rests on,
  and `webSocketFactory` being an injected seam is what keeps it a property of what gets INJECTED rather
  than of either module. The socket-cut fixture holds a real `ws` socket on **both** ends of a real
  upgrade, so it is the only place the hazard is expressible: wiring the client's own `on('ping')` to a
  text `{"type":"pong"}` draws `{type:'error', workspaceId:null, code:'bad-message', …}` from the
  unmodified `badMessage` path — a complaint, not a disconnect. **Measured as an excluding pair on one
  connection**, the same server-side `.ping()` twice with only that listener added in between, so the
  complaint is attributable to the added frame and not to the connection or the heartbeat; the control
  half is production's own behaviour, every thirty seconds, on every socket. The residual 12.361 records
  is untouched by this: the owner rule at both `webSocketFactory` defaults is still a docblock, and a
  case showing what breaking it costs is not a check that it is kept.
  `apps/server/src/stream/routes.ts`, `apps/server/test/dual-client/socket-cut.test.ts`
- ✅ **Visibility that widens because the READER's reach grew, not the ticket's** *(closure 5b, case
  12.283)* — `membership.granted` and `project.member_added` reveal tickets whose history sits below the
  client's cursor, the identical gap. It could not be another entry in the ticket-event trigger list, for
  a structural reason rather than a scoping choice: these are roster events filed against the roster
  entity, so there is no ticket to start a subtree walk from, and the question inverts with the widening
  — not who can now see this ticket, but which tickets can this viewer now see. It answers with what the
  reader can see NOW rather than what they gained, because there is no before-image to subtract, using
  the same visibility predicate every read endpoint uses rather than a second definition of it. It
  therefore over-names, which is affordable only because the client drops ids it already holds without
  asking the server anything. `apps/server/src/visibility/grant-backfill.ts`,
  `apps/server/src/visibility/visible-events-for.ts`
- ⚙️ **A contest filed against a ticket that never came to exist reaches nobody** — surfaced by the
  reopen scenario and asserted as product behaviour: `canSee` is false for a ticket with no
  `proj_visibility` row, so the child's `claim.contested` is streamed to no one. The claimant's only
  record of it is the outbox stub. *What is permanent is the non-delivery, not any cursor lag — an
  earlier version of this bullet said the cursors stay one behind the head for good, and the next
  visible event moves them past.*
- ⚙️ **The fixture-mirror inventory.** 157 fixtures across `app-core`, `sync-client`, `apps/web`,
  `apps/server` and the periphery, each classified against the producer it models: 80 MIRROR (a
  protocol owned elsewhere, with no round trip pinning it), 24 WITNESSED, 53 N.A. (the fixture
  implements an interface its own package owns). The discriminator is whether some OTHER process
  authoritatively defines the shape the fixture encodes. Recorded in `docs/lanes/executor-state.md`
  with owners; the buildable subset is witnessed by the file above, and the rest carry ❌ cases
  (12.326–12.328) naming what remains unwitnessed and why.

## 10. Workflow builder & ticket types

The authoring half of spec §4: a Jira-style visual builder plus a template gallery — no AI drafting.

**A dictated sentence this section transcribed and measurement refutes.** The plan's own §10 preamble reads *"All views live in `packages/app-core` (shared with desktop); `apps/web` contributes pages and the DataSource adapter"* (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-20-08-workflow-builder.md:7086`), and the first version of this section shipped it almost verbatim. It is false on this branch, and it is the fourth dictated sentence §10 has had to correct against the code. The *screens* do live in `packages/app-core` and are shared with desktop — canvas, inspectors, panels, both list screens, the gallery, the type editor — and every route below mounts one of them for the authoring itself rather than keeping a second copy. But `apps/web` authors view code of its own, with its own user-facing copy: six route pages, two of which render four distinct states each, plus `WiringNotReady`'s three non-`ready` arms. The constraint that is actually *enforced* here is a different one, and it is the one worth stating: nothing in `packages/app-core/src` outside `src/online/` speaks HTTP (amendment 10), and that is held by a scanner (`packages/app-core/test/no-http-in-views.test.ts`), not by where a file happens to sit.

The rule was present and the canvas was still invisible, which is why the witness asserts a **measured** height and not a rule or a class name, and why it cannot be a jsdom test (jsdom has no layout engine, so `getBoundingClientRect()` returns zeros for everything and the assertion would pass on the broken tree). The fix is one declaration, **`display: grid`**, on `.gn-workflow-canvas`; `min-height: 480px` is untouched and load-bearing for the narrow-screen layout — the pair is the fix. Measured both states in a browser: `.react-flow` **0px → 480px**, the first node's box lying inside the canvas **0px² → 6923px²**. **What does NOT discriminate, and is therefore not asserted:** the container's own height (480 in both), the FIRST node's height and width (75.27 / 91.98 in both — the nodes are not all the same height, but every one of them is non-zero, which is all the argument needs) and the node count (4 in both) — React Flow sizes each node intrinsically inside a container that draws none of it, so DOM-shape assertions pass on the broken tree. The case carries a planted control that reproduces the pre-fix cascade in-page and must read 0, through the same helper as the measurement. A sweep of `ui.css` + `globals.css` for the same shape found **no second invisible canvas** — the three other `height: 100%` sites either sit under a definite (`inset: 0`) parent or have intrinsic content height; It was simply the wrong instrument for a claim about REACHABILITY: a `Link` is one way to arrive and `router.push` is another. **The two `new` routes carry a route-level role gate**, which the coordination doc recorded as owed against "Plan 8 Task 13" and which shipped in the same commit as the pages: `TemplateGallery` takes no session and its `onPick` is unconditional, so a member who typed `.../workflows/new` was handed the gallery `WorkflowListScreen` deliberately hid, picked a template, and landed on a read-only builder — an authoring entry point offered to someone with none. Both `new` routes now answer `ReadOnlyBanner` plus a link back to the list, gated on `canAuthorRole` imported from app-core and never re-spelled as a role comparison, so one predicate serves four screens and two routes and cannot drift into two surfaces disagreeing about one person. **The two `[id]` routes render four states each** — loading, `missing`, a rejected read as a `ShellRefusal` carrying the cause's own words, and loaded — because a spinner left up for a rejected read is the shell claiming an answer is on its way; `getWorkflow`'s 404 is already `null` (Plan 6's read affordance folds "no such thing" and "not yours" into one body), so `missing` and a rejection are different facts with different sentences. `[typeId]` finds its type inside the whole-workspace list, because neither the gateway nor the server has a `getTicketType(id)` at all — which is also what makes *No ticket type has this id in this workspace.* a measurement rather than a guess. The two ticket-type editor pages (`[typeId]` and `new`) now wrap `TicketTypeEditorScreen` in a breadcrumb link back to the list and a title row carrying a `Cancel` link to the same place — page-level chrome, not props on the shared screen, so `access.test.tsx`'s enumeration of the screen's own controls (rendered standalone, with no page around it) is untouched. **STALE as of Round 19e (§1's "workspace card" bullet carries the current entry): "nothing in the app links to any of them" is no longer true of the ticket-type editor — `/settings` (`app/settings/page.tsx`) now inlines it, and this bullet's own `[typeId]`/`new` chrome paragraph was extracted into `apps/web/src/ticket-type-editor-pane.tsx` so both callers share it.** `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/settings/workflows/page.tsx`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/settings/workflows/new/page.tsx`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/settings/workflows/[workflowId]/page.tsx`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/settings/ticket-types/page.tsx`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/settings/ticket-types/new/page.tsx`, `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/settings/ticket-types/[typeId]/page.tsx`, `apps/web/test/authoring-routes.test.tsx`
- ⚙️ **The role wiring behind those routes — a failed read is not a role** — `useBuilderWiring(workspaceId)` answers a four-arm union (`loading` | `signed-out` | `refused` | `ready`) where the plan's snippet returned `{ gateway, session } | null` and every page rendered `null` for it, collapsing four situations into one blank screen. Where the role comes from is the substance: `GET /v1/me/workspaces` carries one, but `getMyWorkspaces` refuses whole (`ServingGapError`, `online/mappers.ts`), and a role-only mapper over the same route would be routing around a refusal this step may not weaken — so the role is read out of the roster (`GET /v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/members`), where the caller's own row is the server's answer rather than this shell's inference. A 404 is `'guest'` (the no-guests door turned the caller away, or they are not a member); a 200 that does not list the caller is *also* `'guest'`, deliberately not `'member'`, because inventing a role for somebody the roster does not list would be a claim about membership nothing made; anything else — a 500, a dropped connection, an unparseable body — is `refused`, never a default role, since defaulting either way would tell an owner they may not change what they own or offer authoring to someone whose authorization was never established. `WiringNotReady` renders the three non-`ready` arms once for all six pages so none of them can quietly render `null` for a refusal, and its copy is user-facing: a `role="status"` spinner, a *Sign in to open settings* link carrying `?next=` back to the current path, and a `ShellRefusal` headed *Your role in this workspace*. The cost is stated rather than hidden: this reads the roster and `WorkflowBuilderScreen` reads it again — two requests for one list, accepted over a cache whose staleness would be the exact failure the union is built to avoid. `apps/web/src/authoring/builder-wiring.tsx`
- ⚙️ **Draft store & auto-layout** — immutable `WorkflowDraft` store (cascade-edges-on-delete, never rewrite authored references); deterministic layered layout from `initialStateId`; layout is presentation and never published. `packages/app-core/src/workflow-builder/draft-store.ts`
- ⚙️ **Authoring gateway, split by seam, not a single adapter** — the builder's one interface to the world (`WorkflowAuthoringGateway`), with an in-memory fake for tests, and in `apps/web` a real implementation that is not one uniform `DataSource` adapter: `getWorkflow`, `listTicketTypes`, `submit` go through Plan 6's `DataSource.query`/`ingest`; `listWorkflows`, `getStateOccupancy`, `getTypeWorkflowPopulation` and `migrateTypeToWorkflow` go straight over the online HTTP client, because `DataSourceQuery` has no member for them at all (server routes exist; `data-source.ts` does not). `listMembers` also bypasses `DataSourceQuery.getMembers` deliberately: that method returns `Actor[]` (`{ id, name }`), not the `WorkspaceMember[]` (`{ userId, displayName, role }`) the builder needs, and no cast reconciles the two shapes — the adapter's docblock states the choice and names the alternative (widening `DataSource`) it declined, so as not to force the offline replica and the fake to answer for a migrate and an occupancy count they have no offline story for. **`AuthoringReadRefused` is declared in that contract file since E2-39 (2026-09-21)** — declared there and re-exported by the adapter, so `packages/app-core` can narrow on a refusal it formerly could not even name; the rule-editors bullet carries the defect that closed and the two cases pinning it. `packages/app-core/src/workflow-builder/gateway.ts`, `apps/web/src/authoring/data-source-gateway.ts`

Day cells take `--gn-surface-raised` in-month / `--gn-fill-quaternary` out, 1px gaps revealing the tray as hairlines. **The event list (`.gn-calendar__items`) is deliberately PINNED to `--gn-surface`, not the tray it visually sits inside** — this is not an oversight; it is the fix for a real regression a follow-up review caught: nothing between `.gn-calendar__items` and the new `.gn-calendar__grid` wrapper painted an opaque ground of its own, so every item (the custom-field marker's unchanged `--gn-custom-marker` text included) silently moved onto `--gn-surface-sunken`, and `customMarker` on `hig`/`minimal` LIGHT's `surfaceSunken` measures 4.310 — below 4.5, where the SAME pairing on the plain `--gn-surface` it was actually last measured against is 4.935 (`neo`'s cited 4.807 is unaffected either way, since `neo` collapses `surface`/`surfaceSunken` to one hex). Pinned back explicitly. **Ruling 24 (coordinator, 2026-09-16) corrected how this is gated**: the first attempt (case `11.213`, `packages/ui/test/tokens.test.ts`) computed the ratio from `tokens.ts` role lookups alone, duplicated a `CONTRAST_PAIRS` row that had already existed since Plan 9, and — because it never read `ui.css` — could not have caught this exact regression (deleting the CSS declaration left it green). Retired same-day; the real gate is case `11.214` (`packages/ui/test/in-transit.test.ts`), which reads the actual stylesheet and is proven to redden when the declaration is removed. **The today ring moved from a whole-cell outline to a 24px accent circle around the day number** (`onColor` = `--gn-accent-text`, the same pair the Filters sheet and the Timeline bar already use for "accent ground + onColor" — never `--gn-text-inverted`). **The accent-ground event pill, previously bar-only, now applies to every non-custom item** (markers included) — ONE declared exception: the custom-field marker keeps its plain `--gn-custom-marker` text treatment and does NOT become a tinted pill (measured: no purple wash clears contrast on both grounds a day cell can have; no `--gn-tint-purple` role exists or was added). This is a DECLARED architectural divergence from the prototype's single 42-cell grid: this product still renders a week's events in a separate list below its day numbers rather than inside each cell, so the 420px floor is a minimum on the whole grid, not a per-row stretch. No new token role — every `var(--gn-…)` referenced was already declared. Case `11.212`. **AN EPIC'S OWN CLAIMED DATES ARE NOT DRAWN HERE (owner, 2026-09-20).** `hideEpicRows` drops the rank-1 ticket inside `buildCalendarModel`'s `visible` filter, before any item is built — so its bar, its markers and its custom-date claims all go, and its children's claims stay. Joining `visible` rather than filtering the inputs is deliberate: a removed epic therefore counts as a NARROWING, and `narrowedOutOfGrid` still gates `CALENDAR_ALL_HIDDEN_COPY`'s exhaustivity claim off. **Every day cell now names its own full date, and a bar's date span is a linked accessible description (E4-28, batch B15, 2026-09-21).** Day cells carried only `data-day`/`data-today`/`data-outside`/`aria-current` — an assistive-tech reader landing on one heard a bare number with no month or year; each now also carries `aria-label={formatDate(day)}` (e.g. "23 Aug 2026"). A bar's rendered text is its ticket title alone, and its date span lived only in the hover-only `title` attribute; it now also carries `aria-describedby`, pointing at a visually-hidden span repeating the exact `title` string — the accessible NAME stays exactly the ticket title (nothing already depending on it broke), and the dates are linked as a DESCRIPTION rather than folded in, the same ARIA shape `apps/web/app/w/[workspaceId]/page.tsx`'s `WorkspaceLinks` already uses and documents. A marker is untouched: `item.label` already names its own date as the rendered, accessible text.
