Both refusals (`invalid_unread`, `invalid_kind`) are **loud**, because `unread=yes` or `kind=mentons` is a caller who believes they narrowed and did not, and the failure mode is concluding the inbox is empty. **A filtered empty never reuses the unfiltered sentence** — *"Nothing in your inbox"* is a claim about the whole set and is false under a filter. Cases 13.969–13.975. Its HTTP adapter is `packages/app-core/src/online/notifications.ts` — moved there from `apps/web/src/` on 2026-09-07 to sit with its three siblings, which is what made the consumer round-trippable from a server test at all. **And the header carries the BULK action with its Undo** (2026-09-20, door C) — `Mark N read` over **exactly the rows the page has drawn**, on ONE bidirectional route: `POST /v1/me/notifications/read`, body `{ ids, read }`, answering `{ changed }`. The label states the drawn count rather than the prototype's *"Mark all read"*, and the difference is a correction: the ruling kept a **non-id-scoped "mark all" out of scope**, so "all" would claim the whole inbox for an action scoped to the page. **⚠ The Undo un-reads the ids the SERVER reported changing, not the ids the page sent** — those differ for any requested row that was already read, and un-reading such a row would put a notification back on screen that nobody took away. That is why the route answers with a list, and the statement behind it is `UPDATE … SET read = $1 … AND read IS DISTINCT FROM $1::boolean RETURNING id`: **`RETURNING` alone reports every row the `WHERE` MATCHED, not every row whose value CHANGED**, which the bulk route's own case caught. The unread direction did not exist before this — `markNotificationRead` was one-way — and it is the SAME statement carrying the flag rather than a flag on the per-id route. The `ids` list is bounded at **`MAX_LIMIT` (100)**, this route file's own ceiling on one page of the read, and **refused whole rather than truncated**; the route is registered in `HTTP_ORIGIN_PROTECTED_ROUTES` by exact `routeUrl` (the neighbour string does not cover it), and the security suite's drift guard compares the two sets for equality in both directions. The Undo's surface is the shared **`Toast`** — `packages/ui/src/components/toast.tsx`, the product's FIRST transient surface, built shared because the prototype's serves 66 call sites — dismissing itself after **15 s** (owner-ruled) and pausing while the pointer or focus is inside it. **Named absence: a non-id-scoped "mark all read"**, excluded by the ruling and not built. **⚠ AND THE SINGLE-ROW READ AND THE UNDO NOW SPEAK WHEN THEY FAIL (E5-10, 2026-09-21 — cases `13.1108`/`13.1109`):** (filed independently as E2-26 as well, whose case `17.071` pins the ROW-vocabulary choice below) both had `void gateway.…().catch(() => loadFirstPage())` — a reload and NO sentence, which is the exact first-version defect the BULK arm's own docblock records as fixed. The row's is the same split in the row's own wording; **the row splits by KIND where the bulk arm splits by STATUS**, because the bulk route's 400 is its bound and the single-row route's only status is the 404 that "not yours" and "does not exist" share, so an `HttpError` of any status is the server adjudicating. The Undo's is said BESIDE the toast, in its own slot, because the toast the Undo just closed can no longer carry the sentence it contradicts. `apps/server/src/routes/notifications.ts`, `apps/server/src/notifications/store.ts`, `packages/ui/src/components/toast.tsx`, `apps/web/app/inbox/page.tsx`, `packages/app-core/src/inbox/`, `apps/web/app/inbox/`
- ⚙️ **Saved filters** — named FilterSpecs stored via `/v1/me/preferences`; applying one is a view act, never a data act. **⚙️ and not ✅ deliberately: nothing mounts `SavedFiltersMenu` and no `PreferencesGateway` implementation exists outside the test fake**, which `saved-filters.ts`'s own docblock already concedes — so the store, the schema and the menu are all real and tested, and no user can reach any of them yet. *Owner: whoever mounts the menu and writes the gateway against Plan 5's whole-document `GET`/`PUT /v1/me/preferences`.* `packages/app-core/src/preferences/`
- ⚙️ **Reporting scope guard** — an executable scan across seven client and server source trees (`packages/app-core/src`, `packages/domain/src`, `packages/rule-engine/src`, `packages/ui/src`, `apps/server/src`, `apps/web/src`, `apps/web/app` — the last two added because that is where days are finally drawn) keeps velocity/burndown/forecast vocabulary out of every one of them, and keeps the zone string and the day regex to their single origin in the domain. `packages/app-core/test/reporting-scope-guard.test.ts`

## 13. Deployment & dogfooding

*(Plan 11's own Task 16 opens this section by convention, held until Tasks 1–15 merge. In practice it was
opened early, incrementally, by Tasks 1–15 across five parallel lanes — so what Task 16 did was give it
its FINAL SHAPE, reconciling what was already here rather than writing it fresh. **All sixteen tasks have
now landed**, and the runbook named throughout this section exists at `docs/runbook.md`. What remains
outside it is the live production deploy itself, which is out of scope by the owner's instruction: the
DigitalOcean spec is written and quarantined in `deploy/do/`, and provisioning is verified at deploy time
(`13.21`), not by CI.)*

- ⚙️ **Go-live day fixes (2026-09-22)** — the first production boot on DigitalOcean found two defects the dev stack could not: the backup worker's 30-day orphan-sweep timer overflowed Node's 32-bit cap and ran in a tight loop (`startScheduler` now arms in chunks ≤ 2^31-1 ms, case `13.1282`), and the image's migration step could not verify the managed cluster's certificate (`apps/server/docker-entrypoint.sh` writes the bound `DATABASE_CA_CERT` to a file and migrates over `sslrootcert`, case `13.1283`). Spaces lives in SGP1, not BLR1 — BLR1 refused bucket creation for this account (`deploy/do/README.md` step 2).
- ⚙️ **Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM / SIGINT** — `installShutdownHandlers(app, pool)` is installed by
  the one non-test boot path BEFORE `app.listen`, and runs `app.close()` (bounded 5 s) → `pool.end()`
  (bounded 2 s), then lets the event loop drain to exit 0; a whole-process watchdog exits 1 at 8 s if
  something still holds the loop. The bounds are sized under `docker stop`'s 10 s default, the smallest
  grace period this image meets in the wild. **The defect it closes is a PID-1 one, measured against
  the built image, not reasoned about**: `apps/server/Dockerfile`'s entrypoint `exec`s node, so node is
  PID 1, and PID 1 has no default signal dispositions — with no handler installed, SIGTERM was
  **ignored** and every deploy ended in SIGKILL after the grace period (`docker stop -t 3`: 3197 ms
  ignored vs 172 ms handled), severing in-flight requests and leaving the snapshot writer's interval,
  the stream hub's sockets, the notification fan-out's subscription and the pool all unreleased. A
  second signal is logged and dropped (`pool.end()` twice throws). Process-level `unhandledRejection` /
  `uncaughtException` handlers are deliberately NOT installed for the life of the process — they
  suppress Node's own crash — with ONE narrow exception, installed only for the duration of a shutdown
  and removed after it: avvio runs `onClose` hooks synchronously, so a hook that throws
  **synchronously** never rejects `app.close()`'s promise and is not catchable there; measured without
  the exception, that fault skipped `pool.end()` entirely and exited 1 in 12 ms — a graceful stop
  reported to the orchestrator as a crash. `apps/server/src/shutdown.ts`, called from
  `apps/server/src/index.ts`
- ⚙️ **Seed plumbing** — `seedUlid(namespace, key)` mints a deterministic, `ULID_REGEX`-valid id from a SHA-256 digest, so re-running a seed regenerates identical event ids and a re-run can recognise its own prior work rather than duplicating it. (The recognition is a ledger lookup BEFORE submission, not the plan text's `duplicate-event-id` refusal — measured in Task 9: the permission gate and the rule engine both answer before `insertEvent` ever reaches the primary key, so that refusal is unreachable for most seed events at either door.) `plainTextDoc(text)` builds a ProseMirror doc from a seed string: since the owner's 2026-09-20 ruling (*"both"*) it **parses markdown** (`markdownToDoc`, its own module) and `literalTextDoc(text)` is the renderer that keeps text literal — one paragraph per line, by delegating each line to the domain's own single-paragraph `plainTextToDoc` rather than duplicating its paragraph-shape logic. `seedDescriptionDoc(parts)` composes a description from `markdown` prose and `literal` record lines, told apart by the builder that wrote them rather than by inspecting the text. `findUserIdByEmail` looks a person up in better-auth's `"user"` table by email — seeds never invent people. `apps/server/src/seed/{seed-ulid,doc-text,users}.ts`
- ⚙️ **`checkErrandTemplate` — the executable pin on the errand-with-waits template, and Ruling P29's tripwire** — verifies Plan 8's `ERRAND_WITH_WAITS_TEMPLATE` can structurally carry the Convenience Corner tracker board before any seed event is built: every tracker state the seed maps to is present and reachable from the initial state in exactly one transition (no fabricated intermediate history), `waiting` carries `blocked: true`, every door into `done` is guarded by `require-comment`, and — the tripwire — every one-hop transition the seed relies on carries **zero** rules, because the seed submits a bare `ticket.transitioned` with no comment or evidence and any rule there would make the real engine refuse the seed's own event at ingest. This last check is what reddens if a copy of the template ever grows a rule on one of the two paths (`later`→`waiting`, `next`→`waiting`) that Ruling P29 deliberately leaves rule-free — a test pins `adviseWorkflowDef`'s two `rule-bypassable` advisories on the real template by identity, proves a single-edge "fix" genuinely silences one advisory while `checkErrandTemplate` still reddens, and proves guarding both edges clears the advisory panel to zero while `checkErrandTemplate` still refuses it. `workflowFromTemplate` clones a template into a live, published-shape definition at version 1. `apps/server/src/seed/templates.ts`
- ⚙️ **Convenience Corner seed mapping — frozen record in, events out, nothing invented** — `readCcBoard` reads the frozen `reference/convenience-corner-tracker/board.data.js` snapshot read-only through a `vm` sandbox and refuses (naming the path) a file that does not define `window.CC_TRACKER` with the expected shape. `buildErrandEvents` maps one tracker item to its full ticket event sequence: `ticket.created`, a `description` whose PROSE is parsed (the record's body and its quoted ask — headings, lists, bold, italic, code and links) beside its machine-ish `— tracker record —` block kept **literal**, an optional `counterparty` custom field, an origin-dated `startDate` claim (built-in field, `{date, note?}` shape) only when the record itself dates it, a `dueDate` claim derived from `needed_week` by the tracker generator's own published week arithmetic with the derivation named in the claim's note, and at most one `ticket.transitioned` (payload key `to`) mapping the tracker's `later/next/in-progress/blocked` states onto the template's `later/next/in-progress/waiting`. Refuses — never guesses or fabricates — on a `done` item (checked by both the state string and the done flag, so the two disagreeing can never slip a completed item through as open) and on any unmapped tracker state. Every event id is a `seedUlid` derived from the item's own tracker id, so two builds of the same item are identical and a re-snapshot cannot collide event ids across items. `apps/server/src/seed/{cc-board,cc-map}.ts`
- ✅ **Convenience Corner seed runner — the shop's real errands through the product's own door** — `seedConvenienceCorner` founds the **Convenience Corner** workspace, the **Shop operations** project, the **Errand** ticket type (one custom field, `counterparty`; `startDate` and `dueDate` are built-ins and need no declaration) on a clone of the errand-with-waits template, the two epic tickets **Registrations** and **Open questions** titled verbatim from the snapshot, and the 23 shop errands with their bodies, dates and states — 118 events, every one submitted through `ingestClientBatch`, the **gated client door** a person's own action goes through. The seed is handed only that door (`SeedIngest = Pick<IngestService,'ingestClientBatch'>`), so reaching for the ungated internal one is a compile error; envelope-origin is `'web'`, the founding sequence is the server's own and is never re-emitted, and any result other than committed/already-present fails the run loudly, naming the refusal. The accountant is staged: `--allow-missing-guest` seeds everything but the guest surface, and a later run — once the accountant has signed in — adds exactly the guest membership plus explicit visibility on the four errands whose record names them, with the owner kept on every explicit list. Idempotent by construction: every event id is a deterministic `seedUlid`, the runner asks the ledger which ids it already holds and submits only the rest, so a second run commits nothing and a partial first run resumes cleanly. CLI `apps/server/src/seed/cli-seed-convenience-corner.ts` (`--owner-email` / `SEED_OWNER_EMAIL`, `--accountant-email` / `SEED_ACCOUNTANT_EMAIL`, `--allow-missing-guest`, `--board-path`), wired as `pnpm --filter @gisik-nokma/server run seed:cc`. `apps/server/src/seed/{seed-convenience-corner,cli-seed-convenience-corner}.ts`
- ⚙️ **What the client door costs a seed, recorded** — a dogfooding seed meets the refusals a person meets, and two of them are not in the plan text. The owner must **join their own project** (`project.member_added`, `projectAdmin: true`) before any `ticket.created`: `checkVisibilityPermission` requires the actor be on the target project and there is deliberately no admin shortcut. And a `ticket-type.defined` is filed against a **fresh entity ULID** with the stable type key in the payload — `entitySchema` admits a non-ULID entity id for `membership` alone. Both are in `seed-convenience-corner.ts` with the measured refusal quoted beside them.
- ⚙️ **`readPlanSeries` — the plan documents are the record** — reads `docs/superpowers/plans/`, skipping plan 00 (the coordination doc — an interface authority, not an execution plan, with no `**Goal:**` line of its own), and returns each plan's verbatim H1 title, `**Goal:**` line, and every `### Task N:` heading, refusing (naming the file) a plan with no H1 rather than inventing one. `apps/server/src/seed/plan-series.ts`
- ✅ **Gisik Nokma dev seed — the plan series, seeded into the product's own build** — `seedDevWorkspace` founds one **Build — the plan series** project inside the `Gisik Nokma` workspace (founded by the bare `workspace.created` event alone; Plan 4's `bootstrapWorkspace` supplies the built-in `epic`/`task` types and workflow for free, so this seed never re-emits a `workflow.defined` or `ticket-type.defined` of its own), one **epic** ticket per plan document and one **task** ticket per `### Task N:` heading, titled verbatim from `readPlanSeries`. Same client-door discipline as Task 9's Convenience Corner seed: submitted only through `ingestClientBatch` (`CcSeedDeps`/`SeedReport` reused, not redefined), `origin: 'web'`, the owner joins their own project before any `ticket.created`, and every event id is a deterministic `seedUlid` so a second run commits nothing. **It DOES claim a priority** (spec 2026-09-22): every seeded `ticket.created` carries an explicit level, cycling P1 → P2 → P3 off the ticket's position in the series, so a fresh database shows the whole ladder — without it every ticket would take the reducer's birth default and the dev stack would read as a product with one priority. ONE counter across epics AND tasks, not an index per plan: a per-plan index (`planNumber % 3`, the shape the plan text sketched) leaves a two-plan corpus with only P2 and P3, which is exactly this seed's own test fixture. Deliberately claims no dates and no transitions — the plan series has no dates of its own, and execution state belongs to the humans doing the work, not to a seed script. CLI `apps/server/src/seed/cli-seed-dev-workspace.ts` (`--owner-email` / `SEED_OWNER_EMAIL`, `--plans-dir`, default `docs/superpowers/plans`), wired as `pnpm --filter @gisik-nokma/server run seed:dev`. `apps/server/src/seed/{seed-dev-workspace,cli-seed-dev-workspace}.ts`

  other package), and `e2e` (checks for Plan 11 Task 13's one known artifact, `docker-compose.dev.yml`,
  but does NOT attempt to run anything even once it exists — see the case below for why). A `gate` job

  `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- ⚙️ **Silent-skip guard for gated test suites, plus a coverage trip-wire for where it doesn't reach** —
  `check-no-silent-skips.mjs` reads a shard's vitest JSON report and fails if any file using `.skipIf(`
  contributed zero passed-or-failed tests — the case where a runtime guard (a missing binary, a missing
  env var, or a guarded loop over an empty fixture list) eats an entire suite while the run still exits 0.
  It is wired into `server-tests` only; `check-skipif-coverage.mjs` closes the gap that leaves open — it
  fails the (cheap, no-build) `check-env` job if any `.skipIf(` usage appears outside `apps/server/test/`,
  the one place the guard actually runs, converting an uncovered guard into a loud CI failure rather than
  a silent one. ⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-09-21 (E6-6): this sentence read "no file in this repo uses `.skipIf(`
  yet; Plan 11 Tasks 11/12 will add one around the restore-drill suite", and Plan 11 landed** — two files
  carry the guard today (`apps/server/test/ops/pg-dump.test.ts`, `…/restore-drill.test.ts`), both inside
  the covered prefix. **⚠ And the guard could not fail on its own universe**: every rule was applied to
  `report.testResults ?? []`, so an empty or mis-shaped report printed `ok (0 skipIf-guarded file(s)
  checked, none fully skipped)` with EXIT=0 — a run that examined NOTHING and a run that examined
  everything and found nothing wrong were the same output. An empty report now REFUSES and names the
  guarded files the tree holds. **It refuses on the report being EMPTY rather than on the shortfall, and
  that is measured, not cautious**: `ci.yml` calls the script once per `server-tests` shard with that
  shard's own report, the two guarded files can land in different shards, and refusing the shortfall
  would fail three healthy shards out of four — a check that cannot pass is the mirror of one that cannot
  fail. The shortfall is stated in the output instead, and the union-of-shards form is a recorded gap.
  `.runIf(` is recognised as the same guard inverted. `scripts/check-no-silent-skips.mjs`,
  `scripts/check-skipif-coverage.mjs`
- ⚙️ **DigitalOcean deploy spec (file only, not applied)** — `deploy/do/app.yaml`: server, web and a

- ⚙️ **Deployed-database timezone assertion** — `scripts/check-db-timezone.mjs` connects with a bare
  `pg.Client` that sets no startup options and issues no `SET TIME ZONE`, so a pass proves the
  **database's own default** is `Asia/Kolkata`, not merely that the app pool asked for it (which a
  connection pooler can silently drop). Verified falsifiable against a throwaway database explicitly
  `ALTER`ed to `UTC` before being trusted — the shared dev Postgres's cluster-wide `-c
  timezone=Asia/Kolkata` GUC makes every ordinary database (including the admin `postgres` db) answer
  IST regardless of any per-database `ALTER`, which is exactly the unfalsifiable-demo trap the plan's own
  suggested proof text would have fallen into. **It is the one of the nine `scripts/check-*.mjs` that no
  CI job invokes, and that absence is a recorded decision rather than an oversight (F8)**: it asserts a

  database it should point at — the `server-tests` service only approximates IST through a `TZ` its own

  beside the other checkers in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `check-env` job and in this script's own
  docblock; the occasions it is *for* (provisioning, a restore, managed-database maintenance) are the
  runbook's. `scripts/check-db-timezone.mjs`, root `package.json`'s `check:db-tz` script
- ⚙️ **Backups — a nightly `pg_dump`, a weekly ledger export, and a daemon that phones home when
  either fails (Task 11)** — `exportLedger` writes the whole ledger as gzipped ndjson, one envelope per
  line, in `readLedger`'s canonical replay order, to `ledger/YYYY-MM-DD.ndjson.gz`. **This export, not
  the dump, is the fundamental recovery artifact**: every projection rebuilds from the ledger (Plan 1's
  rebuild path and the verify-projections gate prove it continuously), so the ndjson alone is
  sufficient. **Known ceiling, recorded rather than discovered:** `readLedger` materialises the whole
  `events` table before a byte is written, so this job's peak memory scales with the ledger even though
  its gzip/upload half is streamed — the multipart-streaming claim below is true of `pg_dump` and not of
  this. On the `basic-xxs` (512 MB) worker the deploy spec provisions, it is the one job whose OOM means
  no recovery artifact (case 13.34). `dumpDatabaseToSink` streams a custom-format `pg_dump` straight to
  `pg/YYYY-MM-DDTHH-mm.dump` without buffering it — the *convenient* restore — and on a non-zero exit it
  **discards the key it was writing to** before throwing, because the sink was handed `child.stdout`
  before the exit code existed and a truncated archive at a normal-looking dated key is what a restore
  drill reaching for "the latest dump" would pick up. Its connection password travels in `PGPASSWORD`,
  never in argv, where any process on the host could read it. `msUntilNextUtc` computes the delay to the
  next `HH:MM` UTC, optionally constrained to a day-of-week — refusing, by name, a value that is the wrong
  shape (`9pm`) AND one that is the right shape but no time of day (`25:00`, `23:60`, `99:99`), which
  `setUTCHours` used to roll over silently (E6-23; cases 13.1200–13.1201) — and `startBackupDaemon` runs both jobs on
  that clock, writing **every** failure to stderr as structured JSON *itself* and then handing it to an
  `ErrorAlerter`, and re-arming rather than dying, because a backup that fails silently is a lie about
  being backed up. The stderr line lives in the daemon and not in the alerter on purpose: every alerter
  the daemon can be handed may be silent (Task 3's `NoopErrorAlerter` is empty, and the default
  deployment gets it), so an alerter-only witness would have gone quiet the moment the shim below was
  retired. `backup-daemon-main.ts` is the worker entry `deploy/do/app.yaml` names (`node
  dist/ops/backup-daemon-main.js`, confirmed against `tsconfig.json`'s `rootDir`/`outDir`); `--once` runs
  **both** jobs to completion — ledger export first, neither able to veto the other — reports both
  outcomes and exits non-zero if either failed, which is what the manual/runbook backup uses; `SIGTERM`
  stops the schedule and ends the pool.
  `apps/server/src/ops/{schedule,export-ledger,pg-dump,backup-daemon-main}.ts`, `apps/server/package.json`'s
  `ops:backup-once` script
- ⚙️ **The scheduler generalised to N jobs, and two more Plan 11 "ops errands" registered on it** —
  `startScheduler(jobs: ScheduledJob[], alerter)` extracts the daemon's private `loop`/`onFailure`
  primitive above into a standalone function over an arbitrary list of `{name, run, delayMs}` jobs, arming
  every job's first timer SYNCHRONOUSLY at construction and re-arming each independently after it settles —
  one job's failure or schedule never touches another's. `startBackupDaemon` becomes a thin wrapper over it
  with an unchanged external signature, so its own existing tests (the stderr shape, the
  `` `backup:${name}` `` alerter key, the two-timer construction) pin the wrapper byte-for-byte with no
  edits — but **`backup-daemon-main.ts` itself now calls `startScheduler` directly with all five jobs**
  (four when this bullet was written; Task 8 of the second wave added `auto-close`), not
  `startBackupDaemon`: one scheduler, one `stop()`, one `'backup daemon scheduled'` log line, for the
  two backup jobs and the three errands below alike. `startBackupDaemon`'s only remaining caller is its own
  test file, kept because it is what pins `startScheduler`'s stderr/alerter contract in one place; a
  `sweep-orphans` failure in production alerts through that SAME contract, as `` `backup:sweep-orphans` ``
  with `msg: 'backup job failed'` (cases 13.25/13.27's naming, extended to the two new jobs by construction
  rather than by a fifth case). `backup-daemon-main.ts` puts two more jobs on the SAME scheduler as the
  nightly dump and weekly export: **`sweep-orphans`**, running `sweepOrphanObjects` against the worker's own object store on a
  fixed 30-day interval (first run 30 days after boot; "monthly" in the calendar sense would need real new
  day-of-month logic this maintenance sweep does not need enough to justify) and logging COUNTS only, never
  the swept key list, at `info` level; and **`sweep-notifications`**, running the existing
  `runNotificationSweep` on `NOTIFICATION_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS` (optional, default one hour — unset or empty
  both mean "use the default," the same equivalence `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL || null` already draws elsewhere in
  this file, because an unset App Platform binding resolves to `''`). Neither new job runs under `--once`
  — that flag is "run the two BACKUP jobs right now," and folding an unrecoverable delete into it silently
  would surprise whoever reaches for it expecting only a backup — and `requirePositiveIntervalMs`, beside
  `msUntilNextUtc`, REFUSES rather than clamps a non-positive, non-finite or non-integer interval, naming
  the bad value, so a mistyped variable exits the worker 1 on its first `delayMs()` call rather than
  spinning it at 100% of a core or never firing at all. Construction is ALL-OR-NOTHING: `startScheduler`
  now calls every job's `delayMs()` up front, before arming any of their timers, so a later job's refusal
  (review-round fix, 2026-09-06) leaves zero timers live rather than orphaning the earlier, correctly-
  configured jobs' timers with no `stop()` ever returned to cancel them.
  `apps/server/src/ops/{schedule,backup-daemon-main}.ts`
- ⚙️ **The backup object sink — a second, deliberately separate S3 client, and why it is not the
  attachment one** — `s3TargetFromEnv`/`s3SinkFromEnv` build a near-put-only `ObjectSink` (multipart via
  `@aws-sdk/lib-storage`, so a multi-gigabyte dump never lands in the worker's memory; plus a `discard`
  that aborts an in-flight upload and deletes the key, so a failed dump leaves nothing behind — abort and
  delete are both needed, because an unaborted multipart upload leaves paid-for parts no listing shows)
  and `fetch-backup.ts` is its read half, pulling one object down for a restore. It reads the **live**
  `OBJECT_STORE_S3_*` credential names — the plan's own `S3_ENDPOINT`/`S3_ACCESS_KEY` draft names
  nothing reads are not used — and takes only its BUCKET from a separate variable (`BACKUP_S3_BUCKET`),
  so backups can never land in the attachment bucket. `deploy/do/app.yaml`'s backup worker recorded that
  reuse as an **UNRESOLVED** assumption and this settles it, amending that file in the same change set:
  the worker now sets endpoint, region and path-style alongside the credential pair. It has to.
  `s3TargetFromEnv` REFUSES to boot without `OBJECT_STORE_S3_ENDPOINT` and `OBJECT_STORE_S3_REGION`,
  naming them — **stricter than `createObjectStoreFromEnv`, deliberately**, not a mirror of it. An
  earlier revision required only bucket and credentials and defaulted the region to `us-east-1`, and
  that was measured to resolve `https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/gisik-nokma-backups` from the literal
  environment the worker supplied: DO Spaces credentials posted at Amazon, nightly, invisible in dev
  because `.env.example` sets both for MinIO. A backup destination has no local-disk fallback to degrade
  to, so an unset one is a boot-time refusal rather than a default pointing at another provider. It
  deliberately does **not**
  reuse `attachments/object-store.ts`'s `assertValidObjectKey`: that validator refuses any key
  containing a dot and is right to, because attachment keys derive from caller-supplied input where a
  `..` is a traversal attempt (its own planted-defect test pins that). Backup keys are server-generated
  from a timestamp and legitimately carry dots, so widening a live security control in one subsystem to
  suit another was rejected in favour of two separate implementations — the reasoning is recorded in the
  file so nobody "fixes" it back. Every credential is destructured off `env` rather than read as
  `env.NAME`, the one shape `scripts/check-env-example.mjs`'s D2 detector can see — load-bearing for a
  future backup-only variable rather than for these five, which the gate already attributes to
  `attachments/store-config.ts` (its `record()` is first-write-wins and the walker reaches `attachments/`
  first); proven by adding a genuinely new name to this file's destructuring and watching the gate fail
  naming this path (case 13.20).
  `apps/server/src/ops/{object-sink,fetch-backup}.ts`, `apps/server/package.json`'s `ops:fetch-backup`

- ⚙️ **The restore drill — `restore.sh`'s scratch-only guard, and the automated proof that a restored
  database still verifies (Task 12)** — `scripts/restore.sh <dump-file> <target-database-url>
  [--force-live]` runs `pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges` and then prints the `verify:projections`
  command, because **a restore is not done until the freshness gate is clean** — the script deliberately
  does not claim success on its own. Its guard reads the database name out of the target URL and
  **refuses any name not containing `scratch`, `restore` or `drill`** unless `--force-live` is passed:
  restoring over a live database is a deliberate act, not a typo away. The guard runs BEFORE the
  dump-file existence check, so a mistyped target is answered with the target, not sent looking for a
  file. `apps/server/test/ops/restore-drill.test.ts` dumps a seeded database, restores into a bare
  scratch database and accepts the restore only when **the row count crossed** (the restored `events`
  count matches the count measured in the source, with a `> 0` floor) **and** `verifyProjections` is
  clean **and** the restored ledger still refuses an UPDATE; a planted-drift case corrupts
  `proj_entity_heads` and requires the gate to name that table. The count check is not decoration:
  measured by restoring `--schema-only`, the verify-clean case still PASSED against an empty database
  while the count case failed `expected +0 to be 21` — an empty structure verifies clean, so verify
  alone could never have proven a restore restored anything. The script itself is executed by the suite
  rather than described by it — refusal, the same invocation one word different in the name getting past
  the guard, `--force-live`, the usage text, and a real happy-path restore into a second scratch database
  whose row count is then read back from the database.
  **For a URL-shaped DSN, the password never reaches argv or the terminal.** `restore.sh` splits it in bash — the
  same split `src/ops/pg-dump.ts`'s `splitDatabaseUrl` performs for the daemon (case 13.31), including
  the percent-decode, so the two halves of the pair agree on one DSN — and hands the credential to libpq
  through `PGPASSWORD`. `pg_restore` is invoked with a password-free URL, and the `verify:projections`
  next-step line it prints is password-free too, with a note telling the operator to re-supply it. This
  is an operator script run on the ops box during an incident, where argv is world-readable (`ps -ef`)
  and terminal scrollback outlives the incident. Both halves are asserted, and the exit-0 restore beside
  them is what shows the credential was REROUTED rather than merely deleted. **The stated limit:** a DSN
  the split cannot parse — libpq's non-URL conninfo form, `host=... password=...` — falls through
  untouched and keeps the old argv behaviour. That is the same fail-open-on-parse choice
  `splitDatabaseUrl` makes, for the same reason (refusing would break a form the tool accepts), and it is
  a real remaining exposure for anyone who restores with a conninfo string rather than a URL.
  **Version rule, and the one thing here NO automated test covers:** the `pg_restore` used must be at
  least as new as the `pg_dump` that produced the archive AND no newer than the target server's major
  version. Measured 2026-09-06: `pg_restore` 18.4 opens every restore with `SET transaction_timeout = 0`
  (PG17+), which a 16 server rejects — the data lands and the exit code is still non-zero. The rule is
  printed by `restore.sh` on the path that actually restores (not only by `usage()`, which an operator
  who typed the command correctly never sees), and stated in `deploy/do/README.md`.
  **Skew is the ONLY thing allowed to skip the round trip.** The suite gates on client-major ≤
  server-major, not merely on the binaries existing, and skips loudly (naming both majors) on a skewed
  workstation rather than reddening; CI runs it on the matched pair `ci.yml` already pins
  (`pgvector/pgvector:pg16` + `postgresql-client-16`). Every OTHER reason a version probe might come back
  empty — no `psql`, no libpq on `PATH`, Postgres down or not yet ready, unparseable output — is a
  **failure**, asserted by an always-running precondition test that names the probe and quotes its error.
  It has to be: the probes used to fail open, `check-no-silent-skips.mjs` cannot see a partially skipped
  file (the four ungated guard cases always contribute passes), and a readiness blip in CI would
  otherwise have turned the whole round trip — count, verify, and the only execution of `restore.sh`'s
  happy path — into a green skip. The trade is disclosed: a machine with no libpq at all now reddens
  here where it used to skip. The guard cases need only bash and are ungated, so they run everywhere.
  `scripts/restore.sh`, `apps/server/test/ops/restore-drill.test.ts`, `deploy/do/README.md`
- ⚙️ **Deployment config surface, CA-aware pool, versioned `/healthz` (Task 1)** — `loadConfig` grows
  nine deployment knobs (`WEB_ORIGIN`, `TRUST_PROXY`, `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX`, `RATE_LIMIT_EVENTS_MAX`,
  `RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SEC`, `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL`, `SMTP_URL`, `MAGIC_LINK_FROM`, `DATABASE_CA_CERT`) plus a
  tenth not in the plan, `DEPLOY_SHA`, every one refusing loudly by name via `ConfigError`.
  `WEB_ORIGIN` shipped **required, with no default** — a deviation from the plan's optional
  `string | null` — because it is the host of every invitation link. `httpUrl()`/`smtpUrl()` close a
  real bug: `z.string().url()` accepts `localhost:3001` (the WHATWG parser reads `localhost:` as a
  scheme), which would have minted unfollowable links. `createPool(databaseUrl, tls)` strips six `ssl*`
  query parameters before attaching an explicit `ssl: { ca: caCert }`, because `pg` otherwise
  `Object.assign`s the parsed connection string over the caller's `ssl` option — every DigitalOcean
  managed-Postgres URL carries `?sslmode=require` and would silently discard a configured CA under the
  unmodified library behaviour. `/healthz` answers `{ status, sha }` — **not `{ ..., version }`** as the
  plan specified — on both its 200 and 503 branches (Ruling P33), `sha` from `DEPLOY_SHA` defaulting to
  `'dev'`. **Two defects were found and deliberately left open, recorded rather than fixed:** an
  `options=` query parameter still clobbers the pool's timezone startup parameter through the same
  `Object.assign` (asserted as present, not hidden); and `sslcert`/`sslkey`/`sslrootcert` cause `pg` to
  `readFileSync` at client construction, turning a missing file into an `ENOENT` at pool creation — this
  one has no test at all. `apps/server/src/config.ts`, `apps/server/src/db.ts`, `apps/server/src/app.ts`
- ⚙️ **CORS, three rate-limit buckets, and an HTTP-Origin (CSRF) check (Task 2)** — `httpOriginRefused()`
  refuses a `POST` to one of seven `HTTP_ORIGIN_PROTECTED_ROUTES` only when the request carries a
  `Cookie` header (an ambient credential) and `Origin` does not match normalized `WEB_ORIGIN`; matched
  against the route **pattern** (`request.routeOptions.url`), not the raw URL, so a query string cannot
  buy a bypass. `makeFixedWindowLimiter`/`rateLimitKeyFor` key rate limiting on the **rightmost**
  `X-Forwarded-For` entry, not `request.ip` — the plan did not specify a keying strategy, and the obvious
  one (leftmost, under `trustProxy: true`) is attacker-choosable; this was caught and fixed before
  shipping. Three independent buckets — `authMax`, `eventsMax`, and an **`inviteMax` not in the plan's
  two-bucket design**, added because invite-issuance mints a credential per request and had no bucket
  under either of the plan's two; `POST /v1/attachments`, previously unlimited, now shares the `events`
  budget. `webOrigin: null` turns off CORS **and** the CSRF check together, by design — no independent
  switch. Three routes (`/v1/workspaces`, the ticket-type migrate route, mark-notification-read) were
  found missing from an initial "exhaustive" protected-route list by forging a request at every
  non-GET route in the assembled table, not by re-reading the list; the suite now asserts set-equality
  between the protected-route table and the production list so that drift reddens. **Three more** were
  found the same way and added later (E3-14): `PUT /v1/me/notification-preferences`,
  `POST /v1/me/invitations/:inviteId/accept` (membership-granting) and its `/decline` sibling — distinct
  from the invite TOKEN accept and `PUT /v1/me/preferences`, both still deliberately outside the set by a
  recorded ruling. Case 13.197. **The drift guard itself was found unable to catch a route missing from
  BOTH the test's named table and the production set (E3-15) — the exact shape of the E3-14 gap.** Fixed
  by a TEST-ONLY `onRoute` seam on `buildApp` (wired before any route is registered, since a hook attached
  by a caller afterward misses every root-level route — `printRoutes({ commonPrefix: false })` was tried
  first and rejected: MEASURED, it silently drops `/api/auth/*` from its tree). Case 13.198 asserts every
  mutating route the real, assembled app serves is either in `HTTP_ORIGIN_PROTECTED_ROUTES` or a
  commented, reasoned allow-list of the six public doors (two recorded rulings, a POST that reads and
  writes nothing, two pre-session MCP device-flow routes, and better-auth's own CSRF middleware on
  `/api/auth/*`). **Not covered:**
  `rateLimitKeyFor` has no standalone unit test, only indirect HTTP-integration coverage; whether
  `apps/web`'s proxy actually forwards `Origin` on same-origin requests is undemonstrated in this repo.
  `apps/server/src/http/http-origin.ts`, `apps/server/src/http/rate-limit.ts`, `apps/server/src/app.ts`
- ⚙️ **Error alerting hook on 5xx, contained against its own failure modes (Task 3)** — `setErrorHandler`
  lets sub-500 errors pass through unchanged; a 5xx is logged, alerted via `alertWithoutWaiting` with the
  request URL redacted (`redactRequestUrl`, which wraps the invites module's `redactInviteToken` and also
  blanks query-string credentials, so an unspent invitation or sign-in token never lands in a chat webhook), and answered with the fixed `INTERNAL_ERROR_BODY` — **not** the
  plan's `{ error: 'internal_error' }` shape. `alertWithoutWaiting` exists because the plan's own wiring
  snippet (`void alerter.notify(...)`, no try, no catch) would let a promise rejection float and end the
  process on default Node settings — "the monitoring hook becoming the outage" — so it carries both a
  `try` (for a synchronous throw) and a `.catch` (for a rejection), proven by a real
  `process.on('unhandledRejection', …)` collector asserting nothing escapes either way, and it never
  waits for the alert to settle before the response is sent. `WebhookErrorAlerter` POSTs `{ text }` with
  a 5s `AbortSignal` timeout and swallows its own failures. **Deliberately NOT built, against the plan's
  Step 3:** process-level `unhandledRejection`/`uncaughtException` handlers — installing them would
  suppress Node's own crash-and-restart behaviour; the one narrow exception (active only during a
  shutdown, for a synchronously-throwing close hook) is a later, separate commit
  (`installShutdownHandlers`, above). **`/healthz`'s 503 branch deliberately never reaches this
  alerter** — the database-down case, named in prose as exactly the failure an on-call webhook exists
  for — and nothing here coalesces repeated failures into one page. Neither boundary is guarded by a
  test; both are asserted only in source comments. **This is the real implementation Lane C's
  `error-alerter-shim.ts` bullet (above) was written against as still-unmerged** — it has since landed on
  this branch, so that shim is now retirable by the one-line change its own file header already names

- ⚙️ **SMTP magic-link sender, and phone/OTP sign-in refused rather than logged (Task 4)** —
  `SmtpMagicLinkSender` sends a real, **plain-text-only** magic-link email via nodemailer (subject
  `MAGIC_LINK_SUBJECT`), constructed with explicit 10s connect / 10s greeting / 20s socket timeouts —
  nodemailer's defaults (2 min / 30 s / 10 min) would hold a sign-in HTTP request open for minutes
  against an unreachable mail host, since sending is awaited inline; measured with a real TCP listener
  that accepts and never speaks, asserting rejection bounded both above and below the configured
  timeout. `NullOtpSender` **refuses** every OTP send with a 501 (`PHONE_SIGN_IN_UNAVAILABLE`) —
  a bigger, security-relevant deviation from the plan, which asked for `OtpSender` to stay wired to the
  dev-only `LogOtpSender` (silently logging codes) in production; `selectOtpSender()` is asserted to
  never return `LogOtpSender`. `selectMagicLinkSender`/`selectOtpSender` (`select-senders.ts`, not in
  the plan at all) extract the choice into pure, config-only functions so it is unit-testable outside
  `main()`, which opens a Postgres pool on its first line. Verified over the real mounted route
  (`app.inject` against `/api/auth/phone-number/send-otp`): the 501 body is exactly `{code, message}`
  with nothing extra, and the identical request against `LogOtpSender` (a positive control) still
  succeeds, ruling out a broken route as the explanation for the 501. **Not covered:** whether
  `requireTLS` should be forced on the SMTP transport (deliberately left off, to keep working against
  Mailpit's plaintext `smtp://`); that a refused OTP request still leaves an expiring verification row
  in better-auth's own storage (documented as an accepted side effect, not tested).
  `apps/server/src/auth/{smtp-magic-link-sender,otp-sender,select-senders}.ts`

- ⚙️ **The dev stack serves BUILT images, rebuilt from the branch the primary checkout stands on** —
  `pnpm dev:stack` brings it
  up, `pnpm dev:stack:rebuild` rebuilds and brings it up. The stack is `docker-compose.dev.yml` **alone**:
  `web` on :3001, `server` on :3000, real Postgres on 54330, MinIO, Mailpit. **There is no bind-mounted
  source and no watcher**, so the served code equals that branch exactly as of the last build. It is run from
  `/Users/kiro/my_projects/gisik-nokma` — the MAIN folder — because the images bake `SERVER_ORIGIN` and
  `NEXT_PUBLIC_SERVER_URL` as BUILD args and `next build` serialises them into `.next`: **an image is a
  snapshot of the tree it was built from.**
  **WHICH BRANCH — amended 2026-09-23 by owner instruction** (*"on the next rebuild launch the dev stack from
  the release branch so that I can verify"*): the stack follows the primary checkout's **current branch**,
  now a `release/<date>` branch rather than `main` — a merge to `main` deploys to production, so work
  integrates on the release branch and a stack pinned to `main` would serve code nobody is working on.
  `ctl rebuild` reads `git branch --show-current` and pulls THAT branch, accepting `main` or `release/*` and
  refusing a task branch or a detached HEAD (`scripts/ctl/verbs/rebuild.sh`). **This does not loosen the
  2026-09-19 "main folder" instruction quoted below: that named the FOLDER** — the only checkout holding
  `.env` and the baked build args, where a worktree compose resolves the secrets to `""` and silently turns
  sign-in OFF — **not the `main` BRANCH.** The folder is still fixed; only the branch it stands on moved.
  The evidence limit: no sha is baked into the image, so the branch and sha in `ctl rebuild`'s OK line are
  read from git HEAD at build time — nothing inside a running container can be asked which tree it came from.
  **`ctl rebuild` ends by pruning the build cache and unused images older than 24 h** (owner standing rule,
  2026-10-01): `docker builder prune -f` and `docker image prune -a -f --filter until=24h`, run only after the
  stack has been proven good, output to the log, a failed prune reported in the OK line rather than turned into
  a FAIL. **Never a volume** — no `docker volume prune`, `docker system prune` or `--volumes`: the dev Postgres,
  MinIO and the test Postgres live in volumes. The OK line carries a disk line (image and build-cache size with
  what is reclaimable, plus how full the Docker VM disk is) and `--dry-run` prints both prune commands. Why: a
  full Docker VM disk made the test Postgres refuse connections and failed a whole gate. `scripts/ctl/lib.sh`
  (`ctl_prune`, `ctl_disk_line`), `scripts/ctl/verbs/rebuild.sh`, `scripts/ctl/test/lib.test.sh`.
  **The rebuild rule is the load-bearing part, and its failure shape is this repo's recorded
  stale-serving class.** Merge to `main` and skip `pnpm dev:stack:rebuild`, and the app keeps serving the
  PREVIOUS build while `/healthz` answers 200, both containers are `Up`, and `:3001` returns its usual
  307 — every signal green, the code older than `main`. With the watchers gone the rebuild is the only
  thing that closes it, and no health check can tell you. `--env-file .env` (which both scripts pass) is
  what converts a MISSING `.env` from a silent empty substitution — server healthy, **Google sign-in
  OFF** — into a hard stop.
  **HOT-RELOAD MODE WAS RETIRED HERE ON 2026-09-19** by owner instruction: *"no more hot reloads. rebuilt
  once they hit the main, is fine. that means the servers are to be run from the main folder instead of
  from the executor's branch."* No executor's branch is ever live any more, which also retires the
  ":3001 belongs to executor 1" rule that existed only because the container mounted that worktree.
  `docker-compose.hot.yml` is **kept and deliberately no longer composed by anything**, because a deleted
  file takes its reasons with it — the rename-over save shape not crossing the Docker Desktop mount;
  `tsx watch` losing its watch **permanently** on the first such save; `node --watch --import tsx` measured
  failing even on a write made INSIDE the container; busybox `kill -0` succeeding on an exited-but-unreaped
  child, so a liveness supervisor cannot fire; `compose` v2 shell-word-splitting a string-form `command`.
  **The incident that motivated hot mode is why the rebuild rule is written in this register**: the running
  server image was built **2026-09-09T12:32Z** while the first `closed` fold reached
  `apps/server/src/read/ticket-cards.ts` on **2026-09-17**, so the owner's Backlog tab read cards with no
  `closed` key from a server eight days behind the client, and the mapper refused it
  (`list.groups[0].cards[0].closed: expected an object`). The mapper's refusal stays strict — a `closed`
  that defaults to `null` when absent is what hid case 13.603 the first time.
  `docker-compose.dev.yml`, `docker-compose.hot.yml` (retired; kept for its measurements), `package.json`,
  `apps/server/Dockerfile`, `apps/web/Dockerfile` (both keep `dev` stages that no shipped command targets
  any more, and both stage comments now say so; **their `dev` stage's position is still load-bearing** —
  see the rebuild rule), `docs/runbook.md`,

  `pnpm check:migrations` compares `apps/server/migrations` against the base ref's (`origin/main`, with a

  absent from the base whose numeric prefix is not strictly above the base's highest. **It is the one
  gate that can see this class at all**, which is why it is separate: a migration numbered below one
  already applied can never run — `node-pg-migrate`'s `checkOrder` refuses it as *"preceding already run
  migration"* — but a FRESH database applies every migration cleanly in numerical order, so the whole
  server suite is green on the broken tree by construction, and the hot stack (which migrates only at
  container start and aborts on failure) goes down instead. Measured on the real incident rather than
  reasoned about: PR #459's branch tip is **refused** against its fork point (`1789300000000` vs the
  already-present `1789400000000`) and commit `73c40ea3`, which renamed it to `1789500000000`, is
  **accepted**. The baseline is the base ref's TIP and not the merge base, deliberately: the merge base
  cannot see the case that actually broke the stack, where `main` gains a higher-numbered migration while
  a branch is open. The comparison runs over two real DIRECTORIES through one reader, so the self-test
  plants fixture directories rather than arrays — `6 planted defects caught, 5 known-good accepted`,
  including a duplicate prefix, a non-numeric prefix the runner reads as `0`, an empty baseline that must
  refuse rather than conclude, and a **17-digit `utc`-format prefix whose instant is below the highest
  present**, which a bare `Number()` would read as `2.026e16` and wrongly accept. Two honest
  non-coverage notes: it does not refuse a migration removed or renamed from the base set (a rename of a
  not-yet-applied migration is legitimate and indistinguishable from this side), and it cannot see a
  lower-numbered migration that reached the base ref before the branch existed. **The CI job passes the
  pull request's own base** (`--base origin/${{ github.base_ref }}`), not `main`: review measured that a
  branch stacked on another branch which outranks it is **accepted** against `main` and refused against
  its real base, and that shape is used here — 14 of the last 400 merges were based on a non-main
  branch. **The refusal names the convention it rests on, because nothing else did** (E6-7): the
  migrations here are hand-numbered on a counter rather than stamped from the clock — each of the last 13
  is a multiple of `1e8` ms and the gaps between neighbours are `1e8` (10 of the 12) or `2e8` — so the
  sequence can sit ahead of the wall clock, and a stamp fresh from the generator the plans document lands
  below the head and arrives at this refusal. The message states the convention and the remedy, and the
  self-test pins that sentence as a required name of the below-max plant, so deleting the record reddens
  the check rather than passing quietly. `scripts/check-migration-order.mjs`, `package.json`,
  `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, cases 13.902–13.906

## 14. MCP server

*The assistant-facing door. An MCP server a person runs on their own machine, signed in as
themselves, whose writes are attributable in the ledger as an assistant's rather than a person's.
Mirrored by `test-cases/14-mcp-server.md`. The envelope-origin half of this feature lives in §3,
where the ledger's provenance vocabulary is defined, rather than being restated here.*

- ✅ **An assistant can operate gisik-nokma as you** — at first nine tools over stdio (the workspace and project tools joined them in MCP CRUD plan Tasks 6–7, below): five reads (`list_workspaces`, `list_projects`, `search_tickets`, `list_tickets`, `get_ticket`) and four writes (`create_ticket`, `transition_ticket`, `add_comment`, `assign_ticket`). It has no permissions of its own — every call is the call you would have made, judged by the same permission gate, rule engine and visibility rules as the web client, and every write is a real domain event through `POST /v1/events`. Driven end to end against the live stack: a ticket created at seq 1, a comment at seq 2, a bad transition refused as `refused by unknown-state: The workflow "Errand with waits" has no state "no-such-state".`, and the ledger reading `web 123 · server 6 · mcp 2`. `packages/mcp-server/src/tools/`, cases 14.60–14.88. The same nine tools, the same code, also run behind the hosted `/mcp` (hosted remote MCP plan, Task 7) through `hostedSession` (`apps/server/src/mcp/in-process-fetch.ts`) — the API's own routes called in-process with the caller's token and network identity, so the rate limiter sees the real caller and a write is still `origin: 'mcp'` with the caller as `actorId`; the package now exports `registerTools`, `allTools` and `lazySession` from its index. Cases 14.250–14.254

- ⚙️ **`@gisik-nokma/mcp-server` — the package scaffold and its configuration** (MCP plan Task 1) — a workspace package for the assistant-facing MCP door, with `loadMcpConfig(env, home)` as the one place its configuration is resolved: it REQUIRES `GISIK_SERVER_URL` and names it when absent, defaults the token cache to `~/.gisik-nokma/mcp-token`, and strips a trailing slash so later URL joins never double it. The env arrives as a PARAMETER rather than being read from `process.env`, which makes the three cases pure functions of their inputs — and, as a side effect nobody wanted, makes the file invisible to `pnpm check:env`, whose detectors all require the string `process.env` to appear (recorded in `.env.example`; owner: whoever next touches `scripts/check-env-example.mjs`). - ⚙️ **The MCP credential store — device-code grants and personal access tokens** (MCP plan Task 2) — two server-owned tables, `mcp_device_codes` and `mcp_tokens`, both hashed at rest (sha256 of 32 bytes from `randomBytes`; a plain hash rather than a password KDF is correct here for the same reason it is for `invite_tokens` — the input is 256 bits of uniform entropy, so there is no dictionary to stretch against). **Neither is a projection and neither is rebuildable**, deliberately: what they hold is absent from the ledger, because anyone who can read a workspace's history can read an event id and a payload. Neither name may ever appear in a projection's `tables` array — `reset()` empties what that array names, and a rebuild that emptied `mcp_tokens` would sign every MCP client out with no way to put them back. Single-use is enforced by `DELETE … RETURNING` in the statement that reads the grant, not by a read-shaped guard. A revoked token and a forged one resolve to `null` identically, because every distinction is an oracle. The user code uses a no-vowel, no-0/O/1/I/5/S alphabet so it can neither spell a word nor be transcribed into a different valid code. Cases 14.10–14.16. `apps/server/src/mcp/token-store.ts`, `apps/server/migrations/1788600000000_mcp-device-auth.sql`
- ⚙️ **The MCP device-authorization flow — four routes** (MCP plan Task 3; the DENIAL route added 2026-09-19) — `POST /v1/mcp/device/code` mints a grant, `POST /v1/mcp/device/approve` binds it to the signed-in person, `POST /v1/mcp/device/deny` **refuses** it, `POST /v1/mcp/device/token` exchanges it once. **Two of the four carry no session by design**, because the point of a device flow is that the thing asking for a credential does not have one yet; neither gives anything away, since the credential is created by the APPROVAL. **Both the approval AND the denial are cookie-authenticatable POSTs and both are inside `HTTP_ORIGIN_PROTECTED_ROUTES`** — without that, a page the victim visits could approve the ATTACKER's device code on the victim's ambient cookie, or kill a grant out from under whoever was mid-approval, and `SameSite=Lax` does not help because the product and API are same-site siblings of one registrable domain. All four are charged to a **fourth rate-limit bucket** fed by the existing `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX` (the `inviteMax` precedent, no new environment variable): before it, a route under `/v1/mcp/...` matched no bucket at all, leaving the 8-character user code an unlimited brute-force surface. That budget is also what fixes the TTL and poll interval the spec left open. **Denial is a DELETE of the grant row rather than a `denied` flag**, and that is what makes it work in both states — an unapproved code can no longer be approved, and an already-approved one can no longer be collected by the CLI. Every downstream answer is then `unknown_code`, deliberately not a distinct "denied" state that would confirm a guessed user code had been real. **Approve and deny now refuse an MCP-token caller (E6-16):** `requireSession` accepts either a real better-auth session OR an MCP personal-access-token bearer as `currentUserId` (`require-session.ts`), and nothing previously distinguished them — so a token could approve (or deny) a device code, including a SUCCESSOR device code that survives revoking the very token that minted it, making the consent page's "it lasts until you revoke it" false. `requireSession` now also stamps `request.authKind: 'session' | 'mcp-token'`, and both routes refuse `403 mcp_token_may_not_decide_device_grant` when it reads `'mcp-token'`, before the code is even looked up. A forged token and a revoked one are refused identically. The cost is stated: a request that falls THROUGH to the PAT branch performs one indexed single-row write, because the lookup stamps `last_used`; a better-auth session never reaches it. Two assertions exist because a declaration table creates two ways to be green while covering nothing — the hand-off is measured from BOTH ends (what section 4 handed over must equal what section 4b received by declaration; an exemption leaves the element in NEITHER population, green), and a renamed entry reddens rather than dying silently. All three mutations witnessed, each isolated: undeclare a label → section 4 names it at 16px; rename one → the stale guard fires at a width where section 4 is silent; collapse the selector to its base → *"section 4 handed 17 … but the label sweep received 0"*. `apps/web/e2e-viewport/type-scale.ts`, `apps/web/e2e-viewport/responsive.spec.ts`
- ⚙️ **A type-scale floor, and the sweep that could not see the text it was about** (owner-assigned, 2026-09-08) — the other half of the ruling whose tap-target half shipped in #328. `responsive.spec.ts` had swept body copy against 16px since item 7, but its population is `p, li, dd, dt, td, figcaption, label`, and every element the pre-launch finding named — `gn-board-card__provenance`, the chips — is a `span` or a `div`. The reading came from one manual measurement and had no guard. `e2e-viewport/type-scale.ts` sweeps that population as a plain module (not a spec: importing a sweep from a spec loads its `test()` registrations into the other config), ratcheted per route in both suites. **The floor is 12px and it is NOT a WCAG number** — no success criterion sets a minimum font size; 1.4.4 is resize-to-200%, 1.4.12 is text spacing. It is the bottom rung of this product's own scale, seventeen rules at `0.75rem`, and the checklist itself judged the 12.5px and 12.8px labels legitimate. Five declarations sat under it across the three shipped stylesheets and are now at `0.75rem`. **One of the five is witnessed by a ratchet, and the other four were chased until unwitnessable was a MEASUREMENT** — `.ticket-type-list__badge`, 4 → 0 on `/settings/ticket-types`; the other four render only on the workflow editor canvas, inside a description editor, or on a card with an assignee (no seeded card has one), and are fixed but unproven: the workflow editor renders no canvas at all at 390px (`flowNodes: 0`), and the seed assigns nothing. The witnessed rule also carries a `MUST_EXAMINE` coverage assertion, because a ratchet at 0 for a rule that stopped rendering reads exactly like a ratchet at 0 for a healthy one. Widening the population to `a`/`button` put the checklist's own named element under a guard for the first time: `button.gn-board-card__provenance`, 12.48px x26, above the floor and previously invisible to every sweep because it is a `<button>`. The claim that justifies two sweeps rather than one — disjoint populations — is measured, not asserted: an element matching both selectors lands in `bodyOwned` and reddens by name. Cases 13.264–13.265. `apps/web/e2e-viewport/type-scale.ts`, `apps/web/e2e-stack/viewport.spec.ts`, `packages/ui/src/ui.css`, `packages/editor/src/styles/editor.css`
- ✅ **Every control renders in the product's font, not the browser's** (owner-assigned, 2026-09-08) — `<button>` with no `font` rule inherited Chrome's UA default (`13.3333px Arial`), so thirty controls were painted in a typeface the product never chose. `button { font: inherit; }` in `apps/web/app/globals.css`, an ELEMENT selector at specificity 0,0,1 so every class rule still wins — which is what keeps the owner's "and no further" true rather than promised: `.gn-board-card__provenance` stays at 12.48px x26 and every non-13.3333px bucket in the sweep is unmoved. The count grew 26 → 30 by measuring before writing the rule: `/sign-in`'s two `.gn-view-tabs` tabs were never in the signed-in enumeration, and **`/help`'s two `.gn-help__tab` were at 16px in Arial** — `ui.css:1321` sets `font-size: 1rem` and no `font-family`, so their SIZE was right and no font-size instrument could ever have seen them. *(`.gn-help__tab` no longer exists as of 2026-09-15: `/help`'s document switch is the shared `SegmentedControl`, and the one remaining user of the class — `apps/desktop`'s help toggle — carries `.gn-help__toggle`. The finding and its argument stand; only the selector it was found on has been renamed out from under this sentence.)* **30 is a floor**: ten of nineteen routes are swept by neither suite. Guarded by a font-FAMILY reading rather than an assertion about the `13.3333px` bucket, because the bucket form passes over the `/help` pair and would pass again the day a UA constant changes. Cases 13.266–13.267. `apps/web/app/globals.css`, `apps/web/e2e-viewport/type-scale.ts`, `apps/web/e2e-viewport/responsive.spec.ts`, `apps/web/e2e-stack/viewport.spec.ts`
- ✅ **The magic link lands you in the app, not on the API's 404** (owner-dispatched P1, 2026-09-08) — `sign-in/page.tsx` handed better-auth a RELATIVE `callbackURL`, which the browser resolves at token-verification time while sitting on the API origin (that is where the emailed link points), so every magic-link sign-in ended on raw JSON. Measured: `:3001/workspaces` 200, `:3000/workspaces` 404. **Not dev-only** — `deploy/do/app.yaml` ships production as two sibling subdomains, the same split, so this was every new user's first screen. The callback is now absolute on `window.location.origin` (the web origin by definition, with no env var to drift), for the magic link **and for Google, which had the identical shape and was not in the report**. `?next=` is constrained to a same-site path in the same change, because making the callback absolute would otherwise have turned an existing client-side open-redirect into an authenticated one. The e2e guard is the other half: its only assertion was that the path no longer contained `/sign-in`, **which a JSON 404 satisfies** — it asserted the user left, never that they arrived. It now asserts the landing ORIGIN. Cases 13.268–13.272. `apps/web/app/sign-in/page.tsx`, `apps/web/e2e-stack/helpers/sign-in.ts`, `apps/server/test/auth/trusted-origins.test.ts`, `apps/web/test/sign-in.test.tsx`
- ⚙️ **One rate limiter on `/api/auth/*`, and it is ours** (controller ruling, 2026-09-08) — better-auth ships its own limiter and it could not tell clients apart here: `createRateLimitKey(ip ?? NO_TRUSTED_IP_KEY, path)` with `getIP()` falsy is **one shared bucket per path for everybody**, so one person retrying sign-in could refuse every other user. Measured on the dev stack with two clients on different addresses and no proxy in the path: the one that had spent nothing was refused on its first request. `auth.ts` now sets `rateLimit: { enabled: false }` and our limiter — which keys per client address under `TRUST_PROXY`, taking the RIGHTMOST `X-Forwarded-For` entry — is the single authority. Chosen over fixing better-auth's IP resolution because that means reading a caller-written header, putting a spoofable bucket beside a hardened one on the same path; our coverage is already a strict superset. **`RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX` is untouched and finally means what everyone assumed it meant.** The named loss: better-auth's per-path tightening on the magic-link route (`window || 60`, `max || 5`, which overrides the generic `/sign-in*` 10s/3) goes away; a sign-in-specific bucket in our limiter is a recorded follow-up, **now built — see the entry below**. Cases 13.273–13.274. `apps/server/src/auth/auth.ts`, `apps/server/test/http/security-middleware.test.ts`

- ⚙️ **A tighter bucket for the sign-in family, charged on top of the general one** (2026-09-08, the follow-up the ruling above recorded) — disabling better-auth's limiter took a named loss: it gave `/sign-in*` and `/magic-link*` tighter rules than its global default, so afterwards the whole mount sat behind one flat `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX` and a client could spend its entire auth allowance on sign-in attempts. A fifth bucket now repays it, and it is the first that classifies by PATH rather than by Fastify route pattern — every auth path arrives under the wildcard mount as `/api/auth/*`, so telling a sign-in from a session read means reading the caller-written `request.url`. **Additive, never replacing:** charging a matching path to the new bucket *instead of* the general one would hand a client `authMax + signInMax` where it gets `authMax` today, a loosening under a parity headline; charging both means the smaller budget binds, and a path the matcher misses degrades to exactly today's behaviour. The budget is `signInMaxFor(authMax)` — half, so at the shipped `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX=10` it is **5**, while the dev stack's 60 leaves the e2e suite the headroom its single proxied client key needs. **That 5 is NOT parity, and an earlier version of this entry said it was.** better-auth keyed per (ip, *path*), so `/sign-in/magic-link` and `/magic-link/verify` each had their own 5-per-60s budget — five complete sign-in cycles — while this is one bucket across the whole family and a cycle costs two of it: **two complete cycles per window, measured, so between 2.5x and 5x tighter than what it replaces.** The direction is the one the ruling wanted and it is kept, but it is named as a tightening beyond the authorised parity rather than sold as parity, and the cost is named with it: where one client key covers many people — a NAT'd office egress, or the single proxied key the dev stack itself has — the whole key gets two sign-in cycles a minute. Under `TRUST_PROXY` in production the key is the real client address, so there it is per-person. No new environment variable (the `inviteMax`/`mcpMax` precedent) and `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX` still untouched. The matcher deliberately **over-matches** — dot segments, doubled slashes, trailing slashes, mixed case and percent-encoding all resolve toward matching — because a false positive costs the caller one unit of its own budget on a path that then 404s, while a false negative hands it a budget twice the size; only one of those is a bypass. `/phone-number/*` is deliberately outside it: better-auth bounded it at 10/60s, exactly the shipped default, so nothing was lost there and including it would exceed parity rather than restore it. `retry-after` on this path is a LOWER bound, deliberately and now pinned by a case: the two buckets' windows can open at different instants, so a caller told 1 second was measured being refused for 59 more — a hint that is too short, never a bound that admits too much. Cases 13.275–13.280. `apps/server/src/http/rate-limit.ts`, `apps/server/src/app.ts`, `apps/server/src/index.ts`

- ✅ **You can see and revoke the assistants connected to your account** (MCP plan Task 12, owner ruling 5) — `/mcp/tokens` lists them and revokes one in a click, replacing the plan's default of a hand-written `DELETE`. It is a PER-USER screen, not a workspace setting: an MCP token carries your permissions in every workspace you belong to, so a path with a workspace in it would say something false about what revoking does. The row shows when the connection was approved and when the assistant last used it — "Never used" when it has not, rather than a date invented to fill the column — and the page says why there is nothing else: only a one-way hash of the connection is stored. Showing last-used was an owner ruling (2026-09-08); the column was already being written on every resolution, so only the display was open. Revoking ends access at the assistant's NEXT request rather than interrupting it mid-task. `DELETE /v1/me/mcp-tokens/:id` is scoped to the caller inside the statement and answers the same 404 for "not yours" and "does not exist", so it is not an oracle for which tokens exist. Cases 14.90–14.103. **Round 21 (2026-09-16), owner: "lets move MCP tokens to the account page. as this should not be scoped to a workspace." The screen now lives on `/account`** as its "Connected assistants" section, and left BOTH workspace-scoped surfaces it had drifted into: the workspace home's section cards (five doors down to four) and `/settings`' sidebar tab (three tabs down to two, `SettingsTab` down to `'ticket-types' | 'workflows'`). This does not reverse Round 19d's ruling that it "should live inside settings" — it moves it to the settings shell it belongs to, since `/account` IS a person's settings and `/settings` is a workspace's. The same round made the nav's Settings link workspace-conditional, which is what makes leaving that shell safe: `/settings` with no `?workspaceId=` is no longer a destination the bar offers, so the tab that used to be the only thing working there is not stranding anyone. `/mcp/tokens` still resolves and still mounts the same shared component — nobody asked for a URL to die. `McpTokensScreen` gained one `variant` prop (`'page' | 'account'`) deriving three things from a single decision so they cannot disagree: the heading class, the card's max-width, and — the one that is not cosmetic — the sign-in `next` path, since the signed-out branch promises "you land back here" and a hard-coded `/mcp/tokens` would have made that sentence false on `/account`. Case 13.415. **A read that FAILS says so instead of saying "No assistants are connected"** (E2-44, 2026-09-21 — case `14.150`): the load's rejection arm was `() => setTokens([])`, and `[]` is exactly the value the empty arm asserts over, so a 500 was drawn as a confident claim about the person's account — on the one screen whose subject is which assistants still hold access — and sent them to the connect page to approve a second one. `tokens` now stays `null` on a rejection and a separate arm renders the server's own words when it sent any, else *"Your connected assistants could not be loaded — reload to try again. The list is unknown, not empty."* `apps/server/src/routes/mcp-tokens.ts`, `apps/web/app/mcp/tokens/page.tsx`, `apps/web/src/mcp-tokens-screen.tsx`, `apps/web/app/account/page.tsx`, `apps/web/app/settings/page.tsx`
  Hosted (remote-MCP plan Task 8; `routes/mcp-connections.ts`, `src/mcp-tokens-screen.tsx`): the screen now also lists the assistant APPS a person connected by URL — name and web address, connected, last used, **Disconnect** (deletes the connection and its tokens at once; owner-scoped, Origin-checked) — and a **Connect an assistant** panel with the URL (from `GET /v1/mcp/public-url`, absent when the hosted door is off), a Copy button and a How to connect link. The two lists are read independently. Cases 14.270–14.277.
- ⚙️ **The HTTP-Origin CSRF control covers all four mutating methods, not just POST** (found by MCP plan Task 12) — `httpOriginRefused` returned early on `method !== 'POST'` under a comment reading "mutations only". Every protected route happened to be a POST, so the control looked complete while being unable to protect a PUT, PATCH or DELETE added to the set; the forged-`Origin` DELETE reached `requireSession`, which answered 401 for the wrong reason. `security-middleware.test.ts`'s route table now carries a method column, because a table that cannot express a non-POST route cannot catch it. `apps/server/src/http/http-origin.ts`, case 14.95
- ⚙️ **The task ledger refuses a row that cites a PR which never merged** (2026-09-08) — `done` rows are validated by sha reachability, but a non-`done` row requires no evidence by design, so a wrong status carrying a stale PR number was invisible to every other check in the gate. It went wrong for real: `mcp-server/12` read `in-flight 324` while the work had landed through #329, because merging #323 deleted #324's base branch and GitHub auto-closed it. Case 13.262. `scripts/check-task-ledger.mjs`

Access tokens live in `mcp_tokens` as `kind='hosted'` with a one-hour `expires_at`; refresh tokens rotate and a reused one deletes the whole connection. Everything hashed at rest. Device-flow tokens are `kind='local'` and never expire, as before. Cases 14.200–14.209.

Form-encoded or JSON. Cases 14.240–14.249 (14.247's pending-consent half lands with Task 3).
